#6194. We've Tested Dozens of Toiletry Bags—These Are Our Top Picks

If there's one travel truth I live by—and hold dear to my heart—it’s that a dream vacation deserves a dream toiletry bag. After all, what’s a perfectly packed carry-on without a designated home for your favorite lipstick, beloved serums, sunscreen, and all those little beauty essentials that somehow multiply before every trip? The best toiletry bags make room for the whole glam squad, without adding any more suitcase chaos to the packing equation.

On all of our worldly journeys, Condé Nast Traveler editors (myself included) have tested dozens of travel toiletry bags to find the ones worth your precious packing space, from streamlined makeup pouches for the less-is-more crowd to roomy, cleverly compartmentalized cases for those who believe in a 10-step skincare routine. It's no easy job finding the best ones: Some tear after just a few months of use, others have awkwardly sized compartments. Many are too big for a standard carry-on, while others have proven too small to fit the simplest of our travel necessities.

With wipe-clean linings and durable construction, plus smart pockets and ultra chic designs, the carefully selected, editor-tested toiletry bags that earned a spot on this list are the crème de la crème. Read on for our recommendations to keep your essentials organized and your travel beauty routine in check.

Tested by: Jessica Sulima, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? About a year now, and despite how much it’s melded to different parts of my suitcase, the leather has stayed nicely intact.

What is it best for? It's best for longer trips, when you need to carry full-size toiletries. That being said, it also works if you don’t have that much to pack, because the leather folds down however you’d like. I like that the products stay upright for the most part, so you don’t have to worry about bottles squeezing open. The shape makes it so that you can rifle through your things comfortably without dumping everything out.

How much does it hold? My entire skincare routine—cleanser, toner, moisturizer, sunscreen—plus my daily makeup. There’s even room for my vitamins too.

Tested by: Madison Flager, commerce director

How long have you been using it? I've been using this Peak Design toiletry bag for five or six years.

What is it best for? If you're in search of a toiletry bag to keep up with an extended itinerary, this is your solution: It's ideal for longer trips of five days and more. Sometimes I pack it on weekend trips too, but it's a bit bulky, so I find it better suited to checked luggage, or trips where I'll need a good amount of product.

How much does it hold? This is one of the toiletry bag's best features—it truly holds so much. Everything in my routine fits like a glove, each with a dedicated space. I usually bring along shampoo, conditioner, body wash, face wash, moisturizer, eye cream, contact solution, a toothbrush, toothpaste, and floss, plus smaller items like tweezers and nail cutters. There's an exterior pocket sized for a toothbrush, and one inside with a magnetic snap where I store a razor. Plus, there’s a hook on the outside, so you can hang it up in the bathroom.

Tested by: Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? This gem is a newer addition to my travel rotation. I've traveled with it for around two months now—and knew it had to be mine when I saw it came in a glazed dark cherry colorway. (That's now sold out, but there are loads of other fun colors to choose from in the same style.)

What is it best for? Given its spacious yet puffy, cloud-like design, the Luka bag is ideal for any trip where you have some extra room in your carry-on, or are bringing a checked bag. It's a bit bulky for a weekender or duffel bag, though I'd try to squeeze it in if I was packing light. For any of these trips, you can use the hanging clip for easy access.

How much does it hold? It's a bit deceiving just how much this toiletry bag holds—which is much more than it gives off at first glance! I bring all of my beauty products in here, from foundations to lipsticks and moisturizer galore. And though he packs way lighter than me, it can fit my partner's personal care items, too: a face buzzer, hair gel, a toothbrush, and so on. As well as the main pocket with a zippered enclosure, it has two convenient, grab-and-go side pockets as well as an enclosed compartment on the back.

Tested by: Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor How long have you been using it? I’ve had Away's large toiletry bag for just over two years now, and have been obsessed with it ever since.

What is it best for? This is my travel companion for holding my go-to skincare products and toiletries, and it comes with me on every trip. I do also keep all my everyday products in there at home, so it's proven to be always at my ready. It's so chic—especially because it has my initials embroidered on the front—and keeps everything contained. I love that it has so many interior compartments, both zippered and clear, to keep small objects like hair ties, jewelry, and Band-Aids separated from my bigger tubes and bottles.

How much does it hold? Full disclosure: I don’t travel light. But this bag truly holds so much. It fits my entire skincare routine, toothbrush case, deodorant, hair products, body wash, razor, and beyond with ease. The two halves make it easy to find a place for everything.

Tested by: Bridget Knowles, associate social media manager

How long have you been using it? Elizabeth Scarlett’s eponymous label is a London-based luxury accessories brand I discovered during a bout of retail therapy in East London eight years ago. I’ve never looked back since—it’s an unspoken “it-girl” possession.

What is it best for? For longer trips, the Wash Bag is really great to keep everything organized. It has a wipe-clean lining fit for all lotions and potions, and you can personalize it with monograms too, which makes for a great gift. For shorter trips and everyday use, I use the Everyday Pouch—which I strongly suggest adding to your cart. (It’s my life companion in many ways.)

How much does it hold? I put everything in the Wash Bag: daytime makeup, going out makeup (you get me), my nighttime routine, and my morning routine. It’s lined with pockets so you can easily organize brushes, and—I mean—my electric toothbrush even fits in it. That’s how good it is.

Tested by: Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor

How long have you been using it? I've been using—and in love with—this toiletry bag for around two years now.

What is it best for? I promise, my adoration of this bag comes from more than just its good looks. I've been reaching for it nonstop to carry my very extensive skincare routine with me wherever I go—and it's made packing easier than ever. I think I've finally cracked the code to keeping my toiletries organized and ready to go whenever I am. The extra roomy toiletry bag is designed to be packed in your checked luggage, where you have more suitcase space and no restrictions on the amount of liquids you can have inside.

How much does it hold? I used to keep all of my reusable toiletry bottles and miscellaneous minis in a small storage bin underneath my bed. And when it was time to pack for a trip, I'd sift through it and decide what I needed for a particular trip. I decided to put all of my go-to toiletries inside The Kit, including cleanser, body wash, moisturizer, shampoo and conditioner, dry shampoo, tooth paste, floss, and even contact lenses. Now when it's time to travel I can easily grab the pre-packed kit and throw it right into my personal item. I don't even open it anymore to see what I need—it's already stocked up and ready to go.

Read a full review of the toiletry bag here.

How long have you been using it? I ordered this Calpak train case in unison with the aforementioned Luka toiletry bag—so around two months now.

What is it best for? With its boxy, clear, and haute look, the train case is best for extended trips where a checked bag is obvious. Otherwise, it's a superb makeup bag at home for those who don't love too many compartments, and like to have their ready products in view: The transparent panels let you quickly locate what you need without digging. (Not to mention, it looks super cute with the Luka, given the matching colorways. I'm obsessed!)

How much does it hold? When this bad boy arrived at my apartment, it was (luckily) bigger than I expected. It's tall, so it can easily hold my toner bottles, makeup brushes, and blending sponges.

At home, not only does it store my everyday beauty products, but a stock of my next-on-the-lists and just-in-cases—it's where my unopened moisturizers, different lip shades, and nail care products go. My favorite part? There's a hidden, dedicated interior organization pocket attached to the top compartment, which holds the products I wish to keep separate.

Before he ran United Airlines’ MileagePlus program, Jarad Fisher was the type of traveler who went “all-in” for elite status.

He read TPG, collected miles and occasionally went on ambitious end-of-year “status runs.”

“My wife thought I was nuts,” he joked, recalling an epic out-and-back trip to Hawaii 12 years ago — where he never even left the airport — in order to qualify.

Now, Fisher is in charge of United’s loyalty program as it undergoes one of its biggest transformations in recent memory.

Ironically, one of his first orders of business was eliminating flight segments as a status metric.

Starting in 2027, “Premier Qualifying Flights” are out. That means United loyalists will no longer be “graded” on how many actual flights they rack up.

Instead, the carrier will rely exclusively on PQPs, which are based on a combination of members’ spending, both on flights and on their United credit cards.

United has framed the change as a way to make qualifying for status simpler — though it could make it more challenging for some United flyers.

It will also end the need for eleventh-hour “segment runs” that once had frequent flyers (like Fisher) crisscrossing the country in December to rack up enough elite-qualifying flights.

“That was an old relic,” he said, speaking about United’s recent changes in an exclusive interview with TPG.

"You’re taking seats away from people who actually want to get to a certain destination. It’s not great for the environment. It’s not a great use of time,” he explained. “We thought it made more sense for them to have one, consistent metric."

That’s not the only change United has made to MileagePlus in 2026.

Earlier this year, the carrier upended several of its loyalty policies, heavily tilting its program toward members who carry one of its credit cards.

Together, these moves were among the most aggressive any U.S. airline has made to nudge flyers toward its cobranded credit cards.

It’s part of a larger strategy Fisher often sums up with this mantra:

“It’s good to fly United, it’s great to be a MileagePlus member,” he said. “But the best way to engage with us is to be a MileagePlus member and actually have one of our cards.”

Speaking publicly this year, United's chief commercial officer, Andrew Nocella, has hinted that United's loyalty shakeup isn't done.

It appears some changes may have to wait until the airline can re-negotiate its credit card deal with banking partner Chase.

“While we continue to work under a long-term cobrand contract,” Nocella said on an earnings call in April, “We’re making changes to what we can control today.”

United’s current Chase deal is set to run through 2029, according to past TPG reporting.

For now, the carrier has significantly upped the incentives for customers to carry one of its cards in the first place: Over the past year, United's cobranded credit card holders have clearly gained the upper hand in its program.

Fisher said the airline plans to continue adapting the program in ways “that will be more consistent” with that ethos in the coming years.

“And so I think as a function of that, we’re looking at not only the core loyalty program, we're looking at our partnerships," he said. "And we’re trying to make it so that we will continue to be — not just the best airline loyalty program — but we’re really aspiring to be the best loyalty program in the world."

What future changes could MileagePlus members ultimately see when they go to redeem miles, earn on their Lyft rides or enter a United Club?

And Fisher will play a big part in those decisions, after taking the helm of MileagePlus this year with an intriguing pedigree.

Seven years ago, he was heavily involved in the launch of Apple Card.

Before that, he spent time at top rival Delta Air Lines, helping turbocharge its partnership with American Express — which today is the industry's most lucrative tie-up, set to bring Delta $9 billion this year.

That resume has Fisher thinking beyond earn rates and status benchmarks as he looks to build on changes that gave United flyers plenty to digest in 2026.

“We’re really trying to think about what will truly help us break away from the pack,” he said of the carrier’s future plans.

Of course, that’s easier said than done in the airline world.

Flight delays are inevitable. Loyal flyers can grow frustrated when they go to book a redemption and are shocked by how many miles they’ll need.

Not to mention, complimentary status upgrades don’t clear as often as they used to, as first-class seats are increasingly filled by customers who actually paid for their tickets. By the way, balancing paid first-class seats with those long upgrade queues is a dilemma Fisher said the airline is “consistently looking at."

"More folks are paying for [premium seats], which of course is putting pressure on the system," he acknowledged.

But for an airline that has made plenty of waves in recent years — from its on-board internet to its international routes — it's safe to say United won't shy away from trying new things on the loyalty front, either.

And it's a likely bet that customers who carry its credit cards will benefit most.

“If you think about the amount of time people spend with us, and on board our aircraft, we want them to feel known. We want them to feel recognized," he said. “You will continue to see us become even more focused and deliberate about that approach."

#6192. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Thatched Cottage Tucked Away in the Cotswolds

Choosing the perfect place to hole up for a weekend getaway is not always straightforward. But this spring, the decisions seemed to make themselves. After a relentlessly busy start to the year, I was looking for a place to escape. And the place needed to fit certain criteria: Somewhere my partner and I wouldn't have to speak to anyone but each other; somewhere we could sleep for 12 hours a night and take the days slow and easy without guilt; somewhere within a couple of hours’ drive from our home in northwest London; somewhere rural, where I wouldn’t be woken up by the neighbors’ bathroom light or the sound of the tube; and somewhere we could have the place to ourselves, but still be close to some nice pubs or restaurants, so we wouldn't have to hunt and gather our own dinners, God forbid.

An Airbnb in the Cotswolds was the obvious choice. Luckily, I remembered I’d saved a cozy-looking cottage on Instagram a few months prior to feeling the sudden urge to get away. I revisited my staycation wishlist and found Strawtop Cottages: two 16th-century thatched-roof cottages that sit side by side on a quiet street in the quaint little village of Adderbury. I booked one of them, Strawtop Two, for a long weekend in April.

We checked into Strawtop Two after a speedy drive from London on a Friday night. As we unlocked the front door, we found switched-on lamps casting a cozy glow across the beamed living room; kindling ready to be lit in the wood-burning fire. In the egg-yolk yellow kitchen, a fresh loaf of sourdough was sitting pretty on the chopping board for us; organic eggs and marmalade on the counter; Daylesford butter, bacon, and rosé in the fridge. My partner prepared a simple supper while I nosed around the rest of the cottage, discovering a sweet dining room with floor-to-ceiling windows and an enormous bunch of fresh flowers around the back, as well as a boot room with Barbour jackets, Wellies for stomps across the fields, and umbrellas (likely a requirement, considering we were visiting in April).

I learned that the sister properties are owned by local content creator Josie Irons (@Josieldn on Instagram) and her husband Charlie Irons (who manages the properties), who have been custodians here for just a small part of the cottages’ centuries-long history. Their meticulous renovations have restored the spaces beautifully, preserving all the Grade II-listed original features that make staying here feel like a journey back to a simpler, more peaceful time, while adding plush finishing touches that feel every bit as cosseting as those of the area’s top-of-class hotels.

I originally saved this cottage because of the kitchen, drawn in by sunshiny pictures and clips of its buttery-hued walls, vintage copper pans, and an old-school kettle whistling on the Aga stove. But as I nipped between the two bedrooms—one on the first floor with minty green walls, one folded into the eaves on the top floor with tongue-and-groove woodwork—I found there’s a lot more to love here, like the Bamford pillow mist left next to the beds, and the blackout blinds creating one of the darkest and quietest bedrooms I’ve ever drifted off in. Wrapped up in the bed linens, I snoozed more peacefully than I’d managed to in months.

After homemade coffee sipped while listening to the Roberts Radio on Saturday morning, we headed a few minutes up the road to The Yurt at Nicholsons restaurant. This was one of a handful of recommendations that Charlie had sent us ahead of time. Normally, I’m a stickler for doing my own research (read: a snob and a control freak), but in the name of keeping things as relaxed as possible, I decided to put my faith in his suggestions. I shouldn’t have hesitated: a gooey camembert croissant, cut through with umami bacon, and a full English breakfast with melty pork belly chop and smoky baked beans hit the spot.

Our supper, also recommended (and booked for us) by Charlie, at The Norman Knight was every bit as impressive. I ordered perfectly blushing steak frites and felt smugly like I’d uncovered a hidden gem. Our Sunday lunch at The Duke of Cumberland’s Head, where we shared bowls of cauliflower cheese and crispy potatoes, was one of the tastiest roasts I’ve had in a while. Trust me, having Charlie as a de facto concierge is one of the biggest unsung perks of booking a stay here.

Back at the house, we hibernated on the sofa, reading the paper and watching Netflix in the dinky living room. I took mental notes of my favorite design details: the antique coffee table laden with magazines, the books plopped into recesses in the stone chimney, the deep-green rainfall shower stocked with Bamford products, the Steamery steamer and Dyson hairdryer in the bedroom vanity, and the Soho Home robes. If I could make my London flat one-tenth as comfortable as this little countryside cottage, I’d be thrilled. For now, I’ll bookmark the cottage next door for my next escape.

#6189. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Cabin on a Vineyard Just 2 Hours From London

I'm always on the hunt for a new cabin stay in the British countryside. Having visited at least two a year since 2020, I'd now dub myself something of an expert. Living in East London, sometimes all I crave is solitude, and I find that a slightly rustic spot, kitted out with all the necessary amenities, can be more restorative than a jam-packed, buzzy hotel stay.

I don't drive (hey, I'm a Londoner), which can be a rather large obstacle when planning cabin stays. But Liba Vineyard, a luxury glamping site made up of three pod-style homes in Porton, just a 15-minute taxi ride from Salisbury station, presents no such problem. The pods are all bookable on Airbnb, and I scooped up the Hawthorn Pod for a stay this autumn, eager to hunker down and work on writing my upcoming book. Door-to-door from London, I managed to reach it in two hours, armed with enough books and food to last two nights.

Once I'd settled into the Hawthorn Pod, I realized the Wi-Fi was excellent, and I wouldn't need to leave at all during my stay. The pods are dotted along winding wood-chip paths, which branch off towards the three cabins: Hawthorn, Beech, and Elder. All sleep four people and have a wood-fired hot tub, although Hawthorn is slightly more snug than the other two and better suited to solo visitors and couples. Beech is best for anyone traveling with children, while for larger groups, renting all three would be a fun way to celebrate a birthday. It's a spot that can be both solitary and social, depending on what you're after.

Inside, the pods are neutral, bright, and cozy. Draped curtains add a sense of grandeur to the French doors, while the bathroom—the biggest test of any cabin—was a welcome sight. A flushing toilet and strong water pressure are unsung luxuries, and things I'm always relieved to find in a cabin. The kitchen has everything you'd need, but there's also an outdoor barbecue firepit, making cooking here a genuine joy.

Nearby, there are plenty of sightseeing opportunities, pubs, day trips, and activities: UNESCO World Heritage Site Stonehenge is just a 15-minute drive away, while Cranborne Chase National Landscape and the New Forest are both under a half-hour drive. The property itself is full of life as well, with alpacas grazing, chickens clucking, and a muster of peacocks running between hedgerows. On Mondays and Wednesdays, you can join a yoga class in a studio above the winemaking barn.

Each morning, I'd wake to the sound of peacocks, open the drapes to soft golden light trickling in, and breathe in the fresh air before lighting a fire to get breakfast started. Since returning home, I've longed for the calm of those mornings and the methodical mindfulness of cooking over a flame.

The owners have big plans in the works. Soon, wine will be available from the vineyard, which is expected to produce up to 10,000 bottles a year over the next few years. Chris Reynolds, who owns the land with his wife, Louise Marshall, gives every pod guest a tour, something that will become an even bigger selling point once wine is available to taste. Ahead of this, visitors can sponsor a vine through a subscription model in exchange for wine, pod stays, and events such as harvest parties. Liba is already certified organic and is working towards biodynamic certification within the next nine months.

Next summer, the 10-acre farm will be bookable for weddings, while early discussions are underway about an on-site café and additional activities to complement the existing yoga studio.

#6188. Report: Alaska to Lay Off 200 Employees

Alaska Air Group, the parent company of Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, and Horizon Air, will lay off about 200 workers as financial losses tied to the higher price of jet fuel grow.

The Honolulu Star-Advertiser obtained an email sent to employees Friday morning acknowledging the cuts.

“Despite having the right strategy and strong momentum, fuel prices and geopolitical challenges are putting significant financial pressure on our business,” CEO Ben Minicucci wrote. “If current conditions persist, we could lose as much as $700 million this year, which would be our first adjusted pretax loss outside of the pandemic since 2003.”

According to the Star-Advertiser, 125 workers in Washington state will be laid off, and 48 in Hawaii.

The affected employees will be out of a job Nov. 13, but will continue to receive pay through the end of the year.

Alaska’s leadership said no front-line, non-management positions have been affected, suggesting the eliminated jobs are management-related.

Separately, Hawaiian Airlines CEO Diana Birkett Rakow said in an email to staff that, of the 48 affected positions at Hawaiian, 40 roles will be eliminated entirely, and eight people will be be offered other jobs within the airline.

Birkett Rakow also said that two senior leaders – Jim Landers, head of Hawaii operations, and Shelly Parker, head of guest operations – will retire at the end of the year. Both of their positions will be eliminated following their departure.

#6187. Bilt Rent Day Promotion November 2026: Up To $150 Off Hotel, Up To 100% Gift Card Bonus

Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus new ways that housing rewards are offered.

There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With it now being a new month, I’d like to post a reminder of the November 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a gift card redemption bonus and a hotel booking promo code. While there’s no transfer bonus to a travel program, I imagine this will still interest some.

There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

Bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

On the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

On November 1, 2026 only, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for gift cards. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:

This same bonus is available for all 125+ gift cards that Bilt Points can be redeemed for. There’s no option to use Bilt Cash to increase your bonus here.

For what it’s worth, ordinarily Bilt points can be redeemed for 0.7 cents each toward gift card purchases. That means a Blue member would be getting 0.875 cents per point of value, while a Platinum member would be getting 1.4 cents per point of value. For me that’s a hard pass, though I suppose for some Platinum members, it could be an interesting way to “cash out” points, if that’s what you’re looking to do.

For the November 2026 Bilt Rent Day promotion, we’re actually seeing an additional offer as well. Bilt members can unlock up to $150 off a hotel stay booked in the Bilt Travel Portal during Rent Week, so it’s available for bookings between 9AM ET on October 28 and 3AM ET on November 2, 2026.

The catch here is that different members are eligible for different offers, so members have to log into their Bilt account, and they will see a targeted chart delineating different savings of up to $150 for hotel bookings. Here are the key details:

On the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for November 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on gift card redemptions, which can get you at most 1.4 cents per point of value. That’s not terribly exciting, in my opinion, but maybe others will appreciate it. The other offer is for up to $150 off a hotel stay booked through the Bilt Travel Portal. There are different offers there that members will be eligible for, so you’ll want to check in the Bilt app to see what you’re targeted for.

#6186. "Short-Sighted": Delta CEO Vows To Fight Heathrow’s Move To Split It From Virgin Atlantic

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian has publicly criticized Heathrow Airport's decision to move the airline to Terminal 4 in 2028, calling the decision "short-sighted" and "bad for airline consumers." The criticism comes after a once-in-a-decade review at Europe's busiest international airport resulted in five airlines being ordered to move terminals in 2028, including Delta.

This change has been met with upset after both Delta and Virgin Atlantic, in which the American carrier holds a 49% share, argued that it will move the US carrier away from its UK partner and put the airline at a disadvantage to its competitors. Bastian has vowed to "pursue all available remedies" to reverse the decision.

As part of Heathrow Airport Limited's review, Delta will be required to relocate to the airport's Terminal 4. This comes after more than a decade in which Delta and Virgin have cohabitated in Terminal 3. This one-terminal approach for the two airlines has enabled convenient connections, premium shared amenities, and a collaboration to provide travelers access to the airlines' two extensive long-haul networks.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Having the two airlines co-located in Terminal 3 has provided a valuable competitive alternative to other legacy carriers operating transatlantic flights. When separated, this will undermine the years of investment that the two airlines have spent in the last decade, and it is suggested that the decision has disregarded the customer benefits that are offered by the co-location. In a lengthy statement released on Monday, Bastian said:

"Heathrow Airport Limited’s decision to relocate Delta’s operation to Terminal 4, away from our partner Virgin Atlantic, is short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers . . . Separating our operation undermines years of investment and disregards the tightly integrated customer benefits that we offer in our co-located terminal."

As detailed in Bastian's statement, both Delta and Virgin are planning to fight this decision, and Delta is urging Heathrow Airport Limited to reconsider the decision. Virgin is considering its legal options, and SkyTeam, of which both airlines are partners, has argued that the move would put its members at a disadvantage to other airlines sharing terminals.

For Delta, the move matters as they are arguing that the relocation to Terminal 4 would split the airline from its joint venture partner after more than a decade. This would result in connecting passengers between the two airlines being forced to connect across the airfield by bus transport.

Heathrow Airport Limited has said that the once-a-decade review would free up available capacity at the airport, while easing congestion at one of the most slot-controlled airports in the world.

Heathrow's decision to separate Delta and Virgin Atlantic sparks competition concerns and potential legal challenges.

For US carriers, Delta is tied second with United Airlines by total destinations served at Heathrow, with both airlines serving seven year-round US gateways. They trail behind American Airlines, who operate year-round to nine US airports, and add a sole seasonal service.

Virgin Atlantic operates year-round to ten destinations in the US, with a seasonal service added during the Northern Hemisphere summer season to Seattle. The full Heathrow network for both airlines is below:

Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Detroit (DTW), Minneapolis/Saint Paul (MSP), New York-JFK (JFK), Salt Lake City (SLC), Seattle/Tacoma (SEA)

Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Las Vegas (LAS), Los Angeles (LAX), Miami (MIA), New York-JFK (JFK), Orlando (MCO), San Francisco (SFO), Tampa (TPA), Washington-Dulles (IAD), Seattle/Tacoma (SEA) – seasonal

Antigua (ANU), Barbados (BGI), Bengaluru (BLR), Cancún (CUN), Cape Town (CPT) – seasonal, Delhi (DEL), Dubai (DXB), Grenada (GND), Johannesburg (JNB), Lagos (LOS), Malé (MLE) – seasonal, Montego Bay (MBJ), Mumbai (BOM), Seoul (ICN), St. Vincent (SVD), Toronto (YYZ), Phuket (HKT) – seasonal

In Heathrow Terminal 3 currently, Delta and Virgin share a number of facilities and infrastructure, including the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse, providing an iconic lounge for eligible business class passengers and top-tier frequent flyers. Travelers also have access to the Virgin Revivals Lounge, which provides lounge facilities for arriving passengers.

Shared ground labor, check-in, and transfer coordination also see the two airlines working collaboratively for the benefit of passengers and airline operations.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

This is sad and funny at the same time. I'm cheering for the Delta CEO

British Airways is most likely behind seperating Delta Air Lines and Virgin Atlantic terminal locations being separated !!!!!!

The airport needs to work for the airlines, not the other way around.

The issue also includes the fact that shared routes code-shared and passengers can currently be easily moved to another joint flight in case of delay. That won't be so achievable with a terminal split, especially of this distance.

Also shared facilities like engineering and ramp handling will be split and add cost

Don't like it? Take Virgin with you to Gatwick then.

M. Bastian needs to realize that he's not dealing with the French here. Given the long history of support for commercial aviation in the UK, perhaps that 49% ownership in Virgin Atlantic is now unwanted and the airline needs to be give the opportunity to succeed without American interference.

A few years ago, on a damp evening in late March in London, I learned the hard way that countries don’t all change their clocks for daylight saving time simultaneously. After ordering a glass of white wine at a cozy bar in Bermondsey, I mindlessly scrolled on my phone while the bartenders chatted about the clocks jumping forward that coming Sunday. I nearly spit out my Chablis.

Back home in New York City, I had already skipped ahead one hour on the second Sunday in March. As I frantically Googled, I learned that in the United Kingdom, the clocks go forward one hour on the last Sunday in March (and back one hour on the last Sunday in October).

Don’t be like me and lose two hours of sleep in one month. When you travel, remember the following to avoid daylight saving time-related snafus and other time zone mistakes — and if you're in the U.S., most states fell back one hour on Sunday, Nov. 1.

The U.K. isn’t the only country that changes its clocks on a different weekend than we do in the U.S. For example, most European countries follow the same calendar as the U.K., moving clocks forward one hour on the last Sunday in March and back one hour on the last Sunday in October.

Generally, when traveling in the spring and fall, it’s always best to check when the country you’re going to falls forward or backward — and also whether that country observes daylight saving time at all. In fact, according to the Pew Research Center, about 66% of the world doesn’t.

Though daylight saving time is commonly observed in North America and Europe, many non-European Union countries in Europe — including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Iceland, Russia and Turkey — stay on standard time year-round.

In 2023, Egypt became the only country in Africa to change its clocks when it reintroduced daylight saving time for the first time in seven years. Now, each year, its clocks move forward one hour on the last Friday in April and backward one hour on the last Thursday in October.

It’s also worth double-checking these things even if you're traveling within the U.S. In 48 states, daylight saving time runs from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November. Arizona and Hawaii are the outliers that stay on standard time year-round. While it’s less of an issue on an island like Hawaii, Arizona shares enough borders with other states that do observe daylight saving time that it can be problematic.

“Always double-check timing when flying in/out and on road trips through the state,” Becky Blaine, TPG’s newsletter managing editor and former Arizona resident, said. Otherwise, you can risk missing a flight or a reservation.

To keep it simple, remember that Arizona is in the Pacific Daylight Time zone from mid-March to early November, and the rest of the year it’s in the same time zone as other states in Mountain Standard Time.

It’s a similar situation in Canada. Generally, Canada follows the same daylight saving schedule as the U.S., but most of Saskatchewan, the Yukon and some parts of Quebec and British Columbia stay on standard time year-round.

In Australia, daylight saving time starts the first Sunday in October and ends the first Sunday in April in the Australian Capital Territory, New South Wales, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria; meanwhile, the Northern Territory, Queensland and Western Australia don’t observe it.

Outside of daylight saving time changes, there are some general time zone issues to be aware of while traveling.

In countries as large as the U.S., Canada and Australia, it’s easy to see why there are so many time zones. But Eric Rosen, TPG’s director of travel content, also pointed out that the airport in the Maldives is in a different time zone than some resorts in the tiny island nation.

Technically, the Maldives has only one official time zone: Maldives Time, which is five hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). However, some of the archipelago's private island resorts add an hour to Maldives Time to maximize their guests' evening light.

For example, The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Resort sets its clock one hour ahead of the official clock to what it calls "Island Time," but also provides guests with butlers who coordinate transfers to and from the airport so nobody accidentally misses a flight.

Before you go to the Maldives, be sure to check if your resort also does this.

Due to its geographic location, the Canadian island of Newfoundland is 90 minutes ahead of Eastern Time instead of just 60 minutes ahead, as in the rest of Atlantic Canada. On a July trip, Nick Ewen, TPG’s editor-in-chief, found this challenging for calendar purposes.

While traveling in Newfoundland, he received an Outlook invitation to a 7:30 p.m. dinner meeting the following week and accepted it without much thought. However, the actual dinner back home in the U.S. started at 6 p.m. — a detail he completely missed until the reminder popped up 15 minutes before. At that point, he realized he would be late.

Other places offset from UTC by 30 minutes include India, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Iran and some states in Australia. Want to be confused even more? Nepal's time zone is offset by 45 minutes due to its geography.

Even when not dealing with half-hour time zones, it can be easy to make similar mistakes when adding events back home to your digital calendar while traveling in a different time zone.

"Last year, I brought my middle son to a birthday party. We were running a few minutes late, but when we arrived, it seemed like the party was almost over," Tarah Chieffi, a senior writer at TPG, said. "While the kids were eating cake, I double-checked my calendar to make sure we had gotten the time right, and it seemed like we had. But then I went to check the invitation, and we had, in fact, arrived one hour late."

Her mistake? When she entered the party into her calendar while traveling, her calendar app defaulted to the time zone she was in and showed her the incorrect time back home.

"Now, I always toggle the time zone to my home time zone if I enter appointments into my calendar while I'm traveling," she said.

"Outlook lets you have up to three time zones showing on the calendar," Madison Blancaflor, a managing editor at TPG, said.

Go to "Settings," then "Calendar," then "Time zones." Then, check the box for "Show second time zone in Day and Week view" underneath your default time zone. If you need a third one, you can also check that box.

It's also important to remember that it's possible to quickly encounter multiple time zones on cruises — especially on transoceanic cruises, where you'll change time zones daily or almost daily. And if you're on a cruise traversing the Pacific Ocean, you could lose an entire day if you cross the international date line, like Clint Henderson, TPG's principal spokesperson, did when he sailed from Seward, Alaska, to Tokyo last year.

Related: I made a rookie travel mistake that nearly cost me $4,000 — here's how I fixed it

Even on shorter cruises, check if you'll have to change time zones. When I was on a five-day Alaska cruise earlier this summer, I changed time zones twice as we moved in and out of Alaska Daylight Time on a round-trip sailing from Vancouver (which was one hour ahead, on Pacific Daylight Time).

Cabin stewards usually leave notes on your bed at turndown to remind you of upcoming time changes. Clint said he had to set his clocks back between one and two hours each night on his cruise. But you can't always rely on your cellphone to display the correct time when it’s in airplane mode and using satellite-based internet. Bring an analog watch or an alarm clock to ground you if you're unsure whether your device will update properly.

However, some cruise ships may ignore time changes at select ports. "I've had that happen on Royal Caribbean ships in the Caribbean, for example, to avoid the ship time changing three days in a row," said Christine Gallipeau, a senior editor on TPG's points and loyalty team. "So if you're doing shore excursions, make sure you know what time the ship is following, as it may not necessarily match the local time."

Related: Can a cruise help with jet lag? The answer might surprise you

When traveling, don’t assume every country or state follows the same daylight-saving-time rules and schedules as where you live, and be mindful of time zone anomalies. Losing or gaining an unexpected hour can lead to lost sleep, arriving late to an event and, worst of all, missed flights.

#6184. 55 Thoughtful Gifts for Men Who Love to Travel

The holiday season will be here before we know it, which means it’s time to start thinking about gifts for the ones you love. When you’re shopping for a special guy in your life this year, skip the things he doesn’t actually need and go straight for the ones that count: thoughtful pieces he’ll put to good use on his next trip, upgrades to his everyday essentials, and a few small luxuries that make being on the road that much better. The best gifts for men, after all, aren’t necessarily the flashiest—they’re the ones that become part of his routine, whether that means packing them in a carry-on or enjoying them on a quiet Sunday morning at home.

I’ve hand-selected over 50 gift ideas for men who love to travel, featuring many talked-about favorites with a few less expected additions too. From a timeless leather weekender that’s perfect for a quick getaway to at-home accessories that will enrich any guy’s space, I've got you covered with plenty of options he’ll love. Read on for all of the best travel gifts for men or jump straight to the section you think will interest him most.

At Condé Nast Traveler, editors spend a lot of time debating, researching, testing, and re-testing all things travel accessories and luggage. If you’re looking for the best suitcase to buy your guy this holiday season, look here. But if you want something a little unique that will absolutely rock his travel routine for years to come, check out some of the gift ideas below. To make his next long-haul flight more comfortable, consider gifting him a comfy neck pillow, sleep mask, or a pair of compression socks. A ludicrously capacious leather weekender or a luxurious Italian notebook are smart upgrades he’ll cherish forever. And in case of emergencies, a good ol' fashioned flask will more than do the trick.

Here’s the thing about men: There’s a part of us that will always relish having a new toy to play with. This category is for those who will appreciate a wild card gift and savor the element of surprise. A perfect pair of travel-sized binoculars made from the best optical-grade crystal in the world? Jackpot! The latest generation of AirPods with top-notch noise-canceling technology? Bingo! A smart watch that can track his steps on the go? Perfect!

Clothes are a tough gift for the holidays. Everybody is different, every body is different, and a lot of guys are just downright picky when it comes to what they get dressed in everyday. That being said, there are a few tricks of the trade to consider here—when gifting clothes, don’t go too big, too outré, or too outlandish. The secret is to select timeless, quintessential pieces that travel well, age well, and can be styled into any wardrobe: a Barbour jacket, a crisp white shirt, or a navy suit that packs nicely into a suitcase. When in doubt, a pair of high-quality sunglasses in a classic silhouette is generally a win too.

Lovers of the great outdoors are a funny bunch to shop for. They typically have all of their most treasured gear ready to go already, so this is a demographic for whom you need to be on your A-game. Gifts for outdoorsy types need to be the newest of the new with smart details, category-leading engineering, and unassailable durability. Think a lightweight Norwegian cooler that keeps drinks cold without any ice (that’s right—no ice), or a comfortable running shoe that can handle endless wear and tear. Outdoorsy folks will say that they can never have too many puffy layer-type things—so go ahead and consider a thick blanket or the iconic Arc’teryx Atom insulated hoodie. And if all else fails you can get them a beautiful Stanley bottle to keep their favorite soups and beverages warm in even the most wintry conditions.

I hate to stereotype the genders—but a lot of self-care products out there are marketed more heavily toward women, leaving the average guy in the lurch. He may not know the benefits of investing in a Dr. Barbara Sturm skincare regimen, or how an Omnilux LED mask can help slow visible signs of aging. There’s a whole world of self-care products out there! Here, I’ve gathered some of the best items to kick-start his journey—sometimes all it takes is Dr. Dennis Gross’ miracle-working peel pads.

Food is one of my favorite ways to experience travel. If you’re not quite ready to gift someone a trip to sample authentic panettone straight from the oven in Italy, the good news is that the marvels of modern packing and shipping have made some of the world’s tastiest foods closer than ever. A sampler of high-quality spices will upgrade his at-home cooking. A $60 bag of beans is the perfectly fun gift for a coffee snob who might not buy it for himself. And a perfectly unassailable upgrade to his go-to sauté pan (if he even has one), or the investment of a proper stand mixer, are foolproof.

No matter what the recipient’s sense of style is, there are certain upgrades that are likely to fit into most any home. Beautiful linen sheets are always welcome, as is a great bathrobe or pair of slippers to remind him of a luxury hotel. When in doubt, the flourish of a Flamingo Estate candle hits just the right notes.

#6183. Transfer Chase Points To IHG With 80% Bonus: Why It’s Not Worth It

Chase Ultimate Rewards has just launched a new transfer bonus to IHG One Rewards. The bonus is for 80%, which on the surface sounds huge. However, even with such a big bonus, I’d still argue this almost certainly isn’t worth it…

Chase Ultimate Rewards is offering a bonus when you transfer points to IHG One Rewards. Between 12AM ET on November 1, 2026, and 11:59PM ET on December 3, 2026, members can receive an 80% bonus when moving points.

Points ordinarily transfer at a 1,000:1,000 ratio, so with this 80% bonus offer, points transfer at a 1,000:1,800 ratio. You can take advantage of this an unlimited number of times. Transfers from Chase Ultimate Rewards to IHG One Rewards are typically instant.

For context, we typically see a transfer bonus from Chase to IHG two or three times per year, and so far the bonuses have been in the range of 50% to 100%. So this 80% bonus is roughly average as far as these bonuses go, and isn’t quite as good as the 100% bonus we saw earlier this year.

An 80% transfer bonus sounds like it could be valuable, since that’s a big percentage bonus. That being said, I still wouldn’t consider this to be a good deal under a vast majority of circumstances.

Why? Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG One Rewards points to be worth 0.5 cents each, while I value Chase Ultimate Rewards points at ~1.7 cents each. Even when you’re getting 1.8 IHG One Rewards points per Ultimate Rewards point, you’re still only getting under one cent of value per Ultimate Rewards point.

I certainly hope that most people are able to redeem their Chase Ultimate Rewards points for well over a penny each, since that’s a really low cash out value.

Even if you value IHG One Rewards points more than I do, the reality is that IHG frequently sells points for 0.5 cents each, so I would instead buy points at that rate. It would be silly to redeem Ultimate Rewards points when you’re only getting one cent of value vs. paying cash.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is offering a new transfer bonus, as you can get an 80% bonus when you move points to IHG One Rewards. While I’m always happy to see a transfer bonus, I’m afraid that this simply isn’t worth it under a vast majority of circumstances.

Transfers to most of Chase’s partners are generally at a 1:1 ratio. While the simplicity of that is nice, the reality is that points have significantly different values, and this creates a few partners that I would never recommend transferring Chase points to.

Anyone have a different take, and see a reason to transfer Chase points to IHG?

#6181. How Much Do Boeing 747-8 Pilots Make In 2026?

The Boeing 747-8 is one of the largest commercial aircraft in operation. With its distinctive humpbacked fuselage, four powerful engines, and substantial payload capacity, the aircraft requires highly trained flight crews. However, the salaries these pilots receive depend more on their airline, seniority, and position than on the aircraft itself.

In 2026, Boeing 747-8 pilots can earn anywhere from six-figure annual salaries to well over $400,000, particularly at major cargo operators such as UPS Airlines. However, there is no single industry-wide salary for a 747-8 pilot, as first officers, experienced captains, and newly hired pilots work under different pay structures, with contractual guarantees and additional benefits influencing their overall compensation.

Boeing 747-8 pilot salaries vary considerably depending on the airline, years of service, and whether a pilot serves as a captain or first officer. At the upper end of the pay scale, experienced captains at major cargo airlines can earn more than $400,000 annually, while first officers typically receive lower salaries that can still reach six figures after gaining experience.

UPS Airlines offers some of the highest compensation for pilots operating the Boeing 747-8F, the freighter version of the aircraft. Under its pilot pay agreement, the top captain hourly rate reached $401 in September 2025, while the highest first officer rate reached $284. These figures provide a useful benchmark for understanding the earning potential available to experienced pilots in 2026.

Atlas Air, another major Boeing 747-8F operator, follows a different pay structure that takes account of the aircraft, pilot position, and years of service. Its 747-8F captain hourly rate starts at $247 in the first year and increases to $259 in the second year, eventually reaching $332 by the twelfth year. Consequently, the difference between an experienced captain's earnings and those of a newer pilot can be substantial.

Although salary estimates sometimes place the average US Boeing 747-8 pilot's earnings at approximately $135,000 annually in 2026, such figures need careful interpretation. Broad estimates can include junior first officers, contract pilots, and pilots working for lower-paying operators, meaning they may not accurately represent the compensation available to experienced crews at large cargo airlines.

UPS Airlines operates the Boeing 747-8F as part of its extensive cargo network, and its pilots benefit from a compensation structure negotiated with the Independent Pilots Association. The agreement includes a two-year contract extension, with the published top hourly rates providing a strong indication of what experienced pilots can earn when they reach the highest levels of seniority.

At the top of the pay scale, a UPS Boeing 747-8F captain earns $401 per hour, while a first officer earns $284 per hour, based on rates established in September 2025. Estimates put a top-rate captain's earnings at approximately $34,000 per month, equivalent to around $408,000 annually. However, actual earnings can vary according to the pilot's schedule, additional duties, and applicable contractual payments.

One important detail is that UPS Airlines does not pay its pilots according to the Boeing 747-8 alone. Its widebody pilots operate under a common pay scale covering aircraft such as the Boeing 767 and McDonnell Douglas MD-11, meaning that a captain's hourly rate is determined primarily by seniority and position rather than by the particular aircraft flown. The latest data from ch-aviation shows that UPS Airlines' fleet is currently made up of the aircraft detailed in the table above.

Newly hired UPS Airlines pilots begin considerably lower on the compensation ladder, with a probationary rate of approximately $56 to $60 per hour regardless of whether they serve as first officers or captains. This illustrates why the highest published salary should not be treated as representative of every pilot employed by the airline, particularly those who are still building seniority and experience.

Atlas Air operates the world's largest fleet of Boeing 747 freighters and is another major employer for pilots seeking to fly the aircraft. Its compensation system is negotiated through a collective agreement with Teamsters Local 2750, with hourly rates varying according to the pilot's seat, aircraft assignment, and years of service.

For Boeing 747-8 captains, the hourly rate begins at $247 in the first year, increases to $259 in the second year, and reaches $332 by the twelfth year. These rates provide a clear picture of how experience influences earnings, although the captain's annual compensation also depends on the amount of credit earned under the applicable contract and any additional payments.

Atlas Air first officers generally earn between $120,000 and $230,000 annually, while captain salaries range from approximately $250,000 to more than $450,000, according to estimates. These broad ranges reflect differences in seniority, flying schedules, and total compensation, rather than a guaranteed salary for every pilot operating a Boeing 747-8.

Atlas Air pilots have sometimes described their compensation agreement as a contract cycle behind those of major airlines that secured substantial raises after the pandemic. Nevertheless, the airline remains an important option for experienced widebody pilots, particularly those interested in international cargo operations and the opportunities that come with building seniority at a large freighter operator.

Seniority is one of the most important factors determining how much a Boeing 747-8 pilot earns in 2026. As pilots progress through an airline's pay scale, their hourly rates generally increase, allowing experienced first officers and captains to earn considerably more than colleagues who have only recently joined the company. A useful rule of thumb is to multiply the applicable hourly rate by 1,000 to estimate annual earnings.

For example, a pilot earning $284 per hour would generate approximately $284,000 using this calculation, while a captain earning $401 per hour would reach approximately $401,000. This is only a rough estimate, however, because actual pay depends on credited hours and contractual provisions.

At UPS, pilots receive a contractual guarantee of approximately 81 hours per 28-day pay period, alongside potential per diem allowances, extra compensation for certain duties, and retirement contributions. These benefits can make the overall employment package more valuable than the hourly rate alone suggests, although the exact amount depends on individual circumstances and the terms of the applicable agreement.

Mid-career Boeing 747 first officers can often earn between $180,000 and $250,000 annually, while captains at major cargo and international airlines can exceed $350,000 once additional compensation is included. Consequently, comparing salaries requires more than simply examining the published hourly rate, since guaranteed credit, seniority progression, and retirement benefits also influence the final financial outcome.

The distinction between a first officer and a captain is another major factor behind the variation in Boeing 747-8 pilot salaries. Both pilots must meet demanding training and qualification requirements, but the captain has overall authority for the flight and carries additional responsibility for operational decisions, crew coordination, and the safe conduct of the aircraft.

First officers typically occupy the lower end of the pay scale, particularly during their early years with an airline. At UPS Airlines, for example, the highest published first officer rate is $284 per hour, compared with $401 for a captain, illustrating how a pilot's position can affect earnings even when both crew members operate the same Boeing 747-8F.

Promotion to captain generally depends on experience, qualifications, available vacancies, and seniority within the airline. A pilot may accumulate substantial flight experience before securing a command position, and the timing of that promotion can significantly influence lifetime earnings. The aircraft itself does not automatically guarantee a higher salary, as the employer's pay structure remains the decisive factor. Newly hired pilots must also account for the financial realities of entering a cargo airline. Initial compensation can be considerably lower than the salaries advertised for senior captains, and probationary pay arrangements may apply before a pilot progresses through the relevant contract. Therefore, published maximum salaries describe the potential at the top of the career ladder rather than the starting point for every new employee.

The compensation available to Boeing 747-8 pilots in 2026 reflects the continued importance of experienced flight crews to large-scale cargo operations. Airlines require qualified pilots who can manage complex international flights, operate sophisticated aircraft systems, and maintain professional standards across demanding schedules, making experienced captains particularly valuable within the industry. UPS Airlines provides one of the clearest examples of the earning potential available at the top of the market, with its $401 hourly captain rate translating into an estimated annual figure of approximately $408,000 for a senior Boeing 747-8F captain. Atlas Air also offers substantial earning opportunities, although its pay progression and contract structure differ from those at UPS Airlines.

When assessing Boeing 747-8 pilot compensation and comparing it to other aircraft, the airline, the pilot's position, years of service, guaranteed flight credit, and additional benefits must all be considered together. In 2026, experienced captains at major cargo operators can earn more than $400,000 annually, while first officers and junior pilots receive lower compensation as they progress through their careers.

#6180. Transfer Capital One Miles To Air France-KLM Flying Blue With 20% Bonus: Worth It?

Capital One has just introduced its latest points transfer promotion, whereby members can receive a 20% bonus when moving rewards to Air France-KLM Flying Blue. This has the potential to be an excellent deal.

Capital One is offering a bonus when you transfer points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue. Between 12AM ET on November 1, 2026, and 11:59PM ET on November 30, 2026, members can receive a 20% bonus when moving points.

The transfer ratio is usually 1:1, so through this promotion you can transfer miles at a 1,000:1,200 ratio. The 20% bonus should post at the same time as the standard rewards. There’s no registration required, and no limit to how many bonus points you can earn. Transfers from Capital One to Flying Blue are generally instant.

We see bonuses from various transferable points currencies to Flying Blue every so often, in the range of 20-30%. So if you’re in the market for earning some Flying Blue miles, this is a good opportunity.

Air France-KLM Flying Blue is a valuable SkyTeam frequent flyer program. The program has attractive award pricing on Air France and KLM, offering many of the best ways to cross the Atlantic. Admittedly saver award availability can be tough to come by, though if you have Flying Blue Platinum status, you get access to more award space, which is an awesome perk.

On top of that, Air France and KLM make more award seats available to members of the Flying Blue program than to members of partner programs. So even when Flying Blue’s pricing isn’t the best, there are situations where it could make sense to book through Flying Blue (though with all of the Delta SkyMiles devaluations we’ve seen, typically you will find the best pricing through Flying Blue).

I should mention that in September 2026 we saw a Flying Blue devaluation, whereby awards now followed a tiered pricing structure. This means that the cheapest awards are now “Light” fares, and if you want the same inclusions as before, you need to buy up to a “Standard” fare, which costs more miles.

There’s always value in having a stash of Flying Blue miles if you think you’ll be traveling transatlantic in the coming months. I redeem through Flying Blue every year (usually multiple times per year), and consistently get value. I find it to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points.

The only other consideration here is that all major transferable points currencies partner with Air France-KLM Flying Blue, and we see transfer bonuses with some frequency. So I’d be strategic with which program you transfer points from, especially based on how you’d otherwise redeem them.

Through November 30, 2026, you can receive a 20% bonus when you transfer miles from Capital One to Air France-KLM Flying Blue. This bonus is being offered on Capital One’s end, so you should see the bonus right away, and can take advantage of this as often as you’d like.

This has the potential to be a good deal for redemptions on Air France-KLM as well as SkyTeam and other airline partners. If I didn’t already have a stash of Flying Blue miles, I’d take advantage of this.

Do you plan on converting Capital One miles into Flying Blue miles with this bonus?

#6179. Cruising to Alaska? Check if Your Next Port, Bus, or Lodge is Indigenous-Owned

The Huna Totem Corporation was featured on Condé Nast Traveler's Bright Ideas in Travel 2026. Read the full list of winners here.

From April to October, cruise ships tower over downtown Juneau’s Marine Way, a coastal path that connects the port zone to downtown. Should a traveler pause for a moment between ship and souvenir store, they’ll notice Kaagwaantaan Kootéeyaa, a tall, intricately carved pole rising against a backdrop of forest and mountains. At its base, a panel explains that the cedar pole depicts five of the Kaagwaantaan Tlingit clan’s crests: a hat, person, orca, eagle and bear. It is an arresting introduction to the long-overlooked human history of this place.

Since 2023, totem poles have adorned this highly trafficked shoreline, part of Kootéeyaa Deiyí (“Totem Pole Trail”)—a city-wide project led by the Sealaska Heritage Institute (SHI) that represents the cultures of the Tlingit people who have inhabited Juneau for at least 10,000 years, as well as the Haida and Tsimshian who arrived a few hundred years ago. Visible evidence of the region’s Indigenous communities was previously limited, says SHI’s Ricardo Worl (Tlingit), who sees the trail as “an opportunity to reestablish our presence on our ancestral lands.” Noting that more than a million cruise ship passengers land in Juneau each year, Worl hopes the trail “is the beginning of their education about our culture.”

Alaska’s cruise industry has long invited travelers to experience the “Last Frontier” while relegating Indigenous peoples to the margins of the tourism economy. Now, a shift is occurring—one that goes beyond simply incorporating Indigenous culture into the cruise experience. Across Alaska, Native corporations are increasingly owning and shaping the tourism infrastructure itself, from cruise docks and terminals to ground transportation, giving them a greater stake in how destinations develop, and how visitors experience them.

I came to Alaska to see how Indigenous ownership is changing the experience on the ground, following a route that took me from whale watching at cruise ports on the coast to bear and moose spotting at a lodge deep in the Interior. At each stop, I saw how Alaska Native corporations are shaping the places that travelers pass through.

Created following passage of the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Alaska Native corporations are for-profit companies run by and for Alaska Native shareholders. For Huna Totem, a Tlingit village corporation representing shareholders with ties to Hoonah and Glacier Bay, tourism is an important part of its economic development strategy. Its best-known development, Icy Strait Point in Hoonah, is Alaska’s first private cruise destination and has become a model for Alaska Native-owned tourism—creating local jobs, keeping economic benefits within the community and making Tlingit culture part of the visitor experience.

When Icy Strait Point opened in 2004, Huna Totem leadership was focused on “providing economic stability for generations, so the culture can be perpetuated,” says Ruth Banaszak, director of marketing and communications. Icy Strait Point has two cruise ship piers located about a half-mile apart and activity areas for 30 different excursions to distribute visitor flow around the site so that it never becomes overwhelming. To get around the vast site, I made use of the forested walking trails and two gondola systems, one of which took me to the summit of Hoonah Mountain, which I quickly and thrillingly descended via the ZipRider, a six-cable zipline. Walking around the museum exhibits housed inside a 1912 salmon cannery that closed when the fishing industry declined, I could connect tourism's present and future with its economic history. The cannery was once a symbol of loss; now it provides new economic opportunities. “We hire around 350 people for the season,” says Banaszak. “So, in a town of 950, anybody who wants to have a job in the community has one.” The model has also allowed local residents to build businesses of their own, including boat tours to Point Adolphus where, in just two hours, I spotted dozens of orcas, a few humpback whales and uncountable numbers of sea lions and sea otters. In each place, instead of being whisked onto an excursion operated by an outside company, I was experiencing a destination that had been shaped by the community whose ancestral home I was visiting.

“We’ve done this for our own community in Hoonah,” says Banaszak, “so now [we’re asking] how can we take what we’ve learned here and help other rural communities do the same thing?”

That thinking has led Huna Totem around Southeast Alaska and beyond. In Whittier, the corporation opened Glacier Gateway cruise terminal in 2024. Huna Totem and Doyon, Limited, another Alaska Native corporation, have also acquired Portage Glacier Cruises and Alaska Coach Tours, creating Native-owned touchpoints that extend from ship to shore and beyond. In Klawock, on Prince of Wales Island, Huna Totem partnered with Doyon and the local Alaska Native village corporation Klawock Heenya to develop a new cruise port in 2024. The destination uses a single-ship model, with development focused on Tlingit culture, local involvement and community values.

Back in downtown Juneau, Huna Totem is developing Áak’w Landing, a cruise dock and waterfront development targeting its first full season in 2028. The project is designed to improve how cruise visitors move through the city—including eliminating the need for tender boats at the site—rather than simply bringing in more ships. Reflecting its approach of being “culturally driven, community-centric, [and] business-focused,” says Banaszak, Huna Totem sees the project as both infrastructure enhancement and an opportunity to incorporate Alaska Native culture into the visitor experience—two poles from SHI’s Kootéeyaa Deiyí will be raised at the site.

The broader ambition is to create a network of Native-owned tourism businesses across Alaska. “So that Alaska Native tourism grows: culturally-led tourism as it should be done, people telling their own story themselves,” Banaszak says.

The cruise industry may seem an odd venture for Doyon, Limited, which is based in Fairbanks and represents the largely Dene people of the Interior, but, says Jordan Sanford, president of Doyon Tourism, “more than 60% of visitors come to Alaska by cruise, so [we realized] if we wanted to grow, we needed to be involved.”

Deep in Denali National Park, Doyon has operated Kantishna Roadhouse, the park’s only Indigenous-owned lodge, for 30 years. Arriving via a small plane from the park entrance—road access, closed for five years due to a landslide, will return in 2027—I spent blissful days backcountry hiking free from cell service. Evenings were spent listening to presentations by staff, such as an introduction to Dene beadwork and regalia; spotting wildlife including grizzly bears, moose, and caribou, then watching the setting sun light up the slopes of mighty Denali. Since 2004, in partnership with Aramark, Doyon has also operated bus tours, transit services, and campgrounds in the park. The partnership with Huna Totem gives Doyon an opportunity to diversify and grow, while responding to a recent shift in cruise passengers’ expectations: “They’re looking for more authentic experiences,” she explains. “We see that as our advantage. We put shareholders to work, and they share their culture,” she says. “There's a lot of businesses here that have been sharing the culture for so long, but from non-Alaska Natives,” she adds.

Next up is the restoration of the 1925 Chatanika Gold Camp near Fairbanks, which is scheduled to open in 2027 as a northern lights experience center, filling a critical infrastructure gap. Aurora viewing in Alaska today typically means pulling off the side of the road and drinking a hot chocolate, says Sanford. With Chatanika, “we're creating a space [with] cultural programming to make it more of an experience.”

It’s another link in an emerging network of Native-owned businesses across the state. The ultimate goal is “an Alaska Native-owned corridor, where [travelers] are visiting Alaska Native-owned businesses along the way,” says Sanford. For cruise passengers, that means more opportunities to encounter Indigenous culture, while knowing that Indigenous people are benefiting from the industry. And it means that your next Alaska cruise itinerary might begin at a Native-owned port, continue aboard a Native-owned bus, lead to a Native-owned excursion, and end at a Native-owned lodge.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6178. Air France-KLM Flying Blue Promo Rewards: Save 25% On Select Awards

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has its monthly Promo Rewards promotion, whereby members can save 25% on select award tickets over a limited travel period. The program has just published its new Promo Rewards list for November 2026, offering discounted short haul and long haul awards for travel over the coming months.

There are quite a few destinations bookable with this promotion, including several in the Americas, with options in business class, premium economy, and economy. This has the potential to be a great deal.

I’m a big fan of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program, especially for long haul premium cabin redemptions. Not only does Flying Blue largely have attractive award pricing for business class travel, but the program also has access to more Air France and KLM award space than other programs.

The Promo Rewards offer is published every month by the Flying Blue program, and offers 25% discounts off select awards for travel on Air France and KLM. The Flying Blue program has dynamic award pricing, and this promotion specifically applies for the lowest, saver level award costs.

Flying Blue has published its November 2026 Promo Rewards, valid for bookings between November 1 and November 30, 2026. Most of these Promo Rewards have long travel windows, and can be used for flights all the way through April 30, 2027.

As a reminder, Flying Blue has standardized saver award pricing, so ordinarily you’ll pay the following amounts for one-way transatlantic awards between Europe and most of North America, when booking a “Light” fare:

Let me emphasize that with the recent Flying Blue devaluation, the entry level pricing is now for a “Light” fare rather than a Standard fare, so it comes with fewer inclusions. For example, a long haul business class “Light” fare doesn’t offer any flexibility, and also doesn’t offer lounge access.

However, if you have Flying Blue Platinum status, then you still receive most of the perks of a “Standard” fare automatically. So as an example, a Promo Rewards ticket that costs 45,000 miles in business class for a “Light” fare would now cost 56,250 miles for a “Standard” fare.

Here are the awards that are available with the Promo Rewards list this month for travel between Europe and North America, along with the pricing:

On top of that, the Flying Blue Extra program was recently launched (the cost starts at €379 per year), which is essentially a paid membership program that offers extra perks. One of the perks of Flying Blue Extra is access to additional Promo Rewards, so eligible members receive access to the following extra Promo Rewards availability to North America this time around:

There are of course also Promo Rewards opportunities outside of North America, including some business class options to South America, so check out the full list.

All of the lowest priced awards in the above markets through April 30, 2027, should be bookable with the Promo Rewards pricing (though not necessarily the extra award availability that Flying Blue Platinum members receive). You can use all of these awards for travel to and from destinations across Europe, so you can travel beyond Amsterdam and Paris.

If you’re having trouble finding availability, remember to use Flying Blue’s secret award calendar. Also keep in mind that children ages two to 12 receive 25% off Flying Blue award tickets, including Promo Rewards.

One of the things that’s awesome about the Flying Blue program is how easy it is to rack up miles:

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program offers a Promo Rewards promotion, whereby members can book discounted award tickets in select markets. This can be a great deal, especially when you consider how easy Flying Blue miles are to come by, and also how much award space is sometimes available through Flying Blue.

With the latest Promo Rewards, you can save 25% to several destinations in the Americas, with options in economy, premium economy, and business class. This has the potential to be quite a good deal, so if you have any travel you’re interested in booking, this would be a great time to do so.

#6177. American Resumes Service to Haiti After Two-Year Pause

American Airlines on Sunday restarted service to Haiti after a nearly two-year hiatus brought on by gang violence in and around Port-au-Prince.

The carrier is now operating daily nonstop flights between Miami and Cap-Haitien, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

The inaugural flight on Sunday was staffed by an all-Haitian, Creole-speaking crew, the airline said.

“The connection between the United States and Haiti is incredibly meaningful, which is especially true in South Florida,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “We know the critical role air service plays in linking countries and communities, so we’re beyond proud to reinstate such a consequential connection for so many.”

U.S. airlines suspended service to and from Haiti in 2024 amid a rise in gang violence. Toussaint Louverture International Airport in Port-au-Prince was temporarily closed after bullets struck aircraft taxiing on the tarmac.

So far, American is the only U.S.-based carrier to have resumed service to the country.
