#6163. Why Ultra-Long-Haul Flights Still Need 4 Pilots In The Cockpit For Takeoff

Even in the 21st century, flying an ultra-long-haul commercial jetliner halfway around the globe cannot be completed by one or even two pilots. Despite how far technology has come with the advent of fly-by-wire and advanced autopilot, there are still four pilots required to fly the longest 17-or 18-hour ULH missions. This comes down to the Code of Federal Regulations that limits pilots to flying no more than eight to nine hours in a single duty day under Part 117 and dictates that missions over 17 hours require four pilots aboard.

Takeoff is one of the most important and work-intensive phases of a flight for any airplane. So, while not all four pilots will be on duty for the duration of a ULH mission, the two relief pilots taking the second shift will still be in the jump seats to provide an extra pair of eyes as backup during this critical stage in the journey. The backup crew can contribute by reading checklists and scanning instruments during takeoff, and should an unexpected issue pop up or a legitimate emergency occur, they are already on the flight deck to help out.

ULH widebody airliners are enormous and weigh hundreds of thousands of pounds, requiring constant and meticulous monitoring despite the layers of safety tech and automation. Because of the restrictions on aircrew, widebody jets made for long-haul flying have crew rest areas with two or three bunks just for the pilots to sleep. Some aircraft only require three pilots to complete the journeys across oceans and continents if they can reach their destination in less than 16 hours. Yet, for the longest missions, there will be two captains and two first officers to ensure a jet crossing the globe arrives at its destination safely and smoothly.

The colossal aircraft that fly around the world in a single flight weigh hundreds of tons and are loaded with hundreds of thousands of pounds of jet fuel. These planes are giant fuel depots careening through the sky at just under the speed of sound. The margin for error is razor thin, even in the best of cases. If one should be mishandled by a fatigued crew, it introduces catastrophic risks that threaten not only the plane and everyone on board, but also the general public on the ground, as well as the airline and commercial flying industry.

There are a myriad of concerns for aircrews that train to fly these massive and complex machines. They must consider how, in an emergency shortly after takeoff, an ultra-long-haul plane is too heavy to land safely because of its massive fuel load. Widebody aircraft have immense physical inertia. The pilot takes into account that such a large aircraft does not respond instantly to control inputs. Modern automation can maintain an altitude, but it cannot think. Fatigue acts like a chemical intoxicant, progressively shutting down the higher-order brain functions.

In a serious emergency, the two resting pilots are woken up immediately. This gives the aircraft four highly trained minds to manage the situation. With four pilots split into distinct teams, the two active pilots on duty keep each other sharp through strict cross-checking protocols. While technology and automation handle routine flying tasks, they cannot replace human judgment during a crisis. As Lessons From The Flight Deck wrote, this is exactly why four pilots must be present for takeoff on ULH flights like Qantas' upcoming 'Project Sunrise' route.

At 10,573 miles (17,015 km), the journey is no mean feat.

Crew Resource Management on an exceptionally long itinerary is very different from the kind of 'tactical' mindset that pilots flying short to mid-range hops between busy hubs have when they are at the controls. ULH is an endurance mission that requires constant vigilance, discipline, and professionalism to ensure every flight goes off without a hitch. Because a four-pilot crew will spend many hours together, the CRM process begins long before the engines start. The planning process is significantly longer than that of many other commercial flights, reflecting the intensity of the task for every aircrew that embarks on a long-range jetliner.

Paradoxically, one of the greatest hazards in modern ULH flying is not high stress, but extreme boredom during the 14-hour mid-flight cruise phase over oceans. There are a number of productive measures used by crews to actively engage in cognitive tasks to keep their brains stimulated. Some examples include periodic fuel-burn verifications, cross-checking alternative flight paths, and conducting technical 'what-if' scenario discussions about diversions or emergency procedures. Sometimes pilots will take a nap in the cockpit seat for 20 to 30 minutes as well if they are truly exhausted before beginning the scheduled rest time.

Crews are explicitly trained to openly admit to their colleagues when they are experiencing cognitive fog, slow reaction times, or a wave of fatigue. However, because fatigue impairs a person’s ability to recognize their own decline, CRM strategies require pilots to actively monitor each other for signs of fatigue. If a junior first officer notices a highly experienced captain making minor errors during a late-flight approach, the CRM culture empowers the junior pilot to step in, question the action, or take the controls without fear of professional backlash.

The actual flight path an aircraft flies is determined by several factors ranging from efficiency to flight safety and even geopolitics.

Today, Qantas is pursuing a historic goal of establishing the world's longest commercial itinerary. Australia's top airline aims to begin service next year from Sydney International (SYD) on the East Coast of Australia, directly to New York JFK Airport (JFK) and London Heathrow (LHR). Airbus is building a special A350-1000ULR variant, which is a scaled-up version of the A350-900ULR that has successfully been flying for Singapore Airlines on what is currently the longest scheduled flight on the planet. The Qantas jet will fly two to four hours longer on its mission and require four pilots total.

Project Sunrise is expected to take 20 to 22 hours, depending on whether the destination is New York or London, and which direction it is flying, to or from Australia. The itinerary flown by Singapore Airlines from JFK to Changi International (SIN) tops out at around 18.5 hours currently. The Qantas route will be roughly 1,000 miles (1,609 km) longer and take nearly a full day cycle to complete from takeoff to touchdown. Because of how much this mission exceeds the world's longest revenue flight already, many special provisions are being made.

A standard A350-1000 holds between 350 and 410 passengers. Qantas has aggressively slashed this to just 238 seats. The flight crew rest compartment will be located in the upper crown of the jet's roof and physically separated from the already stripped-down cabin to make it the quietest and most restful place possible. It is expected to be equipped with two fully flat full-length berthing bunks. The RCRC will be outfitted with tailor-made ergonomics and warm-toned lights to encourage sleep, as well as blue-wavelength light to help the pilots wake up.

The A380 is no longer a viable aircraft in many airline's fleets.

Qantas will staff the A350-1000ULR jets with highly experienced aircrew to ensure that Project Sunrise is both safe and smooth every time the bespoke widebody takes flight. Instead of using junior second officers as relief pilots, the four-pilot "heavy crew" structure will rely heavily on two fully qualified captains and two experienced first officers. The roster will split the 22-hour time block into operational blocks of a few hours. The crew will rotate so that no individual pilot is at the active controls, so that every pilot receives two distinct opportunities to sleep in the bunk.

The sheer endurance required of the pilots has been a major factor in the development of Project Sunrise. Qantas has worked with the Australian and International Pilots Association to establish a unique op-tempo. The planning phase mandates a clear window of 48 to 72 hours of local time zone rest before a pilot can step onto a Sunrise flight. After they touch down, the pilots will be instructed to take a similar amount of time off in the local area before they can return for duty and fly another ultramarathon mission around the globe.

Implementing a data-driven fatigue risk management system is critical for Project Sunrise because a single catastrophic error on a historic, high-profile mission would permanently damage the airline's reputation. As has happened in the past with examples like the Concorde, one tragic mishap can devastate public trust in air travel and also influence the airspace permissions granted for future routes. The FRMS protects the pilots' executive functioning skills to ensure that the human in the loop is there to guarantee that the jet and every soul aboard is safe at all times.

On top of being required for compliance with ULH regulations to ensure the safety of flight, four pilots make the plane more efficient than trying to push a skeleton crew to the limit of what is legally allowed. With four pilots, the crew splits into two independent, two-pilot teams. Rescheduled rest time matches normal human sleep architecture, ensuring everyone gets deep, restorative sleep. Whereas in a three-pilot operation, the pilot rotation is a rolling cycle.

On a 20-hour flight with three pilots, only one pilot can sleep at any given time to maintain a two-pilot cockpit. If you divide the cruise time evenly, each pilot gets roughly 6.5 hours of bunk time. However, this must be split into multiple short breaks, leaving pilots with fragmented, low-quality sleep that fails to provide restorative REM cycles. A four-pilot crew eliminates this hazard through a clean break in shifts. Plus, if an emergency occurs 18 hours into the flight, like an engine failure or a severe medical crisis, a four-pilot crew can bring all hands on deck.

Midway through a Project Sunrise flight, Team A steps into the cockpit to relieve Team B. A well-rested two-pilot team has the mental energy to actively optimize their flight path, coordinate with air traffic control, and adjust speeds to save fuel. Unlike a fatigued crew, which is more likely to default to passive, rigid flight paths just to minimize their workload. Saving fuel on a 22-hour flight requires constantly analyzing shifting global jet streams and adjusting altitudes, which demands critical thinking and decision-making that considers a long list of variables.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Then there is also the benefit that because the crew gets better sleep on board, pilots recover much faster once they land. This protects their long-term health and allows the airline to build a more predictable, reliable, and sustainable long-haul roster. Otherwise, the physical toll of ultra-long-haul flying can cause chronic sleep deprivation, immune suppression, and early career burnout, which would only serve to hurt the airline, considering the global pilot shortage.

If you have a Capital One credit card, you may be able to earn extra rewards on purchases through Capital One Offers.

Similar to Amex Offers and Chase Offers, the program gives eligible cardholders access to shopping deals that can help them save on purchases they were already planning to make.

Here's how Capital One Offers works, how to use it and what to know before shopping.

Capital One Offers is a shopping rewards platform that gives eligible Capital One customers access to special deals at participating merchants. Offers span categories such as clothing, electronics, home goods and travel.

The platform is available to eligible U.S. consumer Capital One credit card holders, including those with cards in the Venture, Savor and Quicksilver families. (Business credit cards are not eligible.)

You can access available offers through your online account or the Capital One mobile app. However, eligibility varies by account, so you'll need to sign in to see which offers are available to you.

Unlike the standard rewards you earn on everyday purchases, Capital One Offers requires you to select an eligible deal and follow its redemption instructions.

For example, if you find an offer for 5% back at a retailer, you could earn that reward on top of the points or miles you'd normally earn with your credit card, as long as your purchase meets the offer's terms.

Capital One Offers is different from Capital One Shopping. Capital One Offers provides deals through eligible Capital One accounts, while Capital One Shopping is a separate shopping tool that helps users find coupon codes, compare prices and track price drops.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

The deals you'll find through Capital One Offers depend on what's available when you sign in. You might see discounts on clothing, electronics or hotel bookings, with participating merchants and reward rates varying.

Some offers apply to most purchases from a retailer, while others are limited to certain products or categories. Keep in mind that rewards may also exclude taxes, shipping and other fees.

You can find Capital One Offers through the issuer's website or mobile app:

From there, you can browse deals or search for a specific merchant.

How you redeem an offer depends on whether you're shopping online or in a physical store.

Keep in mind that for online offers, the link you use matters, as Capital One relies on tracking information to associate your purchase with the offer.

Be sure to confirm which locations, payment methods and purchases qualify. An online offer won't necessarily apply to an in-store transaction, or vice versa.

Related: How to maximize online shopping portals for your purchases

Capital One says rewards typically arrive in about 45 days, although some can take up to three billing cycles. Certain offers may take longer.

For hotel offers, payouts are issued after you complete your stay, and the reservation must be completed within one year of booking.

Related: The best credit cards for online shopping

There are a few things worth keeping in mind before taking advantage of an offer.

I've gotten into the habit of checking Capital One Offers whenever I'm shopping online with my Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card. Sometimes there's a deal worth using, but other times I'll find a better offer through another shopping portal.

That's why it's worth comparing your options before making a purchase. For example, an offer for 5% back through Capital One, for example, might not be as valuable as a higher reward rate elsewhere.

Just keep in mind that you generally can't stack Capital One Offers with other shopping portals or promotional codes. Using another portal or certain coupons could invalidate your reward, so you'll want to decide which offer to use before checking out.

For travel purchases, I'd also recommend comparing the total price and booking conditions rather than focusing solely on the advertised reward.

Each offer has its own terms, including potential spending requirements, expiration dates and usage limits. Some deals may exclude gift cards, certain products or other purchases, while others may be limited to a single transaction.

Look at the terms before shopping, particularly if you're making a large purchase or planning to use an offer more than once.

You can check the status of your Capital One Offers rewards by opening the menu on the right side of the Capital One Offers page and selecting "Shopping Trips." From there, you'll see a tracker showing the status of your purchases and rewards.

It's also worth saving your offer details and order confirmations, especially for purchases with longer payout timelines.

If your reward hasn't arrived when expected, double-check that you met the offer requirements before contacting Capital One.

Related: Capital One miles: How to earn, redeem and transfer rewards

Capital One Offers can be an easy way to earn extra rewards on purchases you're already planning to make.

Before shopping, check your account for available deals, compare your options and follow the offer's instructions to make sure your purchase qualifies.

Just remember that offers and eligibility can vary, so a deal available to one Capital One customer may not be available to another.

Related: Tips and tricks to get maximum value from your Capital One miles

#6161. Save On Air France-KLM Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Air France-KLM flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel. We’ve seen this offer in the past, and I’m happy to see it return, as I always get significant value from it. However, this offer isn’t quite as lucrative as past ones.

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500 or more with Air France-KLM by December 15, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 25,000 bonus points rather than a $250 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 25,000 points at $425.

For what it’s worth, in the past when I’ve purchased sustainable aviation fuel with Air France in order to earn XP (the metric by which you qualify for status), that triggered an Amex Offers deal. So at least anecdotally, that seems to work. Furthermore, taxes and carrier imposed surcharges on award tickets also seem to qualify.

I’m always happy to see this offer available, though let me note that this isn’t as lucrative as in the past. In past situations we’ve seen a $200 statement credit or 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000+, so as a percentage return, this definitely isn’t as good.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines on up to $500,000 per calendar year and then 1x.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $2,500 ticket, you’d receive a $250 statement credit plus 12,500 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $462.50 on $2,500 of spending, which comes out to an 18.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500+ on an Air France-KLM ticket. If you’re planning travel on Air France or KLM, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

#6160. Save On Etihad Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Etihad Airways flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel (that’s not to say you should or shouldn’t plan travel on Etihad, for a variety of reasons — I’m just sharing a deal!).

To my knowledge, this is the first time that we’ve seen an Amex Offers deal for Etihad purchases, so it’s nice to see another airline join the Amex Offers “circuit.”

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $200 statement credit when you spend $1,000+ or more with Etihad Airways by December 31, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 20,000 bonus points rather than a $200 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 20,000 points at $340.

Let me emphasize that while the terms suggest that you need to book an Etihad flight through the US website that originates in the US, I’ve had similar Amex Offers triggered in the past for flights that didn’t originate in the US, so it’s anyone’s guess how that’s actually enforced here.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $1,000 ticket, you’d receive a $200 statement credit plus 5,000 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $285 on $1,000 of spending, which comes out to a 28.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $200 statement credit when you spend $1,000+ on an Etihad ticket. If you’re planning travel on Etihad, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

Were you targeted for this Amex Offers deal, and if so, do you plan on taking advantage of it?

London routinely ranks among the world’s most-visited cities. It is home to incredible museums, a fabulous theater scene, great restaurants, luxurious hotels and its main airport, Heathrow (LHR), is a hub for multiple airlines, making it a great stopping-over point on a larger trip.

That said, the British capital is well worth visiting on its own for anything from a few days to a few weeks, depending on how much of an Anglophile you are.

Despite the strong U.S. dollar, London is still an expensive destination, so if price points have been putting you off lately, here are some easy strategies to stretch your London trip budget even further using miles and points.

And if you have some strategies of your own to use airline miles, hotel points and credit card rewards to maximize a trip to London, please share those in the comments below!

Where you should stay in London depends on the purpose of your visit. If you are in town for business, you might want to stay near the City of London, while folks who want a quieter neighborhood might like Kensington or Notting Hill. Knightsbridge is best for those who want upscale shopping, while Mayfair has fantastic restaurants and boutiques.

London can get dreary and gray during the winter months and crowded during the summer, so your best bets are fall from September-November and spring from March-May when the temperatures tend to be mild and days will include a mix of sun and rain.

The number of miles you need to fly to London depends on which airline you take and which miles you redeem, as well as the time of year since some mileage programs require more miles during peak travel times. That said, you can find flights on some airlines, like Virgin Atlantic, by redeeming as few as 6,000 miles each way.

American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines all fly to London from various U.S. airports. You’ll also find plenty of flights from over a dozen U.S. cities from the U.K.’s two main carriers, British Airways and Virgin Atlantic.

The cost of a trip to London depends on when you visit, how long your trip is and where you want to stay. The city has options for travelers ranging from budget flights and accommodations to luxury hotels that can cost well over $500 a night. Luckily, many hotels are accessible using credit card rewards and hotel points.

Now that the FAQs are out of the way, here's what else you need to know to start planning your trip to London.

Virgin Atlantic flies to London Heathrow from 11 U.S. cities and using Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points can be a real bargain. Just beware of taxes and fees that can be several hundred dollars, even for economy tickets.

I like using the airline’s Reward Seat Checker tool to price out tickets between city pairs over a month at a time. You can often find economy tickets between the East Coast and London for as few as 6,000 miles each way. Yes, you read that correctly — you can cross the Atlantic for just 6,000 miles. Even better, premium economy starts at just 10,500 miles and Upper Class can require as few as 29,000 miles (though it’s often much higher).

Unfortunately, you’ll be on the hook for anywhere from $450-$1,700 in taxes and fees round-trip depending on your class of service. That’s a lot, but perhaps not so bad considering even some economy flights are costing upwards of $1,400 at the moment, saving a few hundred dollars by redeeming a few thousand miles can be well worth it.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is a 1:1 transfer partner of:

What’s more, some of these partners, including Amex and Bilt, offer limited-time transfer bonuses, so you can score even more of a deal on award tickets.

Related: The best ways to travel to London with points and miles

British Airways is one of the most generous airlines in the world when it comes to releasing award seats in its four classes of long-haul service: economy, premium economy, business class and first class.

The downside is the hefty fuel surcharges and taxes on the airline's flights to and from its London Heathrow hub. There are, however, some ways to mitigate those.

The key is to redeem points and miles from the right programs. The extra charges will still be relatively high, but you can end up saving hundreds of dollars per ticket — each way! To illustrate this most clearly, let's focus on British Airways business class.

While American Airlines AAdvantage would only require 57,500 miles each way in business class for British Airways flights between the U.S. and London, the taxes and fees can cost between $750-$1,000 each way. The same is true if you were to redeem 45,000-70,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points each way – with taxes and fees that can top $1,100.

Instead, you might want to consider redeeming Cathay Pacific Asia Miles. Flights from the East Coast start at 63,000 miles plus $200-$450 in each direction, while those from the West Coast incur the same taxes and fees, but require 93,000 miles.

For its part, British Airways Club would require 88,000-99,000 Avios in each direction depending on which city in the U.S. you’re flying from, plus taxes and fees closer to $400-$500. Yes, that is still a chunk of change, and it’s a lot more Avios or Asia Miles, but it can be well worth it to save close to a thousand dollars per person.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of:

Cathay Pacific Asia Miles is a transfer partner of:

That means that although you’re spending more miles for a ticket than redeeming through AAdvantage or Atmos, you have a lot more transfer partner options to top up your British Airways or Cathay Pacific accounts.

Related: Great award availability but beware the taxes: British Airways business class review

Another way to save on taxes and fees on award tickets as well as sparing yourself a few miles is to redeem United MileagePlus miles for a ticket on United. Not only does United charge far lower taxes and fees than British Airways and Virgin Atlantic, but if you are either a United MileagePlus elite or carry a United cobranded card, you might be eligible for preferential redemption rates on award tickets booked through MileagePlus.

You’ll pay just $5.60 flying from the U.S. to London, in any class of service, and around $200-$400 on the return, depending on which cabin you’re in.

Plus, you can save on the mileage portion of your ticket if you’re an elite or a credit cardholder. Take these flights from London to Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), for instance. Regular MileagePlus members would have to redeem 40,000 miles for coach, 50,000 for premium economy and 80,000 for United Polaris business class. But if you have access to preferential rates, you’ll save at least 10% of the miles and need just 36,000 for coach, 45,000 for premium economy and 72,000 for business class.

If you don’t currently carry a United credit card, consider the United℠ Explorer Card (see ) or the United Quest℠ Card (see ).

United is also a 1:1 transfer partner of Chase Ultimate Rewards if you carry one of the following cards:

Finally, don’t forget that United has a special partnership with Marriott. Normally, when you transfer 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points to one of its airline partners, you end up with 20,000 airline miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus for 25,000 miles total.

With United, however, you get a 10,000-mile bonus, so 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points convert to 30,000 United miles. That’s probably a special-circumstance use for most folks, but still something to consider if you’re swimming in Marriott points.

Related: The best times to apply for Chase’s United cards based on offer history

As you might expect, London is lousy with points hotels, and more are on the way. I’m most excited about the Waldorf Astoria London – Admiralty Arch and the St. Regis London, both of which should open in early 2027.

I’d suggest picking the area you want to stay in and then doing a search with your preferred hotel programs around there. In the meantime, here are some of my top picks with each program.

The swanky NoMad London opened in 2021 and immediately gained a following thanks to its maximalist decor and popular bars and restaurants, not to mention its central Covent Garden location. It’s now part of Hilton, so you can redeem points for stays. Nights start at $550 or 100,000 Hilton Honors points.

I also love the colorful BoTree Hotel, which is part of Hilton’s Curio Collection. It opened in a quiet pocket of Mayfair in 2023 and has bright but sophisticated rooms and is home to an outpost of the see-and-be-seen Italian eatery Lavo. Rates start at $400 or 108,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

I love Mayfair, so my top Hyatt pick for the city is Hyatt Regency London – The Churchill, which sits right on stately Portman Square and is turning 50 years old next year. The room decor is not exactly overawing, but the public spaces are grand indeed and the service is impeccable. Nights start at $440 or 25,000-55,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

TPG staffers also love the Great Scotland Yard Hotel, which is part of Hyatt’s Unbound Collection. Rooms are on the small side, but you can’t beat the history since it’s in a heritage-listed building that was once the Metropolitan Police headquarters. Rates start at $380 or 20,000-40,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

For something a bit hipper as well as budget-friendlier, try the Standard. It’s in a very busy area right near Kings Cross, but chic, 70s-inspired room decor and several buzzy bars and restaurants will make your time here feel like an upscale city experience. Rates start at $305 or 20,000-40,000 points per night.

Related: Which credit cards should you use for Hyatt stays?

Even among quirky Kimptons, the Kimpton Fitzroy is a standout thanks to the magnificent 1900 landmark building that houses it and its central Bloomsbury location. Make time for afternoon tea in Palm Court, which is a veritable London institution. Rates start at $319 or 66,000 IHG One Rewards points per night.

The InterContinental London Park Lane has an utterly convenient location at Hyde Park Corner and features spacious rooms, specialty drinks inspired by the royal family at Arch Bar and an expansive spa and fitness center. Rates start at $433 or 83,000 points per night.

Related: Which credit card should you use for IHG stays?

It might occupy a heritage-listed building from 1910, but the London Edition feels utterly of the moment (even though it opened over 13 years ago). Rooms have Edition’s signature look of white textiles, wood paneling and minimalist bathrooms. It’s worth spending an evening admiring the sculpted ceiling at Berners Tavern while enjoying dishes from chef Jason Atherton’s menu. Rates start at $485 or 70,400 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

Formerly a Renaissance hotel, St. Pancras has since joined Marriott’s Autograph Collection and is a favorite among train enthusiasts thanks to its location in a landmark neo-Gothic edifice attached to the train station of the same name. Rooms feel opulent in a Victorian way, and its Moorish-inspired spa is a treat. Rates start at $280 or 52,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

While hotel points come in handy for saving bundles of money on otherwise expensive stays, if you are looking to splurge while in London, there are still ways to save on luxury hotels.

Travelers with either the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express should check American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, which sometimes has third- or fourth-night free packages at some of the city’s finest hotels. These bookings also come with perks like free daily breakfast for two, a $100 on-property credit, availability-based upgrades and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout.

There are plenty to choose from, but my personal favorite London hotels that participate in Amex FHR include:

Remember, if you have the American Express Platinum Card or The Business Platinum Card from American Express you are also eligible for up to $300 in statement credits biannually for up to a total of $600 per year on prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection or Airbnb Luxe bookings (of two nights or more for THC and Airbnb) through American Express Travel® or the Amex Travel App™. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, those FHR bookings will require two nights or more to be eligible for this credit.

You might also consider booking a luxury hotel through the Capital One Premier Collection if you have the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card or the Capital One Venture X Business for valuable benefits like free daily breakfast for two, up to $100 in on-property experience credits and room upgrades (if available).

Likewise, if you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve or the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business you can book a hotel that is part of The Edit by Chase Travel℠. Cardholders are eligible for two statement credits of up to $250 each (for a total of $500) this calendar year to put toward stays of two nights or more booked through The Edit. During your stay, you are also eligible for availability-based upgrades, complimentary daily breakfast and a $100 on-property credit.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve’s The Edit credit: What to know

Although British food was long a punchline, the city has become one of the world’s premier dining destinations in the past two decades or so. These days, you can find everything from Sri Lankan hoppers and Scandinavian smoked fish to French haute cuisine and sustainable farm-to-table fare.

Prices are high, though, so it’s best to maximize rewards on your spending and any statement credits your credit cards might afford you.

Another favorite tip of mine: You can often find discounts of up to 50% at some restaurants by booking reservations via The Fork. Then, just show your reservation details at check in, enjoy your meal, and the savings will be automatically applied to your bill.

Related: The best credit cards for dining

Taxis and Ubers are easy to come by in London, though rides can be expensive. So if you do go this route, so to speak, make sure to use a card that earns bonus points on ride-hailing services.

It’s also easy to hop on the city’s Tube lines and buses, both of which are easy to navigate and affordable, by simply tapping on with your credit card. If you decide to do so, keep a card that earns bonus points on public transportation at the top of your wallet.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (see ) earns 2 points per dollar on local transit and commuting, for example, and the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card earns 2 points per dollar on local transit purchases.

You might be able to use the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s $300 in annual travel statement credits toward transit purchases as well as taxis and Ubers since these charges often code as “travel.”

Related: The best credit cards for commuting expenses

No matter whether you spell it “theater” or “theatre,” no trip to London would be complete without seeing a production in one of the West End’s magnificent venues. Ticket prices tend to be more reasonable than in the U.S. but can still put a dent in your budget. Luckily, you can take advantage of the Chase Sapphire Reserve Stubhub credit to offset some of that cost.

Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders receive up to $300 per year to use on purchases made through StubHub or its sister site, Viagogo. The credit is split into two biannual credits of up to $150 (activation required; through Dec. 31, 2027).

Among the productions currently available through Stubhub in London are “Paddington: The Musical” (just beware it’s mostly sold out except for last-minute tickets) and “Oh, Mary!”.

A few years ago, Capital One partnered with The Cultivist, a service that grants members free, priority access to dozens of museums around the world. Eligible Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card holders can register for half-price membership that costs $220 per year instead of $440. This auto-renews at the discounted rate for the second year and then is full price after that.

While $220 is a lot, if you visit museums frequently, you can end up saving far more than that on tickets since The Cultivist Enthusiast-level membership available with the Venture X includes priority admission for the cardholder plus a guest. In London, the participating museums include:

Finally, some credit cards levy foreign exchange fees on purchases you make outside the U.S. They tend to add 1-3% to your purchase price, which can add up quickly. Instead, use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees, of which there are many to choose from.

If you travel abroad frequently, you might also want to consider the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card. In addition to waiving foreign transaction fees, the card actually earns 3 points per dollar on foreign transactions, in any category. It’s almost too good to be true, and that makes it one of the best credit cards for trips abroad.

Related: The best credit cards with no foreign transaction fees

#6158. Ouch: Flying Blue Makes Earning XPs Through SAF 50% More Expensive

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has just rolled out a quiet devaluation, and it’s one that many savvy Flying Blue members won’t be happy about. The airline group has increased the cost to contribute toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and in turn, has reduced the ability to earn elite status through this method. And we’re not talking about a minor price increase either…

Personally I consider Air France-KLM Flying Blue elite status to be valuable, not just for the SkyTeam Elite Plus perks, but also for the more Air France- KLM specific benefits, like access to more award availability.

Earning Flying Blue elite status is based on the concept of XPs (“experience points”), and how many of those you rack up. One really innovative thing that Flying Blue has done is that it has been possible to earn XPs through environmental contributions:

As I see it, this is a win-win — this program can genuinely help you earn status, while doing something that’s good for the environment, and also contributing to Air France-KLM’s long term environmental goals.

Well, seemingly overnight, Flying Blue has increased the cost to purchase SAF, and in turn, earn XPs. With these changes, you earn one XP for every €15 contributed toward SAF, compared to the previous amount of €10.

A 50% overnight increase is rough. It gets even worse than that, though. There’s no longer any “rounding” with this, so for short haul economy flights you might find that you’re not offered any XPs if the contribution amount is €14, and you’re offered one XP if the amount is €28.

The past year or so has definitely been rough for the overall value of the Flying Blue program, including for elite members:

This is of course all frustrating, though I guess the other side of the equation is that Flying Blue Platinum status has become more valuable over time, but primarily through punitive measures:

How do we make sense of increasing the cost to contribute to SAF, and in turn, earn XPs? I wonder if Flying Blue management thinks that people will still buy SAF at the same rate as before? I know I certainly won’t, though maybe I’m in the minority (I’ll instead increasingly earn XPs through Flying Blue’s co-branded credit card in the US, since that opportunity was recently improved).

For that matter, I’m curious to what extent the number of people buying SAF matters to Air France-KLM? Does this materially contribute to any environmental initiatives, or is it not a priority?

I still get value from my Flying Blue Platinum status, and don’t have plans to change my strategy. Honestly, that partly comes down to how hard it has become to find award availability in business class on long haul flights through other programs.

But I’m definitely slowly becoming less enthused by the program. Then again, I guess that sums up the reality of miles & points more broadly — this isn’t what it once was, and it’s getting harder and harder to make the case for being loyal. It’s no different than World of Hyatt, where they’re clearly trying to cash in. I guess that is the goal of any for-profit business, eh?

Flying Blue has just devalued the rate at which you earn XPs for SAF contributions. You used to earn one XP for every €10 contributed, while you now earn one XP for every €15 contributed. A 50% increase in cost overnight is huge.

I always thought this was a unique aspect of the Flying Blue program, since it’s a win-win for consumers, the airline group, and the environment. Obviously they’ve decided on a different equation now, and for us members, this isn’t good news.

What do you make of this change to Flying Blue when it comes to earning XPs for SAF?

#6157. Here's What Emirates' 56-Seat Premium Economy Cabin Offers That Singapore Airlines Structurally Cannot Match

Emiratesis internationally recognized for its superb standard of premium economy. The carrier placed second in the last Skytrax classification for the category, one place above Singapore Airlines. Aboard the airline's massive Airbus A380s, passengers have 56 seats to choose from, an enormous premium economy cabin.

Along with creating a premium economy cabin larger than its rivals', Emirates has shown that it can deliver a near-business-class experience, minus lie-flat seating, without charging over standard premium economy pricing. The carrier continues to outshine its rivals like Singapore Airlines.

The most obvious difference is that Emirates' premium economy seats are larger than those of its competitors. Passengers can enjoy 19.5 inches (49.5 cm) of width and 38 to 40 inches (96.5 to 101.6 cm) of pitch, according to Go Guided. The seat also has pop-up calf rests for additional comfort.

These seats are in a 2-4-2 configuration on the A380 and Boeing 777, and 2-3-2 for the Airbus A350, and passengers can expect to pay up to twice as much. Meanwhile, Singapore Airlines offers a 38-inch (96.5 cm) seat pitch as standard, and an 18.5 to 19.5-inch (47 cm to 49.5 cm) width.

Both carriers have the same eight inches (20.3 cm) of recline according to Trip.com. Emirates' mini-business class experience isn't just about the quality of what is included in the product. It also visually looks closer to business class, a clear statement of intent. The seats are decked out with plush cream leather.

Their armrests have sleek woodgrain finishes. The impression created by these design decisions is of a step-down from business class rather than a step up from economy. Meanwhile, Singapore Airlines' premium economy seat design is contemporary and functional, lacking the flair on display from Emirates.

The variation in fleet dynamics means that Emirates is far less constrained by space than Singapore. This is because of the carrier's enormous A380 fleet, with Emirates having access to 116 A380s. The carrier also flies a large number of Boeing 777s, with 144 including freighters. Singapore Airlines' widebody fleet is both smaller in terms of the number of aircraft (139 planes to Emirates' 290 jets) and utilizes smaller aircraft.

For example, its widebody fleet is dominated by midsize aircraft such as the A350 and the Boeing 787. Large aircraft like the A380 and 777 have a much smaller representation. The table below compares the current widebody fleets for Emirates and Singapore, using data from Planespotters.net.

Larger aircraft allow for large premium economy cabins, like the 56 premium economy seats available on Emirates' A380s. It is also notable that the carrier chooses to make this decision when such room is available, whereas others do not. For example, Singapore Airlines configures its A380s with 44 seats in a 2-4-2 layout, all of which are on the main deck.

Constructing a 56-seat premium economy cabin is wasteful for carriers that can't fill it. The carrier can sustain the large-scale demand needed because of both Emirates' and Dubai's premium brand, while still offering competitive schedules and fares. The A380 is central to the premium brand across all classes. In economy, its seats are more spacious than those available aboard its ten-abreast 777s.

First class passengers have access to showers, a rare feature in commercial aviation. Meanwhile, first and business class passengers can use a fully staffed bar on the upper deck. Although not all of the Emirates A380's premium features are available to premium economy passengers, it has helped produce an image of the aircraft in customers' minds that produces an increased demand for the class.

484 (ultra-long-range configuration) to 615 (two-class configuration, being reworked) across four configurations.

Main deck: 21 feet 7 inches (6.58 m). Upper deck: 19 feet 5 inches (5.92 m)

The table above shows the specifications for Emirates' A380s, making use of Emirates' data. Emirates has produced a 'halo effect' around its A380, where one product, the chance to fly on the world's biggest airliner, produces interest in the entire brand. Moreover, the enormous size of Emirates' A380 fleet means it is widely available for people flying long-haul to Dubai, which also generates a consistent experience when flying with the airline.

Food is where Singapore Airlines gets closest to Emirates in the quality of its premium economy product. Passengers flying over 90 minutes can make use of the 'Book the Cook' service, which is also available in Suites, first class, and business class. It allows passengers to pre-select a restaurant-quality meal between six weeks and 24 hours before their flight.

The exact menu will vary depending on the flight that you are on. However, main courses include the lamb ragout, herb-crusted sea bass, and beef bourguignon, along with a range of traditional Singaporean options. Emirates' dining is also of excellent quality, mirroring what the carrier offers business class passengers. For example, you'll be able to try wines that have been pulled from the business-class cellar, including sparkling Chandon.

Food is served on Royal Doulton china tableware with stainless steel cutlery, a luxury step up from the plastic available in economy class. As with Singapore Airlines, the exact menu will vary depending on the flight that you are on. However, Emirates has produced a sample menu to give an impression of what you'll be able to get. Dinner on this menu begins with an antipasti salad, followed by a choice of grilled chicken or Thai pepper beef, with coconut sago pudding for dessert.

Passengers flying on Emirates A380 premium economy class can use its award-winning Information, Communication, and Entertainment (ICE) system. You'll have an enormous library of TV shows, music, games, and movies to choose from on the 13.3-inch (33.8 cm) touchscreen. The airline also provides passengers with noise-canceling headphones, so you can focus on your movie without being distracted by surrounding passengers.

If you can't find anything on the ICE screen to your liking, Emirates also offers WiFi, although you will need to pay extra unless you are an Emirates Skywards Platinum member. Fees range from $2.99 to $19.99 depending on your flight duration and the level of WiFi access you want, from text-only services to full connectivity. The service is provided via Starlink satellites.

The A380 has particularly high-speed Wi-Fi, fast enough for streaming, calling friends, and social media. Emirates describes it as "ground quality." However, it is not totally unrestricted, with Emirates saying that "due to limited bandwidth and satellite data cost, media streaming and some sync services are restricted. Available bandwidth is optimised to provide a better or fairer experience for everyone."

Singapore Airlines also keeps its premium economy passengers entertained through its KrisWorld system, accessible through a 13.3-inch (33.8 cm) touchscreen, with passengers being given noise-canceling headphones. There is a choice of 1,800 movies, television shows, music, games, and more.

You'll find the latest Hollywood movies and iconic comedy series like Friends. Internet connectivity is also available on selected flights. While Emirates offers a unique structural advantage on the A380, its entertainment remains competitive with that of other high-end carriers.

The largest commercial passenger aircraft ever developed is an outlier within the contemporary aviation sector, which is increasingly moving towards smaller and hyper-efficient twinjets, like the Airbus A350, for long-haul flying. Such aircraft make point-to-point aviation possible, whereas the A380 is restricted to the usually obsolete hub-and-spoke model, as it can only serve the world's largest airports.

Emirates will continue to buck this trend, using the aircraft to prioritize capacity and premium products above all else. It flies it to the world's most popular destinations from Dubai, which often have slot restrictions. The size of the aircraft means Emirates could increase its network capacity without having to acquire huge numbers of new slots at immense cost.

Emirates has now built a network of trunk routes to Australasia, North America and Europe. It has put its money where its mouth is with the A380 in recent years, indicating that it hopes to keep flying the aircraft for many years to come. The airline is currently amid a multi-year modernization project.

It has said it is investing $5 billion to refurbish 219 of its aircraft, 110 of which will be A380s. The airline will enter the next phase of onboard upgrades in August 2026, including WiFi connectivity improvements, new cabin features, and an in-flight entertainment upgrade.

#6156. Hotel Guests Report Mold And Mice—It Still Passed Inspection The Next Day

A mother says mice crawled across her sleeping three-year-old at a Wyndham hotel near the Albany, New York airport. Other residents reported mold, cockroaches and soaked carpets. The hotel passed a county health inspection the next day even though the inspector recorded six violations. The rooms with violations weren’t occupied on the day the inspector arrived and were supposed to be repaired before being rented. We trust hotels to do some very basic things: Change the sheets Clean the bathroom Make sure the door locks And the brand on the hotel is supposed to give you confidence! Baymont by Wyndham Latham Albany Airport markets rooms to travelers. It also houses people placed by county social services. That’s often a good indication… One woman, staying with her nine month old daughter, described cockroaches, mice, mold and bedbugs in some rooms. Other residents described wet carpets and a strong smell. A guest said she’d filmed mice crawling over her sleeping child and had stopped letting the girl sleep in her own bed. There were complaints about mouse droppings and dead flies on a bed, and mold and dead flies in a refrigerator. The County moved some social service clients. Another county with one room there relocated their client as a precaution and suspended use of the hotel. What The Inspection Found Albany County inspected the hotel October 13, finding no public health hazards, but six violations: A removed smoke detector. Three exterior doors that didn’t self-latch. A stained bathroom ceiling tile. Evidence of pests in a room. The plan to fix the rooms before renting them helps explain how the hotel could continue operating, though a missing smoke detector matters even in an empty room. And it seems to me that pests in one room can easily spread. There were earlier maintenance concerns, too. A March 13, 2025 entry in New York’s inspection database notes water stains and possible active leaks at this property. You’re Supposed To Be Able To Rely On A Brand A big part of what a hotel brand sells is confidence that somebody has vetted the property. You know what you’re getting. The hotel may be franchised but it’s supposed to deliver to brand standards. Years ago I covered an Inside Edition investigation that found three of nine hotels tested hadn’t provided completely fresh sheets between guests. The beds were re-made with the previous guest’s used sheets. Then came pandemic promises of enhanced cleaning. Inside Edition went back in 2020, using washable marks visible under ultraviolet light. It reported unchanged bedding at a Hyatt Place and a Hampton Inn in Times Square. At Trump International, the sheets had been changed, but the report said a pillowcase hadn’t. More recently, I covered a Hyatt Place guest who went through three rooms and still wound up with filthy bedding. Hyatt refunded the stay and provided 15,000 points. You’re not supposed to have to even check recent reviews and traveler photos, and pull back the bedding immediately on arrival. I Wouldn’t Let An Airline Choose Where I Sleep, Either I’ve made the same argument about hotels airlines provide during overnight delays. I’ve reported on roaches, floors was so dirty they turned guests’ feet black, and worse. Airlines offering lowest-cost rooms aren’t necessarily delvering places you’d ever want to stay. #6155. Denver Air Connection Plans First Florida Service

Denver Air Connection will launch its first-ever service to Florida, and it will be outside the scope of any Essential Air Service (EAS) contract. The only other place in the carrier’s network that isn’t directly part of an EAS contract is its service to Telluride, Colorado, from both Denver and Phoenix.

Beginning January 9, 2027, DAC will begin nonstop flights from Muskegon, Michigan, to Orlando Sanford, with service operating on Saturdays using the 50-seat Embraer E145XR.

While Muskegon itself only has one other destination, Chicago O’Hare, which is also operated by DAC under the EAS contract, DAC will compete indirectly with Allegiant, as it has a sizable operation and a base in Grand Rapids, Michigan, which is located only about 45 minutes east of Muskegon.

The 1,030-mile route from Muskegon to Orlando Sanford on the E145 will become the longest at-risk flight operated by any EAS carrier, and one of the longest commercial airline flights operated by an Embraer E145 in the country, overtaking the current record holder, United’s 830-mile route from Washington Dulles to Mobile, Alabama, by almost 200 miles.

That record for the E145 is a little bit of a technicality, as JSX does operate a handful of flights over 1,000 miles with its Embraer E145s, but the carrier is not considered a commercial airline, and is instead classified as a “public charter operation.”

Muskegon Airport director Ken Efting did have something to say about this new service: “This is a historic milestone for MKG and the communities we serve…This is exactly the kind of opportunity we’ve been working toward, and it’s a testament to our growing community support and strong partnership with Denver Air Connection.”

This isn’t the first time an EAS carrier has operated at-risk service to the state of Florida from an EAS community. These smaller carriers sometimes begin flights to leisure destinations like Florida and other leisure-heavy destinations to entice higher passenger numbers that boost the communities they serve.

Muskegon will join the small but growing list of Essential Air Service communities that are now connected with nonstop flights to the state of Florida, but they will be the only EAS community in Michigan to have Florida flights.

#6154. Belavia Can Once Again Do Business With Boeing, As US Lifts Sanctions On Belarus

Belarusian national carrier Belavia has faced sanctions from the United States and European Union for quite some time, due to a combination of the “hijacking” of a Ryanair flight, along with the country’s support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Well, if Belarusian media is to be believed, these sanctions are now being lifted, so the country’s airline can once again buy planes from Boeing…

Belarusian state owned national news agency BelTA is reporting that the United States Department of Commerce has granted Boeing a license to resume full cooperation with Belavia. This was announced by Valentin Rybakov, the Belarusian representative to the United Nations. If true, this means that Belavia can once again purchase planes and parts directly from Boeing.

This all seems to be related to a visit to Belarus by an American delegation in September, where the country’s president, Alexander Lukashenko, met with US Special Envoy John Cole. This meeting included a larger lifting of sanctions. It also comes at a time when we’re seeing the Trump administration increasingly lifting sanctions on Russia in relation to the invasion of Ukraine.

In 2021, the United States imposed sanctions on Belarus, after the country engaged in what was referred to as a state sponsored hijacking. A Ryanair Boeing 737 was flying between Greece and Lithuania, and as the plane approached Belarusian airspace, an air traffic controller claimed there was a bomb onboard, and that the plane needed to divert to Belarus.

As it turned out, an opponent of the Belarusian government was onboard, so the real motive with this was to have him arrested. Obviously this violates all sorts of international laws and aviation treaties, which is why action was taken against the country. Then in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, additional sanctions were imposed against Belarus, given its support for Russia.

Obviously having sanctions imposed on you by both the United States and European Union makes it challenging to buy new aircraft, given the aircraft manufacturing duopoly we have (unless you consider the aircraft manufacturers in China and Russia to be competitors).

So most of Belavia’s aircraft acquisitions in recent times have been smuggled into the country using shady middlemen. For example, in 2025, Belavia acquired Airbus A330s through an imaginary Gambian airline, as one does.

Belavia can reportedly once again buy aircraft and parts from Boeing, after the United States lifted sanctions that were imposed around five years ago, when the country hijacked a Ryanair plane. This easing of sanctions comes as part of a larger reversal by the Trump administration, as it takes less of a stance against Russia and Belarus.

It’ll be interesting to see what comes of this, and if Belarus places some big Boeing aircraft order in the near future…

What do you make of the US lifting sanctions on Belarus on the airline front?

#6153. Ryanair Weighs Fare Hikes, Pay Freeze As Fuel Prices Soar

Irish discount carrier Ryanair is bracing for a difficult 2027 as jet fuel prices rise and European oil hedges expire.

In its most recent earnings report, the airline said it is considering temporarily freezing pay for workers, lowering crew ratios, and ramping up use of artificial intelligence. The company did not specify how long it would look to freeze wages, or how it would adjust staffing.

Ryanair has over 27,000 employees across its group.

Speaking to CNBC on Monday, Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said ticket prices will rise across Europe as lower-price oil hedges run out.

“The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months,” O’Leary said. “But those hedges are rolling off. There’s still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we’re all facing next year. I believe you’re going to see air fares rise next year across Europe by 10 percent, maybe even 20 percent.”

In its earnings report, Ryanair said that while short-haul air fares will increase “materially,” it will not be enough to offset the expected €2 billion increase in fuel costs, necessitating the additional cost-saving measures.

Fuel prices have prompted several major European airlines and airline groups to cut capacity this fall and winter, and to retire some older, less efficient aircraft. Price volatility also pushed Lufthansa to accelerate the shutdown of Lufthansa CityLine, and made the U.K.’s EasyJet amenable to a roughly $7.7 billion takeover by Apollo Global Management.

The price shock has generally been worse in Europe and Asia than in North America, as those regions are more dependent on Gulf oil and lack domestic refining capacity.

#6152. Passenger Says Delta Flight Attendant Photographed Her Sleeping—‘You Might See It On Facebook’

Tasia Jewel had just arrived in Mexico City and checked into her hotel when she shared the story. She’d been at the Formula One race in Austin, stayed in Texas rather than going home, and was exhausted. She slept for about an hour and a half or so on the roughly three-hour flight.

Then she got to the aircraft door. She says three or four male flight attendants were standing there saying goodbye to passengers. One told her:

Hey, yo friend, I took a picture of you while you were sleeping.

She says the other crewmembers laughed with one adding, “Yeah, she was knocked out.” And the first flight attendant repeated, “You might see it on Facebook.”

Here’s her account, flagged by Paddle Your Own Kanoo:

The woman acknowledges he could have been joking. She also says she hadn’t spoken to him at all on the flight.

My first reaction was that, while Delta has built up its Austin flying, they don’t actually operated Austin – Mexico City. But in a follow-up video she says she flew from Dallas to Atlanta to Mexico City with the flight in question being Delta 602. She says she chose Delta’s Boeing 757 because she didn’t want the Aeromexico Boeing 737 MAX.

And she reports that Delta responded well to her complaint. Her original video caption said she’d filed a complaint. In later replies, she reports a phone call, an apology and an investigation. I guess what matters here was whether there was a fundamental breach or a bad joke. Either way, she says she felt unsafe.

I’ve written about a sleeping passenger who said a man photographed her, where the crew intervened and police met the flight. Here, the person allegedly taking the photos was an employee she was supposed to go to for help.

And last year I covered a flight attendant who caught a passenger secretly filming her and sending her image to someone else. It’s easy to understand why that bothered her. But a passenger can have the same objection when the roles are reversed.

I don’t want a ban on taking pictures inside an aircraft. Passengers need to be able to document how they’re treated. Delta’s customer photography guidance recognizes that people take photos and videos, while asking them to avoid interfering with safety and to be “respectful in your intent” when including employees. Employees ought to show customers that same consideration.

Oh look, another fat ugly woman trying so hard to achieve victimhood status. Omg you got photographed? I can’t imagine a bigger tragedy anywhere in the world.

@Mantis — So, inadvertently, you’re defending the flight attendant? Huh.

(When faced with the choice of punching-down on the worker, or a black woman, we see where your animus really lies…)

Gary, you see that SNL bit on Delta Disruptive?

I would happily punch down on you, retard. But as someone who isn’t retarded, I always assume that people claiming victimhood status on SM with no actual evidence, no witnesses, no proof, and no damages, are just attention seeking terrible people. And then when I see that they are ugly and fat, I use my brain and dismiss the allegations completely. Haven’t you learned yet that these unverified 1st person accounts are almost always false? Oh yeah, I forgot about your disability.

But I wish you wouldn’t give these fools airtime.

It is exactly what they crave – and makes other fools like them think ‘oh, I want my five minutes of fame too – what can I accuse someone of and make a massive deal out of it’?

A passenger has every right to be annoyed if they are photographed without consent. The laws vary from state to state regarding photography in a public place. The US flag carriers are technically “private property” and operate by the carrier’s rules. The flight attendant was not only wrong to photograph the passenger without consent, but was stupid to say that the photo would be posted. IF, INDEED, THE WHOLE SCENARIO IS TRUE! Most likely, since it was noted that the attendant was a male, he was looking for a little “night action”. Fundamental breech or bad joke aside, if true…STUPID. Delta should investigate and, if the attendant was violating company policy, terminated. The younger generation employees at many companies have not been taught manners and “common sense” while growing up. This is partially due to parental and school neglect. Ignorance about something can be corrected. STUPID…forever!

Oh, and “Mantis”…my gawd, is there something wrong with you? YIKES. I’d say more like, “Preying” Mantis would fit the bill.

@Win Whitmire — Yeah, classic @Mantis. (He said he’s going for the It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia character, Dr. Mantis Toboggan, the drunk. Eh.)

I am having trouble understanding why a flight attendant would photograph sleeping passengers. I mean, they see thousands every week. In one year, they could put most likely put 10K+ such pictures.

Circling back to previous blog entries, flight attendants according to a lawsuit say they see people masturbating all the time.

I just did a Google search for “celebrities that claim they had sex on the plane.” The list is long. In fact, according to Google AI, Gwyneth Paltrow “Shared that she once had sex in an airplane bathroom during an overnight flight to Paris.” Yet, this flight attendant is going to photograph a sleeping passenger. I find it hard to believe.

For example, hypothetically, suppose she said “I was out cold”. Then he said, “No worries, I didn’t take a picture and it is not on facebook.” My hypothetical sounds more likely.

OK, gentlemen. I originally thought it was a pain to have to read political comments on a travel site. I’m here for the aviation/travel perspective. I do miss world travel for the government. Eventually I got over it and just accepted Gary’s regular cast of characters. But now, you’re talking about some person somebody deemed “fat and ugly.”

In my past lives, in one part, I might have been able to put such an obnoxious person in jail. And in the other part, well, let’s say “they didn’t make it, Sir.”

#6151. Transfer Amex Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 30% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just launched a new 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While Flying Club is in some ways a niche program, this is a deal that has the potential to offer outsized value, and I’m sure it will interest many people. I’d probably speculatively take advantage of this, except for the fact that I moved a bunch of points last year when there was a 40% transfer bonus.

Between November 2 and November 30, 2026, the American Express Membership Rewards program in the United States is offering a 30% bonus on points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,300 Flying Club points for every 1,000 Membership Rewards points transferred. Transfers are generally instant.

For context, Amex seems to offer a transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club once or twice per year. The last promotion we saw was over the summer, and this is the second offer so far in 2026. When we do see these offers, they’re typically in the range of 30-40%, so this is on the low side of that range, but could still represent a great deal.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

In late 2024 we saw Flying Club introduce dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. While the changes are a mixed bag, what’s exciting is that on the low end, redemptions are cheaper than ever before. It’s now possible to fly one-way Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and the UK for under 30,000 points, and that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 30% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Amex points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through November 30, 2026, Amex is offering a 30% bonus when you transfer points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is definitely more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 30% bonus, award travel on Virgin Atlantic will be an even better value. There’s also lots of value to booking on partners, ranging from SkyTeam airlines, to Air New Zealand, to All Nippon Airways.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this Amex transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club?
