#6150. United Airlines Threw Away A Damaged 25-Year Airbus A320, But Repaired A Fuselage-Wrinkled Boeing 767 Much Older

Michael Derrer Fuchs & Robin Guess | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

On May 16, 2026, a catering truck at Washington Ronald Reagan National Airport (DCA) hit N470UA, a 25-year-old Airbus A320-200 operated by United Airlines. The vehicle struck the plane's rear fuselage and caused severe damage, enough that it was deemed too expensive to repair. This aircraft had, in fact, recently been refurbished with the United Signature Interior, but still, it was simply too old to justify the investment. As such, the aircraft has stayed in DCA ever since the incident and has been taken apart for scraps.

25 years isn't ancient for an airliner, but N470UA was hardly a sprightly bird either. It's normal to scrap an airliner of this age when it sustains severe damage, given the potential cost of repair. What's unusual about this is the context of an earlier decision to repair a damaged Boeing 767 in 2023. This aircraft, registered as N641UA, suffered severe structural damage after a hard landing and was repaired before being returned to service during the 2024 summer season, despite being 32 years old at the time of the incident.

Planespotters.net shows that United Airlines currently has 1,157 aircraft in its fleet. This is split between 68 Airbus A319-100s, 64 A320-200s, 78 Airbus A321neos, 40 Boeing 737-700s, 141 737-800s, 12 737-900s, 136 737-900ERs, 123 737 MAX 8s, 188 737 MAX 9s, 40 757-200s, 21 757-300s, 37 767-300ERs, 16 767-400ERs, 19 777-200s, 55 777-200ERs, 22 777-300ERs, 12 787-8s, 64 787-9s, and 21 787-10s. Altogether, that's 210 A320 family aircraft, 640 737s, 61 757s, 53 767s, 96 777s, and 97 787s.

On average, the 767-300ERs are the oldest aircraft, at over 30 years old, followed by the airline's 757-200s, at over 29 years old. This is followed by the 737-700s, at 27.6 years, the 777-200s/200ERs at 27.2 years, the A320-200s at 26.7 years, the 737-900s at 25.2 years, the 767-400ERs at 25.1 years, and the A319-100s at 24.7 years. While the Airbuses aren't quite the oldest planes in the fleet, the A319 and A320 are also the only types that United has consistently been retiring in recent years.

United's focus coming out of the pandemic has been on domestic growth as part of the 'United NEXT' strategy. As part of this, the airline is taking delivery of a large number of Boeing 737 MAX aircraft (having ordered 514 in total, including some before the strategy was implemented) and 210 Airbus A321neos. The smaller Airbuses, as the oldest narrowbodies in the fleet, are the primary types being replaced by the new narrowbodies, while widebody growth has been slower, even as the airline is still being incredibly ambitious abroad.

Repair cost was an important consideration for United Airlines in both cases, as well as the repair cost relative to the plane's value. The other important consideration, however, is opportunity cost. When making these decisions, United had to determine the value of keeping the extra A320 in the fleet and the value of keeping 37 767-300ERs. This is the main reason why N470UA went away, as United ultimately doesn't need an extra A320, while the Boeing 767 is much more strategically important.

Deliveries of 737s and A321neos have picked up in recent years, and the carrier planned to take over 100 new narrowbodies in 2026, which means that United is hardly short of widebodies. In addition, it's fairly easy for the carrier to cover the loss of one aircraft by adjusting schedules within its domestic network. The A320 is also the third-smallest narrowbody in the United mainline fleet, above only the A319 and 737-700, while United has been focusing heavily on upgauging with larger 737 MAX 9s and A321neos.

The widebody fleet is much smaller than the narrowbody fleet, so the loss of one 767 would have a larger impact. In addition, deliveries of widebodies are generally much slower than those of narrowbodies, with United planning to take 20 787s in 2026. Moreover, this is a record yearly delivery rate for the airline; in 2023 and 2024, when N641UA was being repaired, the airline took delivery of just five 787s (the only widebody that it is currently taking).

What was the reason behind the Star Alliance carrier's decision?

United has long had a much larger long-haul network than its competitors, and this remains an advantage for the Chicago-based carrier. Even for United, a carrier taking 20 787s in 2026, widebodies are a scarce resource. What's more, although the 767 is currently United's oldest type and N641UA is the oldest aircraft in the airline's entire fleet, the airline essentially had no replacement for it in 2023. In 2023 and 2024, retiring a 767 would have meant cutting back its growth plans.

In 2024, United only added one new transatlantic destination during the summer, while also moderately increasing frequencies on select transatlantic and transpacific services. It was not a year of massive international growth, mainly because United took only two 787s in early 2023 and only three in 2024, all of which arrived after the summer season. Losing a 767 would have further capped its 2024 schedule, and this would have been a serious problem as transatlantic demand has been growing with strong yields.

United plans to retire its 767-300ER fleet by 2030, as the 787 will eventually replace it. For now, however, the carrier is not focusing on fleet renewal. Instead, United is growing as much as it can and getting as many widebodies as possible. Although the 767 is old and inefficient by today's standards, United's examples feature modern interiors, while these paid-off planes remain effective on transatlantic routes during the summer, when demand is lower.

The Airbus A320, although it is still regarded as a modern airliner, is actually a very old aircraft type today. Within United's fleet, the A320-200 is the airline's third-oldest narrowbody type, behind only the 757-200 and 737-700. However, United has already retired a significant portion of its A320-200 fleet, and the 757-200 plays a very specific role in United's fleet as a premium narrowbody for transcontinental routes and thin transatlantic services. The replacement for the 757 is only just now arriving in the form of the A321XLR and A321neo 'Coastliner'.

The A320-200s are old, and this size of aircraft is also not particularly relevant to United's goals today. The airline only installs 12 first class seats and 150 seats in total on the A320-200, whereas it's overwhelmingly taking delivery of 179-seat 737 MAX 9s and 200-seat A321neos with 20 first class seats as well as significantly more Economy Plus seating. United is all about large narrowbodies today, and the A320-200 is mainly a tool to use while the airline still owns the aircraft, but it is not a core part of its strategy.

United Airlines Domestic Narrowbody Fleet

United has retrofitted a significant number of its A320s with the Signature Interior, which includes seatback screens, mood lighting, and larger overhead bins. However, this is mainly because the airline has been prioritizing the rapid roll-out of the Signature Interior across its fleet to provide a more consistent experience. Within its domestic fleet, the A320-200s and A319-100s are the types furthest from its current vision.

An increasing number of 777-200s are being sent to the desert.

The A320-200 and A319-100 fleets are set to fully exit by 2030, being replaced by the 737 MAX 9, MAX 10, and A321neo. United is primarily retiring its oldest examples as they age out and is not in a hurry to remove either type, because the carrier's first objective with the domestic network is to grow, followed by upgauging. It's unconfirmed what will happen with the similarly aged 737-700s, but the 737-800s and 737-900s are larger and more economical, while the 737-900ERs are relatively young.

On the widebody side, United is, again, focusing on growing its fleet. While it's now taking 787s at a rapid rate, these planes are intended for a different role than the 767s. The latest 787-9s coming in are a special subfleet with a huge Polaris cabin, mainly used to add premium capacity to high-demand destinations, while the displaced aircraft are used for growth. Eventually, however, these aircraft will leave the fleet and the 787 will take their role, although it will be many years before the fleet is fully gone.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

While United has not yet retired any 737NG aircraft and has not announced plans to do so, the 757-200s will be retired within the next few years. To replace these 40 aircraft, United has ordered 50 A321neo Coastliners for transcontinental routes and 50 A321XLRs for European flights, which will send the 757s away once they start arriving in higher numbers. In addition, the carrier will eventually replace its 777-200s and some 777-200ERs with future 787-10 deliveries, although it's unclear what will replace the remaining 777-200ER fleet.

#6149. Airline Passengers Are Getting Scam Emails With Real Confirmation Numbers—Some Frontier Customers Are Entering Credit Card Details

Frontier Airlines passengers are reporting emails from scammers using their real flight details and confirmation numbers, promising refunds or claiming their bookings haven’t been paid for – and telling them to enter their credit card information to complete purchases or confirm return of funds. Frontier reported an active phishing campaign targeting its customers. That doesn’t tell us where the reservation information came from. A reader sent me a refund email that claims a ticketing error caused duplicate taxes and fees and failed to apply a promotional credit. It promises a full refund after the customer confirms the original payment card. The message even supplies an explanation for why an airline that already charged you supposedly needs your card again: Because the settlement batch for this reservation has already closed, our payment system needs the original payment method confirmed so the refund can be routed back to your card. A closed settlement batch ordinarily means the merchant needs to process a refund rather than void the original transaction. In other words, it’s a made up reason meant to sound plausible. These Emails Are Using Real Reservation Details In a Frontier GoWild! Pass Holders discussion, numerous passengers say they received these emails. Several report that the confirmation numbers matched actual bookings. That includes trips already taken and travel still upcoming. One customer says the supposed refund was about five times what they’d paid. Another reports receiving both versions: a refund offer for a completed trip and a warning that payment hadn’t gone through for an upcoming reservation. A separate Reddit discussion reports the payment problem version, with an email that contained real flight information and confirmation number. Passengers report responding with their credit card numbers. One passenger says they tried several other cards before the site accepted the card originally used to book the flight. And of course a rejection message doesn’t mean the site didn’t collect the card number. Frontier Has Disclosed A Database Incident I wrote in July about a breach affecting 11,482 people. Separately, a security researcher reported that a confirmation number and last name could expose sensitive passenger information through Frontier’s systems. There’s also an October 2 notice from Frontier about a security incident involving its customer care database covering information submitted through its customer care form. They changed the database configuration and are ‘improving monitoring’. Security firm VenariX analyzed leaked samples associated with a group claiming Frontier among its victims. They found booking codes, flight numbers and dates, and evidence pointing to overly broad access permissions on Microsoft customer service portals. This Approach Has Been Used Against Hotel And Cruise Customers I’ve covered hotel scams where the sender knows the guest’s reservation details and uses them to demand payment or card verification. Knowing the hotel, dates and guest’s name makes the message much more persuasive. Norwegian Cruise Line customers reported a similar campaign in October, with messages containing real booking information and demanding payment verification. Norwegian issued its own warning. What To Do If You Received One Frontier won’t email asking you to reconfirm a reservation, re-enter card details, or supply payment information to receive a refund. Check the trip through Frontier directly. Open the app or type the airline’s website address yourself. Use contact information obtained there if something looks wrong. If you entered a card, contact its issuer. Lock it while you report the exposure and arrange a replacement. Include every card you tried, even ones the page said it rejected. Don’t assume leaving before clicking Submit protected the information. Web forms can collect what you type before submission. If you supplied a password, change it through the legitimate site. Change it elsewhere if you reused it. Check the reservation. Make sure the itinerary and contact information remain correct. Frontier’s published instructions say a confirmation code and last name can provide access to changes and cancellations, so changing your frequent flyer password may not close that separate route into a booking. Always check the sender information on an email. That can be spoofed but most scammers don’t go to that level of effort. #6148. Are Authorized Users Eligible For Credit Card Bonuses?

Here’s a topic that seems to cause confusion among some people. If you’re an authorized user on someone else’s credit card, are you eligible for the bonus on that card if you apply outright? The answer is actually pretty straightforward, so let me explain…

Credit cards frequently offer huge upfront welcome offers, whereby you can earn a lot of bonus points for spending a certain amount within a limited timeframe. While there are different credit card application rules for each bank, there are generally restrictions whereby an existing cardmember can’t apply for a card they already have, while also receiving the bonus.

How does that work in the context of authorized users? If you’re the authorized user on someone else’s credit card, can you apply for the card as the primary cardmember and earn the bonus? The answer is universally yes — being an authorized user on someone else’s credit card doesn’t preclude you from applying for that card yourself, and earning the bonus.

When welcome bonus rules talk about existing cardmembers, they’re specifically talking about primary cardmembers, and not authorized users.

You don’t even need to cancel your authorized user card to be able to do this. For example, say you’re an authorized user on your spouse’s Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more), or Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more). You could remain an authorized user, and still apply outright and earn the welcome bonus on the card.

For those in relationships, it can sometimes be difficult to decide under which circumstances it makes sense to apply for a card outright, rather than being an authorized user on a spouse’s card (and vice versa). There are pros and cons to each.

The advantage of adding someone as an authorized user is that it minimizes annual fees, since many cards have lower (or no) annual fees for authorized users, compared to the primary cardmembers. Meanwhile the advantages of having both people in a relationship apply for a card outright is that many cards have big welcome bonuses, and on top of that some cards pay for themselves on an ongoing basis.

For more on this topic, see my post on the best credit card strategy for families.

Many credit cards have amazing welcome bonuses, though you’re generally only eligible for them if you don’t already have that card. The good news is that across the board, being an authorized user on someone else’s card still makes you eligible to apply for that card outright and receive the bonus (assuming you’re otherwise eligible for the card).

Therefore this really comes down to deciding for each card whether the economics of applying outright make sense.

Have you ever applied for a credit card on which you’re already an authorized user?

One of the questions people often ask us is, “How much is a point or mile worth?”

The true answer varies from point to point and person to person. It also depends on your travel goals and how much you maximize a particular loyalty currency. Still, some rewards are worth more than others, and our goal is to give you a sense of how they stack up.

Rove has grown from an intriguing newcomer into one of the most valuable transferable rewards programs we track. So, we've decided to add Rove miles to TPG's valuations at 2.05 cents apiece.

That puts Rove on a par with our valuation of Chase Ultimate Rewards points and behind only Bilt Points as the most valuable transferable currencies we track. Using our updated methodology, we considered the value available when redeeming Rove miles, as well as the number and quality of the Rove transfer partners.

Rove now has an impressive 22 transfer partners, including multiple currencies that have traditionally been difficult for U.S. travelers to earn, such as Japan Airlines Mileage Bank and Lufthansa Miles & More. Most transfers are at a 1:1 rate, and the roster also includes TPG favorites Air Canada Aeroplan, Flying Blue, Qantas Frequent Flyer and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Rove miles are also easy to earn without opening a new credit card. Members can collect miles by booking flights and hotels or shopping online. New members who join through TPG can earn 1,500 bonus miles, then earn another 5,000 miles after making their first hotel booking of more than $500 with code "BRIANKELLY500."

#6145. Buy Choice Privileges Points With 40% Bonus (0.74 Cents Each): Worth It?

Choice Privileges is currently offering a promotion on purchased points, offering up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While this isn’t among the best promotions we’ve seen from the program, it’s still better than no bonus, and there are many situations where you could come out ahead.

Let’s take a look at everything you need to know about this deal, and talk about under what circumstances it makes sense to buy Choice Privileges points. I generally recommend buying points only if you have a short term use in mind, and are sure the math checks out.

Link: Buy Choice Privileges points with a bonus

Between 12AM EDT on November 2 and 11:59PM EDT on November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is offering a sale on purchased points. The accounts I manage show a bonus of up to 40%, which is structured as follows:

Different accounts may very well show different offers, so you’ll want to log into your Choice Privileges account to see what you’re eligible for.

Choice Privileges’ pricing when buying points isn’t linear, and you get a lower cost the more points you purchase, not even factoring in any promotional bonuses or discounts. Before factoring in any bonuses or discounts, the cost to purchase points ranges from 1.28 cents per point (if buying just 1,000 points) to 1.03 cents per point (if buying 180,000 points), and that’s inclusive of taxes and fees.

If you maxed out this promotion, you could purchase a total of 252,000 points (180,000 base points, plus 72,000 bonus points) for $1,854, which is a rate of 0.74 cents per Choice Privileges point.

Note that purchased points will post within 24 hours of completing the transaction, and the points earned don’t count toward Choice Privileges elite status.

Choice Privileges lets you purchase up to 180,000 points per account per calendar year, not factoring in any bonus points.

When Choice offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically either a 30-45% discount or a 35-50% bonus. So this 40% bonus is toward the bottom end of that range. Personally, I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Choice Privileges on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Choice Privileges points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t generally count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. There is one exception — if you use a co-branded Choice Privileges credit card, then these purchases are rewarded in the same way as hotel spending.

Otherwise, I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

While it doesn’t get much attention in the miles & points world, Choice is a huge hotel group, with over 7,000 properties in 40 countries, representing roughly 570,000 hotel rooms. Choice hotel brands include (among others) Ascend, Cambria, Comfort Inn, Sleep Inn, Quality Inn, Clarion, Rodeway Inn, and more.

The catch is that Choice doesn’t have that many aspirational properties. In general there’s the most value outright purchasing points if you have a premium redemption in mind, given that this is the best way to get outsized value compared to the cost of a stay if paying cash.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have a formal award chart, but award pricing usually ranges from 6,000 to 45,000 points per night. In Asia-Pacific, some properties cost up to 75,000 points per night.

There are definitely some properties where you’ll get outsized value acquiring Choice Privileges points at a discount. For example, Choice has an impressive footprint in Northern Europe, where hotels can otherwise be expensive when paying cash, especially in summer.

Let me just give some examples, and let’s just keep the math easy, to show redemptions where you’re getting well over one cent of value per point (which is way higher than the acquisition cost here). Generally the key is to travel during peak periods, since that’s when you’ll get the most outsized value from your points.

For example, if you wanted to travel to Tromso, Norway, in December (to see the Northern Lights), I see two properties charging $560-620 per night, when you could book them for 40,000-45,000 points per night, getting you very nicely outsized value.

If you wanted to travel to Stockholm, Sweden, in July (summer is popular!), I see two properties charging $420-580 per night, when you could book them for 25,000-30,000 points per night, getting you excellent value.

For an example closer to home, say you wanted to go to Dunedin, Florida, in March. I see a property charging $730 per night, when you could book it for 40,000 points per night, also getting you hugely outsized value.

Let me be clear — you won’t always find outsized value in this way. For example, say you need to spend a night near LAX, where you’ll see properties charging $102-149 per night, when a points redemption requires 20,000-30,000 points per night. Paying cash is the much better value there.

The key is to travel places during peak periods, where the cash rate would be significantly higher than usual, while the points rate isn’t as elevated.

Here’s a fun redemption option with Choice Privileges points. While Choice doesn’t manage these properties, Choice Privileges has a partnership with Preferred Hotels & Resorts, which is a group of over 500 luxury independent properties around the globe.

You can redeem Choice Privileges points for stays here, and the hotels cost anywhere from 25,000 to 118,000 points per night. You can find participating hotels and award costs here, and nowadays you can even book these awards online. There are some participating hotels where you can get significant value redeeming this way, though the recent devaluation sure doesn’t help.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have blackout dates, and points can be redeemed for stays up to 50 weeks in advance, as long as a standard room is available.

Choice Privileges points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Virtually any activity that involves earning or redeeming points would be considered qualifying for these purposes.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Choice Privileges points to be worth ~0.6 cents each. That’s a conservative valuation, though if you’re strategic you should be able to get lots more value out of your points than that.

Several transferable points currencies have Choice Privileges as a partner:

As you can see, of those transfer partners, Wells Fargo is going to be the most lucrative, followed by Citi, followed by Amex and Capital One.

Through November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is selling points with up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While I wouldn’t recommend speculatively picking up Choice Privileges points at that cost, with a specific and short term use in mind, there could be value with this offer.

Does anyone plan on buying Choice Privileges points?

#6144. Rosewood Beyond Sale: 30% Off Stays, Plus Rosewood Elite Perks

Luxury hotel group Rosewood has just kicked off its best sale of the year, offering savings of up to 30%, and it’s exclusively available through Rosewood Elite travel advisors. If you’ve been considering a stay at a Rosewood, this would be a great time to book.

With the Rosewood Beyond promotion, guests can save 30% off the best available rate when booking a Rosewood property through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. To cover the basics:

In order to take advantage of the Rosewood Beyond sale, you need to book through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. Ford’s team is happy to help with this, and can be reached at [email protected]. Other travel advisors are welcome to leave their contact details in the comments as well.

Let me emphasize that the 30% discount is off the best available rate, otherwise known as the flexible rate. So you couldn’t get this discount on an advance purchase rate, third or fourth night free rate, etc. So in some situations the savings here won’t be that significant, while in other cases they are huge.

While there are of course some restrictions and blackout dates, this is about as no strings attached as promotions get. The 30% off rate also offers the same flexibility as whatever the flexible rate would be, which of course varies by property.

Since the Rosewood Beyond sale is specifically being offered through Rosewood Elite travel advisors, the good news is that these reservations also unlock additional benefits, including the following:

Rosewood is a really high quality hotel brand, and you can find all the hotels here. If you’re looking for a getaway from the United States, it’s tough to beat the Rosewood Mayakoba, the Rosewood Little Dix Bay, the Rosewood Kona Village, Las Ventanas al Paraiso, etc. Rosewood also has lots of great city hotels, ranging from the Rosewood Hong Kong, to the Rosewood Sao Paulo, to The Carlyle New York.

Rosewood has brought back its biggest promotion of the year, offering 30% off the best available rate. This is valid for bookings confirmed November 3-10, 2026, and for stays through June 30, 2027.

Aside from a small list of excluded properties, this is a pretty straightforward offer that gives you the best deal you’ll find on Rosewood stays. You can even stack this with Rosewood Elite perks, to unlock breakfast, a property credit, a room upgrade, and more.

Just keep in mind that the discount is based on the flexible rate, and not based on any promotional rate you can find.

#6143. Capital One Adds New Airline Partner With 30% Bonus—Book Emirates Business Class Without Fuel Surcharges

All of a sudden Panamanian airline Copa is taking U.S. points transfer programs by storm. Did not have that on my 2026 bingo card! Capital One has added Copa Airlines ConnectMiles as a transfer partner, opening another way to book Emirates business class without fuel surcharges. They’re offering a 30% transfer bonus to launch the partnership, too. But even with that bonus, you’ll get fewer Copa miles than Citi and Rove offer at their regular rates. Beginning November 2, Capital One miles transfer to Copa at 2:1.5. That’s 750 ConnectMiles for every 1,000 Capital One miles. The 30% bonus runs through December 1, 2026, bringing the effective rate to 975 ConnectMiles per 1,000 miles transferred. I like seeing Capital One expand its partner list again. They haven’t done so in a year! I just wish they weren’t quite so tight with the transfer ratio. Citi Added Copa Last Week, Following Rove I covered Rove adding Copa on September 1. Their regular transfer rate is 1:1, and they launched with a 40% bonus through September 30. That meant 1,000 Rove miles became 1,400 Copa miles. Then Citi added ConnectMiles on October 25: Citi Strata Elite, Strata Premier, Prestige and AT&T Access More cardholders receive 1,000 Copa miles per 1,000 ThankYou points. Other eligible ThankYou cards, including the no annual fee Citi Strata, Double Cash and Custom Cash cards, transfer 1,000 points to 700 Copa miles. Here’s how the three programs compare today: Transfer From Copa Miles Per 1,000 Points Rove 1,000 Citi, with an eligible premium card 1,000 Citi, other eligible cards 700 Capital One, regular rate 750 Capital One, with 30% bonus through December 1 975 Capital One’s bonus nearly gets you to 1:1. Transfer 10,000 Capital One miles and receive 9,750 Copa miles during the promotion. Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Copa at 3:1, with the usual 5,000-mile bonus for transferring 60,000 points. That’s 25,000 Copa miles for 60,000 Marriott points. When Rove added Copa, I liked having access to a program that the big U.S. bank currencies didn’t offer. Two months later, Citi and Capital One have followed. Rove’s 40% launch bonus is over, but their ordinary rate still beats Capital One’s promotional rate. The Value In Copa Miles Transfers Copa is a Star Alliance airline based in Panama. Its miles can book United Airlines and other alliance partners, but the redemption I flagged in September was Emirates. Emirates business class from the U.S. to Dubai for 80,000 miles one way, without carrier-imposed surcharges. Taxes and other applicable fees apply. United Airlines premium transcontinental business class for 25,000 miles one way when saver award space is available to Copa. Copa economy awards starting at 15,000 miles one way from its North America 1 region to Panama, Central America, parts of the Caribbean and northern South America. Capital One Now Has 23 Transfer Partners Capital One’s last additions were Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and I Prefer Hotel Rewards on September 23, 2025. It’s been more than a year, so it’s good to see them adding another option. Here’s the complete current list. These are the standard transfer ratios, before temporary bonuses, expressed as Capital One miles to partner miles or points. Transfer Partner Standard Ratio Aeromexico Rewards 1:1 Air Canada Aeroplan 1:1 Air France-KLM Flying Blue 1:1 Avianca LifeMiles 1:1 British Airways Club 1:1 Cathay Pacific Asia Miles 1:1 Copa Airlines ConnectMiles 2:1.5 Emirates Skywards 2:1.5 Etihad Guest 1:1 EVA Air Infinity MileageLands 2:1.5 Finnair Plus 1:1 Japan Airlines Mileage Bank 2:1.5 JetBlue TrueBlue 5:3 Qantas Frequent Flyer 1:1 Qatar Airways Privilege Club 1:1 Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer 1:1 TAP Air Portugal Miles&Go 1:1 Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles 1:1 Virgin Red 1:1 Accor Live Limitless 2:1 Choice Privileges 1:1 I Prefer Hotel Rewards 1:2 Wyndham Rewards 1:1 Capital One manages the economics of its rewards program tightly. They give you 750 Japan Airlines miles per 1,000 Capital One miles, and half as many I Prefer points as Citi offers with its premium cards. Copa is another useful partner, but with a less generous conversion rate. At the regular Copa ratio, earning 2 Capital One miles per dollar on Venture X spending means earning 1.5 Copa miles per dollar. Citi Double Cash earns 2 ThankYou points per dollar on purchases as you buy and pay, and pairing it with an eligible premium ThankYou card gets you 2 Copa miles per dollar. #6142. British Airways Axes 6 Boeing 787 Routes From Heathrow: See Full List Now

All of British Airways' Boeing 787s are currently deployed from London Heathrow Airport (LHR), although 787-10s will eventually operate from London Gatwick. In 2026, the oneworld member pulled the so-called Dreamliner, to use the manufacturer's moniker, from five routes from LHR, with a sixth ending soon.

Few airlines operate all three variants of the 787, but BA is one of them. Ch-aviation shows that the airline has 43 examples of the type: 18 787-9s (215 and 216 seats), 13 787-10s (256 seats), and 12 787-8s (204 seats). The latter variant, with relatively few seats and a less premium configuration, will play an important role in growing BA's future US network to smaller cities.

The UK flag carrier's Dreamliner network from LHR for January to October 2026 was compared to what's scheduled from November onwards. This process identified that the following five routes from the UK's busiest airport have stopped seeing the type. Three have simply switched to other equipment, while one market has been suspended and another has ended completely.

Stopped Seeing The 787 On Which Date (From LHR)?

What Equipment Now Operates (November 2026-October 2027)?

None, as the route is currently suspended. Theoretically set to return next winter, but that remains to be seen. BA's schedule currently extends to October 31, 2027, with no sign of Abu Dhabi yet. That could easily change.

A350-1000 and 777-200ER (from March 2027)

A350-1000, 777-200ER (from March 2027), and 777-300ER (January-March 2027)

Obviously, aircraft deliveries, along with freed-up aircraft, mean the destinations to which they are deployed change. For example, BA started flying the Dreamliner on the very short service from LHR to Madrid in late October 2026, primarily for freight purposes in partnership with Iberia to South America.

Last month was also when the type operated new routes from LHR to San Jose, Costa Rica, and Tampa, along with returning to Johannesburg, with the equipment last used there in March 2024. Most significantly, BA will fly the 787-9 to Melbourne via Kuala Lumpur in January 2027, with a daily operation.

Then there's Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), from which it is usually quicker to reach Manhattan than from New York JFK. BA has two daily flights from LHR to EWR. Until November 7, the 235-seat 777-200ER and 256-seat 787-10 each operate daily. However, things will then change.

Between November 8 and 10, the 777-200ER will coexist with the 258-seat 777-300ER, before the 787-10 reappears between November 11 and 14. The changes continue thereafter, with the only constant being the presence of the 777-200ER. The Dreamliner's penultimate operation is down for November 20, before the variant reappears on November 30. No 787 flights are currently scheduled beyond then, but that could change.

United Airlines has overtaken ANA as the world's largest Boeing 787 operator, with further Dreamliner expansion planned.

Let's narrow the focus from December 2026 until October 2027. As of November 3, the latest information shows that BA's 787s are collectively scheduled to fly from LHR to 46 destinations. Obviously, some places will only see the equipment at certain times. They include service on the 787-9 to Doha, a route that exists in partnership with Qatar Airways, at the end of next October, along with just six departures on the 787-8 and 787-9 to Nashville next March.

In the examined period, all these places will see BA's Dreamliners, whether regularly, seasonally, irregularly, or otherwise. They are Bahrain, Baltimore, Barbados, Bengaluru, Boston, Cape Town, Chennai, Chicago, Cincinnati, Dallas, Delhi, Denver, Doha, Dubai (flights resumed on November 3), Houston, Hyderabad, Johannesburg, Kuala Lumpur, and Lagos.

Then there's the short hop to Madrid, along with Malé, Melbourne (via Kuala Lumpur), Mexico City, Miami, Montreal, Mumbai, Nairobi, Nashville, New Orleans, New York JFK, Pittsburgh, Portland, Rio de Janeiro, Riyadh, St. Louis, San Francisco, San Jose, Santiago, Seattle, Shanghai, Singapore, Sydney (via Singapore), Tampa, Tokyo Haneda, Toronto, and Washington Dulles.

Transfer bonuses can offer lucrative opportunities to help you maximize your points and miles and work your way toward fantastic award redemptions. You can sometimes get significantly more value from your rewards by transferring them to an airline or hotel partner during one of these bonus periods.

Remember, though, that these are limited-time offers: You’ll need to act fast if you find one that suits your travel plans.

We’ve compiled transfer bonus updates for most major programs with transferable rewards to make it easier to track these offers. Just note that transfer bonuses are sometimes targeted, so some may not be available to you.

We only recommend transferring points or miles if you have a short-term plan to use them. Transfers are irreversible, and you don’t want to be stuck with thousands of points or miles in a program you have little use for.

If you don’t have a specific redemption in mind but still want to earn points or miles, you’re likely better off earning rewards through card welcome bonuses and everyday spending.

We always recommend verifying award availability before transferring your rewards.

When a program with a transferable currency offers a transfer bonus, it’s important to run the numbers to determine whether it is worthwhile.

Generally, you won’t want to transfer your points or miles unless you have a specific redemption in mind. After all, a large part of the value of transferable points and miles comes from their flexibility, which you’ll give up when you convert them to a partner’s currency. However, a transfer bonus can help you get more value from your points and miles if you frequently use a partner program or plan to redeem them soon.

#6140. New Cathay Pacific “Halo Suites” First Class For Boeing 777-9s

In late 2024, Cathay Pacific unveiled its new Aria Suites business class, which is progressively being introduced on the carrier’s Boeing 777-300ER fleet. While we know Cathay Pacific is introducing a new first class product, it’ll take some time before we see that in service.

In light of everything going on — the introduction of Cathay Pacific’s new business class, the delays to the Boeing 777X, the products being introduced by competitors, etc. — I’d like to cover the latest when it comes to Cathay Pacific’s new first class.

We’ve known for years that Cathay Pacific plans to introduce new first and business class products on its Boeing 777-9s. The airline has 35 of these aircraft on order, and they’re expected to become the carrier’s flagship aircraft.

Note that not all Cathay Pacific 777-9s are expected to get first class. The expectation is that somewhere around 20 of them will feature the cabin, while the remaining will feature business class, premium economy, and economy.

Initially the aircraft was supposed to enter service as of 2020, though due to delays stemming from a variety of reasons, the plane is now slated to be delivered in 2027 at the earliest.

Many airlines were planning on introducing new “flagship” products on their 777-9s, though the seven year delay has obviously not been ideal for that, and has caused many airlines to fall behind with their premium products. I would imagine that Cathay Pacific was planning on debuting its new business class on 777-9s, but now decided to install it on 777-300ERs.

While Cathay Pacific has moved forward with introducing its new business class, the airline only plans to introduce a new first class as of 2027, on Boeing 777-9s. Understandably, one major concern here is when 777-9s will actually enter service for Cathay Pacific.

At this point, the aircraft will enter commercial service in the second half of 2027 at the absolute earliest, and Cathay Pacific isn’t even the launch customer. So it could very well be 2028 before we see the first Cathay Pacific 777-9.

In 2023, Cathay Pacific applied for a trademark for “The Aria Suites,” which is the carrier’s new business class. The airline also applied for a trademark for “The Halo Suites,” and this is specifically intended to cover “luxury and first class air transportation services.”

For what it’s worth, the two patents were filed just a few weeks apart. While we can’t say anything with certainty, I’d be willing to bet with that this will in fact be the name of Cathay Pacific’s new first class product.

We know that Cathay Pacific has been working on developing its new first class product for many years (it was supposed to be ready in 2020, based on the initial Boeing 777-9 delivery timeline). We also know that Cathay Pacific is planning something truly spectacular. However, there hasn’t been any official indication as to what we can expect (though rumor has it that we could get a “tease” in the coming months).

Back in 2019, Cathay Pacific applied for a patent for a new first class product, and… wow! Let me emphasize that I can’t guarantee this will be Cathay Pacific’s new first class, though I think it’s very possible. I’d highly recommend reading the whole application, as it actually contains a couple of different concepts.

Below is the diagram that’s displayed, and if I’m understanding this correctly, the plan is that figures five through eight reflect what Cathay Pacific is hoping to offer.

This appears to be based on Paperclip Design’s Peacock Suites concept. The below pictures should give you a sense of just how spectacular this product might be (though I’d expect Cathay Pacific to have a customized version of this, so don’t expect it to be exactly like this).

This product looks absolutely wild, and I’m in disbelief that we could see anything like this introduced. It almost looks more like The Etihad Residence than a standard first class product. Heck, it almost looks more like what you’d expect on a private jet.

A couple of years back, former Cathay Pacific Chairman Patrick Healy has called the new product “mindblowing,” and “a really, really special product and very impressive.”

This would likely blow away the best first class products in the world, like Air France’s 777 first class, Emirates’ 777 first class, and Japan Airlines’ A350 first class. In terms of other first class products on the horizon, we know that Singapore Airlines will be unveiling a new first class shortly, and Qatar Airways is working on a new first class, but it’s not a sure bet yet.

Due to ongoing delivery delays with the Boeing 777-9, the carrier’s plan to transition its fleet is proving to be anything but straightforward.

Cathay Pacific is currently retrofitting its 777-300ER fleet with the new Aria Suites business class. As the airline retrofits its 777-300ERs, it’s also removing first class from those planes (assuming they have them). We’re seeing a combination of three-cabin aircraft reconfigured (with business class, premium economy, and economy), along with some four-cabin aircraft (with first class).

At this point, Cathay Pacific has just six planes remaining with first class. In the past, the airline has acknowledged that it may hold off on reconfiguring some jets, so that it can maintain even a small fleet with first class seats, for markets where it’s really needed. However, with the extent of the delays, one wonders if Cathay Pacific really wants to put the fleet retrofit project on hold, just to preserve a few dozen first class seats.

Cathay Pacific’s first class is an excellent, spacious product. While this isn’t the world’s most private first class, it is one of my favorites. On top of that, the soft product is very good.

Cathay Pacific plans to introduce a new first class product, though only on the 777-9, and not on the 777-300ER. You can expect this product to be introduced as of late 2027 at the earliest, assuming the Boeing 777X actually gets certified (that’s a big “if”).

Based on some filings, it would appear that Cathay Pacific will name its new first class “The Halo Suites,” and some diagrams suggest that this will be an unbelievably good product. I can’t wait to learn more. Rumor has it that we could get our first official tease of this product in the coming months, though who knows, that may be delayed yet again.

What do you make of what we know about Cathay Pacific’s new first class?

#6139. American Airlines Philadelphia Flagship Lounge Expected To Double In Size, Taking Over The Admirals Club Next Door

American Airlines’ gorgeous Philadelphia Flagship Lounge may finally get the space it should have had from the start. Lounge staff are reportedly telling passengers it’ll take over the Admirals Club next door around March 2027, essentially doubling the size of the business class lounge before next summer’s transatlantic seasonal peak. That’s the change I called for when the lounge opened. But there’s a potential problem for Admirals Club members since there’s no announced replacement for the club they’d lose. A passenger reports being told by the employee managing Flagship lounge entry that it would expand into the adjoining A West Admirals Club “sometime around next March.” Another commenter says an agent separately told them about expanding to the whole floor (which is the same thing), after they gave up on finding a seat in Flagship and went next door. Officially, an American Airlines spokesperson tells me: Nothing set in stone right now, but we are always evaluating how we can best serve our customers during the summer peak next year. In my original review, I showed the connector behind the check-in desk. There’s already ‘swing space’ that can be opened to either lounge. During my visit it was part of Flagship. These are adjoining spaces with the same beautiful design, and they’re already connected. The dimensions of the spaces are: Flagship: 12,500 square feet, with 200 seats. Admirals Club: 11,000 square feet, with 181 seats. Additional flex space: 1,364 square feet. That’s nearly 25,000 square feet across the complex. Moving the Admirals Club space into Flagship would roughly double its footprint. I quite like this lounge. In the morning and early afternoon, it’s a lovely place to spend time. The trouble comes before the bank of transatlantic departures, when the passengers it’s supposed to serve all arrive at once. A business class lounge needs enough seats for people flying business class. And in the summer from Philadelphia that total grows quite a lot with American’s seasonal services. Things are even worse now that the A West terminal has lost the American Express Centurion Lounge for expansion into the British Airways lounge space, expecting to reopen by the end of 2027. I’ve covered the project taking over the British Airways lounge space below. The British Airways lounge is closed, too. I actually think Flagship was already better than both lounges. It’s just crowded (but not as cramped as Centurion was!). American has been investing more in lounge food. At Dallas recently, I found a better buffet, staffed charcuterie and food ordered by QR code that arrived at my table in four minutes. Philadelphia helped introduce that ordering system, coming after the Soho lounge at JFK which is shared with BA. Philadelphia wasn’t built with a separate Flagship Dining room. Those are operating in Dallas and Miami, and I broke the news that Los Angeles reopens this week. Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has talked about rethinking Flagship. Delta was the last of the big three to introduce a separate business class lounge, and I think Delta One lounges now offer the strongest overall product. American’s access rules are much more generous, including eligible elites flying coach on qualifying international trips and oneworld Sapphire and Emerald members from programs other than American and Alaska even on domestic itineraries. That makes having enough space especially important. American had an Admirals Club in A East. They closed it when these lounges opened in May 2025. I argued then that they should keep A East for Admirals Club members and dedicate A West entirely to Flagship. Under the reported plan, the nearest Admirals Club would instead be B/C. Someone paying for a membership, or carrying the Citi Executive card, would lose access to the beautiful A West club without gaining access to the larger Flagship Lounge. American should take back the A East space as well. #6138. Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card Amex Offers Deal: Save $200 On $900+ Flight

The Amex Offers program frequently offers promotions that can save you money on flights, hotel stays, etc. There’s a new Amex Offers deal that seems to be specific to one co-branded Marriott card, and it’s incredibly lucrative.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) seems to have a new targeted Amex Offers deal whereby you can earn $200 back when you spend $900+ on airfare.

This is really straightforward — targeted members just need to register for the Amex Offers deal, and then spend $900+ across one or more transactions by February 28, 2027.

You can reach that spending threshold through one or more qualifying purchases, and the flights need to be booked directly with airlines (so not through a third party). There are no restrictions as to which airline you can book through, so you can use this both for US and foreign carriers, which is awesome.

Officially Amex Offers deals are all targeted, though this one at least seems to be pretty widely targeted. It seems that it’s specific to this card, and that most people with the card are eligible for the offer.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card has a steep annual fee. Personally, it’s a card that I have, and one that I find to represent a good value, thanks to the variety of perks it offers. However, an easy $200 in savings beyond the expected value sure helps even more with making the math work!

The card ordinarily earns 3x Bonvoy points per dollar spent on airfare, and I value those points at 0.7 cents each, for a 2.1% return. So if you spent exactly $900 on a ticket, you’d get a $200 statement credit plus 2,700 Bonvoy points, which I value at an extra $19 return, for a total return of around 24%. That’s excellent.

Even if you don’t have an immediate ticket you want to book, most major US airlines let you bank credit if you buy a ticket and then decide that you no longer want to travel. So you could typically buy a $900 (non-basic) ticket, and essentially pick up that much credit with an airline for around $700. That’s a great value, assuming you can use the credit before it expires.

Amex Offers has a new deal that can save you $200+ on the cost of an airfare purchase of $900+. This seems to be specific to the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card, and it’s widely targeted. This is an easy opportunity to save well over 20% on the cost of an airline ticket with few strings attached, so it’s worth taking advantage of, if eligible.

Are you eligible for this Amex Offers deal, and do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6137. Boeing Predicts China’s Airliner Fleet Will Double To Almost 10,000

2026 has been a largely positive year for Boeing as far as its Chinese prospects are concerned, with improving diplomatic relations between the US and China paving the way for the American planemaker to land several major orders and continue deliveries. Going forward, China is certainly a market where Boeing will want to have a strong footing, given its latest projections for the Asian country.

Specifically, a recent report published by the US-based planemaker has highlighted the fact that, according to Boeing's projections, the fleet of commercial aircraft in China will more than double in the next two decades. This growth will see the country's portfolio of airliners grow to almost 10,000 planes, based on steady annual traffic growth. Most of these are set to be single-aisle passenger jets.

Boeing's latest projections show that, in 20 years' time, China's commercial fleet will consist of more than 9,800 aircraft. This would be more than twice as many as the country has today. Crucially, almost all of these will be newly delivered planes, with Boeing expecting Chinese carriers to take delivery of 9,240 new aircraft in the next two decades. Of these, 42% are set to directly replace older models.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Single-aisle passenger jets will be at the heart of this growth, with 7,215 of the 9,240 projected deliveries (78.1%) falling under this category. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this is where Chinese manufacturer COMAC is currently placing a particular emphasis, with its C919 narrowbody. Boeing also projects many new widebodies (1,460), regional aircraft (405), and freighters (160), with Darren Hulst saying:

"With a partnership spanning nearly 55 years, Boeing jets are the backbone of China’s civil aviation industry growth, connecting people and carrying goods within and across continents."

China's airlines won't be picking up thousands of new aircraft for the sake of it. Rather, projected growth in passenger traffic will make such a fleet expansion a necessity. According to Boeing, China's passenger traffic is set to increase at an annual rate of 5% over the next 20 years, with "an expanding middle class, more visa-free travel destinations, and continued infrastructure investment" being key.

This figure represents a better-than-average rate when compared to the world as a whole. On this front, Hulst, who serves as Boeing's VP of Commercial Marketing, says that "China’s passenger air traffic outpaces growth globally, supported by favorable economic and policy fundamentals that will make air travel more accessible." Likewise, long-haul growth will also outpace rates seen elsewhere in Asia.

However, and perhaps unsurprisingly given the size and scale of China's internal network, domestic traffic will play a particularly important role. By 2045, Boeing projects that "China’s domestic air travel market is expected to become the world’s largest as more people choose to fly for leisure or business." This is where the huge single-aisle demand comes in, although Boeing will have to fight Airbus for orders.

The orders could significantly impact US aerospace.

Despite Boeing's recent positive inroads in the Chinese market, it still lags behind its main rival, the multinational European planemaker Airbus, when it comes to overall capacity in the country. Looking at Chinese domestic flights in November 2026, data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, shows that Boeing aircraft account for 150,354 of the country's 391,760 internal services this month.

This represents a respectable proportion of 38.4%, but still leaves it short of Airbus, whose figure of 209,331 flights accounts for some 53.4% of China's domestic capacity. More seats and available seat miles are also offered on flights operated by Airbus jets, although both it and Boeing remain streets ahead of Chinese manufacturer COMAC. These aircraft account for just 20,616 domestic flights, or 5.3%.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6136. Southwest’s New Credit Card Bonuses Offer Up To 90,000 Points Toward Companion Pass—Last Chance Before Rules Change

Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Southwest’s Companion Pass lets someone fly with you for just taxes and fees, even when you redeem points for your own ticket. For someone who flies Southwest with a partner a few times a year, it’s the single best deal in domestic air travel. And the easiest way to earn it is about to disappear.

There’s still a final window to use an 80,000- or 90,000-point credit card initial bonus toward a pass valid through December 31, 2027. You need to apply by December 2, 2026 and get approved. Neither bonus gets you all the way there on its own, but both give you a huge head start.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. It has a $229 annual fee. This is the premium Southwest co-brand card, really designed for folks who fly the airline. It makes those trips better, and spending helps earn both elite status and Companion Pass®. The travel benefits cover the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation: First checked bag free. Preferred or Standard seat selection at booking, at no additional charge, when available. Extra Legroom seat upgrades within 48 hours of departure, at no additional charge, when available. Boarding with Group 5 or earlier if another benefit qualifies you for a better group. You earn 4 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, including flights, inflight purchases and Southwest gift cards; 2 points per dollar at gas stations and restaurants; and 1 point per dollar on other purchases. There are also 7,500 anniversary points each year. The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Its annual fee is $99. That’s a much lower spending requirement for a bonus that’s only 10,000 points smaller. First checked bag free for the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation. Standard seat selection within 48 hours of departure, when available, for the same group of travelers. Group 5 boarding or earlier if you otherwise qualify. 3,000 anniversary points each year, plus a 10% anniversary flight discount code that excludes Basic fares. The Plus card earns 2 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, and 2 points per dollar at gas stations and grocery stores on the first $5,000 in combined purchases per anniversary year. Other purchases earn 1 point per dollar. I’d choose Plus for the lower cost of getting the bonus. Priority costs $130 more per year, but gives you better seat benefits, 4,500 more anniversary points and a larger initial bonus. For a family that flies Southwest regularly, those seating benefits can easily be worth the difference. How Close These Bonuses Get You To Companion Pass Under the 2026 rules, earning 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year gets you the pass for the rest of that year and the following year. Southwest credit card customers receive a 10,000-point qualifying boost, so they effectively need 125,000 more. Priority: 90,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 100,000. You need another 35,000 qualifying points. Plus: 80,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 90,000. You need another 45,000 qualifying points. The purchases you make to earn the bonus also earn points. Assuming those purchase points post in 2026, spending the minimum at 1 point per dollar reduces the remaining gap to 32,000 points with Priority or 44,000 with Plus. Bonus category spending and qualifying points you’ve already earned reduce it further. Qualifying flights and eligible partner activity can help fill the gap, too. Check your Companion Pass progress in your account. Once you have the pass, book your own Southwest flight with cash or points and add your designated companion, as long as there’s an available seat. Their taxes and fees start at $5.60 one-way. You can use the benefit repeatedly and change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. How Optimal Timing Of The Companion Pass Has Changed As I covered in Southwest’s 2027 Rapid Rewards overhaul, unlimited Companion Pass becomes a benefit of the new Platinum elite tier next year. Initial bonuses generally stop helping you qualify. Anniversary points, referral bonuses and extra points from card bonus categories stop counting, too. Southwest’s transition exception preserves the initial bonus for customers who apply by December 2, 2026, are approved, and meet the offer’s requirements. Even if you finish the required spending in early 2027, the bonus can count toward 2026 qualification for a pass ending December 31, 2027. So the old strategy of waiting until January to earn nearly two years of Companion Pass doesn’t work here. A bonus earned under this exception won’t get you a pass through the end of 2028. And Chase’s terms distinguish the initial bonus from ordinary purchase points. Those purchase points must post to your Rapid Rewards account in 2026 to count toward this pass. Spending after your December statement closes generally posts in January. You also want the 10,000-point qualifying boost credited in 2026; Southwest allows up to 30 days after account opening for it to arrive. You still have to meet the initial bonus spending requirement within the first 3 months from account opening. The transition rule doesn’t extend that deadline. I’m a former Companion Pass holder, and a promotional Companion Pass holder.Southwest still represents about 40% of the seats out of my home airport in Austin. Even with all the changes they’ve made, being able to bring someone along on those flights for just the taxes is huge. Before applying, you can’t currently hold a Southwest personal credit card, and you can’t have received an initial bonus on any Southwest personal card in the past 24 months. Southwest business and employee cards are excluded from that restriction. Chase’s usual 5/24 rule also applies: generally, you need fewer than 5 new credit card accounts on your credit report in the past 24 months. If you’re eligible, can handle the required spending, and have a path to the remaining qualifying points, I’d take advantage of this before December 2. Delta Air Lines is adding another route from its fastest-growing “focus city.”

Over the weekend, the Atlanta-based carrier filed plans to launch nonstop service from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) to Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) outside Bentonville.

Flights will begin in March 2027, with Delta offering service on board a Delta Connection regional jet.

The service will give the Texas capital a nonstop link to northwest Arkansas — not to mention parts of Oklahoma, Missouri and Kansas, which are all a relatively short drive from XNA.

SkyMiles news: Delta announces Medallion qualification requirements for 2027

The airport is also the closest option for travelers heading to the University of Arkansas.

For Delta, it’s the latest in a series of expansions in Austin.

The carrier has grown its flight offerings at AUS at a fast pace over the last couple of years, targeting the airport as one of its top non-hub “focus cities.”

That growth included the airline’s first nonstop service from Austin to Europe, which Delta revealed in August. Those flights to Paris will begin in April.

That’s on top of new routes to major tech hubs like San Jose in California's Silicon Valley and popular leisure destinations like Bozeman, Montana, and Cancun in Mexico.

All told, the airline plans to operate up to 70 daily departures by March, Delta chief commercial officer Joe Esposito told me this summer.

In 2019, it had 28 peak daily departures from AUS.

“The boom is incredible,” Esposito told me in August, noting that a growing number of Delta flyers will also start seeing itineraries with connections in the Lone Star State. That said, Delta has stopped short of saying it will ever make Austin a hub.

“We want to be the business carrier of Austin — we’re quickly moving in on the leading corporate carrier for Austin,” he said. “Then you wind up connecting people.”

It's likely no coincidence, then, that Delta would be interested in service to Bentonville: the region is home to Walmart's corporate headquarters.

As for this latest route, Delta’s service from AUS to Northwest Arkansas will launch on March 7.

It’ll be a late-night departure, with flights taking off just before 9 p.m. The return flight from XNA to AUS will launch the next morning, on March 8.

The service will be on board an Embraer 175 regional jet operated by regional partner SkyWest.

“This new direct route is another example of Delta’s continued investment in Austin and our commitment to making it easier for Austinites to get where they want to go as we continue growing alongside this important community,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement to TPG Monday.

While Delta has grown its flight offerings in Austin rapidly over the past couple of years, Southwest Airlines remains the market leader at the airport.

Southwest, like Delta, plans to offer its biggest schedule ever from AUS in 2027.

The airport will also be home to one of its inaugural airport lounges.

Delta, for its part, is planning a second — larger — Sky Club at AUS for the coming years.

By the way, Delta's new route to Northwest Arkansas will add to a strong run of air service growth for that region, too.

This year, the airport will see 28% more total flights than it did just two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Beyond its future route to Austin, Delta serves Bentonville from five other airports — all hubs: Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, Salt Lake City and New York's LaGuardia Airport (LGA).

#6134. Condor Plans To Open First-Ever Lounge At Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3

Germany’s second largest airline, Condor, plans to open its own lounge for the first time ever. However, some more patience will be required, and details are also still quite limited.

Earlier this year, we saw Frankfurt Airport (FRA) open its new Terminal 3, which is the airport’s first new terminal in decades. We’ve already seen all airlines that previously occupied Terminal 2 move to Terminal 3.

The long term plan is that Terminal 1 will be exclusively for Lufthansa and its Star Alliance partners, while Terminal 3 will be for all other airlines. Meanwhile Terminal 2 may eventually be rebuilt, as Lufthansa hopes to take it over as well, but that’s a very long term vision.

As of now, the only airline that hasn’t yet completed the move to Terminal 3 is Condor, which is Germany’s second largest airline. The carrier still operates out of Terminal 1, and uses Lufthansa lounges for its customers, despite Lufthansa’s disdain for the carrier.

The expectation is that Condor will make the move to Frankfurt Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027. As part of that, the airline also plans to open two lounges in the terminal, as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. The expectation is that one will be a Schengen lounge, while the other will be a non-Schengen lounge.

The catch is that the lounges will only open later in 2027, due to the pace of construction. While the company’s CEO confirmed these plans in a meeting with employees, publicly the airline has only confirmed that “we are currently in discussions with our partners at Terminal 3 of Frankfurt Airport to explore the possibilities for Condor’s own lounge offering.”

No details are yet known about what kind of amenities the lounges will offer… I’m definitely curious to see what they come up with, as it’s always interesting when an airline opens a lounge for the first time!

Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 is getting quite a nice selection of lounges. As things currently stand:

On top of that, we know that Qatar Airways is opening two lounges in the non-Schengen area of the terminal, which will be for passengers traveling on oneworld airlines.

Condor is expected to move to Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027, as it’s the last (and largest) airline to make the move to the terminal. We now officially know that Condor is planning on opening two lounges in the terminal, though they’ll likely only open in late 2027.

It’s exciting to see the airline open lounges for the first time, and only time will tell how this plays out…

What do you make of Condor opening lounges for the first time?

Country singer Jessie James Decker shared video of herself spraying the bare foot of a passenger that had invaded her plane armrest. She holds her nose, takes aim with a small mint-green bottle, and the foot quickly disappears. Then she covers her mouth and laughs. Her Instagram video says, “Someone’s foot smells so bad on the plane.” She asked her followers how they would have handled it. Several suspected she was just messing with her husband, former football player Eric Decker. She refuted that: “Have you seen Eric’s feet? Toeeeee UP.” Jessie James Decker’s airplane video Decker is a country pop singer whose 2017 album Southern Girl City Lights debuted at number one on Billboard’s country albums chart. Her sister is Sydney Rae Bass, whose husband Anthony Bass complained that United Airlines made his pregnant wife clean up their child’s spilled popcorn a few years ago. In April, an American Airlines first class passenger shoved a woman’s feet off their armrest, only to see her put them up on the window. The suggestions in that discussion included spraying cologne. Here Decker puts that into practice. Somehow though this keeps happening? I’d want that foot gone, too. I’d ask the passenger to move it, and get a flight attendant involved if they refused. Some Facebook commenters insist this isn’t the crew’s job. They shouldn’t have to deal with it, and neither should a passenger. Each of us is supposed to contain our bodies within the space of our assigned seats. #6132. I can’t stop making this cabbage

I have a very specific fantasy about the restaurant I would open, should someone ever hand me a set of keys and an unlimited supply of funds and optimism. It would be a little neighborhood bistro, the sort of place where the wine comes in mismatched stemless glasses thrifted from estate sales. The menus would be illustrated by hand, which sounds charming until youâve spent an entire afternoon trying to get the shading right on a watercolor artichoke. There would be personality wallpaper in the bathroom, icy sparkling cocktails, very good roast chicken and a bread service so generous it would probably make an accountant nervous.

Fortunately, I donât have to worry about razor-thin margins in a fantasy. But even if I did, I know one dish that would earn its place on the menu: cabbage.

Specifically, green cabbage roasted in miso butter, then showered with crispy, lemony panko breadcrumbs. Itâs inexpensive, uncomplicated and just a little chic. More importantly, I canât seem to stop making it.

The recipe began with one of my favorite ways to cook: playing matchmaker with ingredients. If Thing A already loves Thing B, and Thing B loves Thing C, perhaps A and C would get along, too. Thereâs a pleasing logic to it, like introducing two friends at a dinner party and watching them discover they have more in common than the host.

I already adored miso butter, with its salty, savory depth. And cabbage cooked in butter is a classic for good reason. Putting the two together was hardly a leap. I chopped up a head of green cabbage, coated it with the miso butter and let the oven do the rest. After about 30 minutes at 350 degrees, with a stir halfway through, the cabbage had softened into silky folds, with a little browning at the edges. The butter made it rich; the miso gave it a subtle funk.

My first instinct was to go the baked-macaroni-and-cheese route: lightly toast some panko, scatter it over the cabbage, then return the whole thing to the oven. In theory, a golden, crunchy topping. In practice, the crumbs more or less fused into a single crust over the slick cabbage beneath. Cutting through it was less delightful than Iâd imagined.

The fix was blessedly simple. I crisped the breadcrumbs separately in a pan with olive oil, red pepper flakes and the zest of an entire lemon, then spooned them over the cabbage just before serving. Now each forkful caught a little of everything: tender, almost creamy cabbage; browned edges; bright flecks of citrus; and individual crunchy crumbs that stayed crunchy.

That last part matters. The contrast is what makes this feel like a dish rather than a vegetable dutifully placed beside dinner.

And beside dinner it has appeared, repeatedly. With salmon and rice. With grilled chicken and sweet potato coins glossed with maple syrup and orange zest. With a skillet of white beans and sausage, plus sourdough for scooping. Different meals, same cabbage. At this point, Iâd be more surprised by a week without it.

Lately, Iâve been trying to make room for more vegetables in everyday cooking, ideally two kinds at dinner. Not as a grim exercise in virtue, but because I want the vegetables to be things I actually look forward to eating. That means finding a few sides that are so appealing, and so low-effort, that adding one more feels less like a chore and more like, âOh, hell, why not?â

Cabbage is particularly good at this. Itâs cheap, keeps beautifully in the refrigerator and demands almost no knife skills. You can even buy it pre-shredded. It sits in the oven while you make the rest of the meal, asking for little beyond a halfway stir. Low-maintenance, low-effort, high return.

I may never open that bistro, and perhaps thatâs just as well for the accountant and the watercolor artichokes. But on an ordinary weeknight, when dinner is nearly done and I find myself reaching for the cabbage again, I get a small piece of the fantasy anyway: something simple enough to make at home, and good enough that Iâd happily order it out.

1 medium head green cabbage, shredded (red works, too! Though it takes on a decidedly spooky dark purple color)

#6131. Park Hyatt Phu Quoc, Vietnam, Opening Soon, And I’m Intrigued!

Back in 2019, plans were announced for an exciting new Park Hyatt resort in Vietnam. The property has been massively behind schedule on its planned 2022 opening. Several months ago, the hotel started accepting reservations for stays as of March 2027. There’s now a positive update, as the timeline has been moved forward to December 2026, so it’s just weeks away.

The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 8, 2026. The delays on this property have been endless, so it’s nice to see the timeline moved forward for once. Here’s to hoping that there are no last minute delays.

For those not familiar with Phu Quoc, it’s Vietnam’s largest island, and half of the island is in a national park and UNESCO site. The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is expected to feature a total of 168 keys, including 114 rooms and suites, and 54 private pool villas. This is Park Hyatt’s first resort in Vietnam, and second property in the country, after the Park Hyatt Saigon.

The resort is located on the southwestern tip of Phu Quoc Island, and is developed on 160 acres of land, bordered by a mile-long white sand beach on one side, and lush hills on the other side. The Park Hyatt is a 30-minute drive from Phu Quoc International Airport (PQC).

Details about the property are fairly limited, though here are some things we do know:

Below are some renderings of the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc. Given that we’ve had the same renderings for years and the property has been delayed year after year, I can’t help but wonder if the actual property looks anything like the renderings.

With the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc bookable, what are rates like? If you’re looking to redeem World of Hyatt points, this is a Category 7 property, meaning that a free night redemption will cost anywhere from 25,000 to 55,000 points per night, assuming a standard room is available. I value World of Hyatt points at around 1.4 cents each, so that puts the “cost” of a redemption at $350-770 per night.

When it comes to cash rates, they seem to start at just over $700 per night, and that’s before the 13.4% in taxes and service charges, so we’re talking about entry level rates of over $800 per night all-in.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

Depending on the award pricing for the nights you’re looking at, redeeming points here could potentially be a very good value.

While I’ve visited major cities in Vietnam several times before, I’ve never gone there for a beach vacation, so I’m intrigued by this property, especially given the value of World of Hyatt points, plus of World of Hyatt Globalist status.

Based on what I’ve heard, currently the top properties on the island are the JW Marriott Phu Quoc, the InterContinental Phu Quoc, and the Regent Phu Quoc. Many people have told me that these properties are among the best of their respective portfolios.

I’m curious, though, for those who have been to Phu Quoc, is it worth a trek from the United States? I’m sure it’s gorgeous and I’ll certainly take Vietnamese food over Caribbean food, but is it otherwise worth traveling that far out of the way?

It’s funny how my preferences in that regard have changed over the years. 15 years ago, I’d almost exclusively take beach vacations in Southeast Asia, given the generally higher standard of everything (service, hotels, etc.), plus the more reasonable prices.

However, as I’ve gotten older, my opinion has changed. For one, the jet lag becomes more challenging the older I get, and can take away from relaxation. Furthermore, flight award options just aren’t as exciting as they were over a decade ago. Like, easily being able to always snag Cathay Pacific first class awards was a great reason to vacation in Asia, as far as I’m concerned. 😉 But that’s no longer so easy.

But I also have another motive here. I’m intrigued by airline startup Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is just taking delivery of some Airbus A330s. So if I can fly an ex-American A330 directly to here, I’d sure find that to be amusing! For that matter, I really love the Capella hotel brand, and I’ve heard the Capella Hanoi is among the best in the portfolio, so I’d really love to visit that, and pair it with a visit here.

A Park Hyatt property is expected to open in Phu Quoc, Vietnam, and it’s now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. This property has been under development for eons, and it’s over four years behind schedule on opening. With the opening being just weeks away, here’s to hoping that the timeline finally actually sticks.

Do you plan on checking out the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc?
