#6121. Voting rights groups, afraid of criminal penalties, cut back on help for Texas’ most vulnerable

This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access.

Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for Votebeat Texas’ free newsletter here.

This story was produced with support from the Pulitzer Center.

ALAMO, Tex. – Eustorgia Santos de Torres has lived here for four decades. Last year, she turned to a trusted Rio Grande Valley nonprofit for help navigating the citizenship application process. The same nonprofit — La Unión del Pueblo Entero, or LUPE — then helped her register to vote, and she cast her first ballot as a citizen in the primary election last March.

Santos de Torres, 67, is retired after years cleaning houses and working as a healthcare aide. She speaks mainly Spanish and is the primary caretaker for her husband, Nemorio, who is blind. “Yo soy sus ojos,” Santos de Torres said — I am his eyes.

But last month, Santos de Torres, a new voter, struggled to help Nemorio, an American-born citizen, understand and cast his mail ballot for the November election. All the information on the ballot is in English, she said, and the letters are small.

So Santos de Torres helped Nemorio to the car and made the familiar 7-minute drive to LUPE’s headquarters in the neighboring town of San Juan to ask for help with her husband’s ballot.

This time, though, LUPE workers reluctantly turned the couple away.

In 2021, Texas’ GOP-dominated state Legislature passed a sweeping and controversial overhaul of election laws known as SB1. Among other changes, SB1 made it illegal for anyone to receive compensation for helping voters fill in their ballots.

That not only makes it illegal for paid nonprofit staff to help voters, but also criminalized common past practices, such as organizations giving volunteers gas money or stipends. Violations are a felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $10,000.

In the wake of the law, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican currently running in the state’s nationally watched U.S. Senate race, investigated and prosecuted voting rights advocacy groups and organizers in heavily Latino communities across the state.

Groups such as LUPE say they have been forced to alter or stop some voter outreach as they worry about running afoul of the law. LUPE used to send workers out walking blocks to help voters. Now it has to instead ask volunteers to do more limited versions of that work.

Latinos and other non-English speaking voters will be key to the outcome of the state’s high-profile U.S. Senate and House races this year. But the law means such voters, as well as those who are disabled and elderly, have fewer options for help.

LUPE is known for providing one-on-one assistance to people in the Latino community, so the restrictions on helping with voting are a real pain point for the organization, Executive Director Tania Chavez Camacho said. Texas has strict rules limiting who is eligible to use mail ballots, but people over 65 may do so. LUPE helps around 30,000 people a year, she said, including people with disabilities and many older people who, each year, “want to vote by mail and they come in wanting help.”

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

Now, Chavez Camacho said, when the group holds public town halls for residents to instruct them on how to vote, if a voter pulls out their mail ballot to ask for help, organizers must ask the voter to leave so paid employees aren’t near the ballot.

And if workers for LUPE’s advocacy arm are canvassing for candidates and a voter shows them a mail ballot and asks for help filling it out, workers have been trained to say they can’t and walk away, Chavez Camacho said.

“We literally have to turn them away,” Chavez Camacho said. “We’ve had to do a lot of training with our staff for the past three years because they were so accustomed to helping folks one-on-one and now they can’t.”

Santos de Torres did what she could to help her husband, who mailed back his ballot about a month ago.

“But I don’t think it’s right that LUPE can’t help us,” she told a reporter in Spanish. “That law is not right. It’s excluding people who need help.”

“What if,” she added, “my husband didn’t have me?”

The Rio Grande Valley, where LUPE is based, covers roughly 4,300-square-miles across Hidalgo, Cameron, Starr, and Willacy counties along the Mexico border at Texas’ southern tip. It’s a diverse community with some residents who primarily speak Spanish. Younger generations of residents easily switch between English and Spanish in conversation.

Many households are made up of families whose members have mixed legal statuses, including some who have lived in the area for generations. The Valley also has a history of activism as the birthplace of the Texas farmworker movement of the 1960’s. Farmworkers – who harvested cotton, vegetables and fruits — organized and marched for roughly 400 miles from the Valley to Austin to demand fair wages and better working conditions. Mexican-American farmworker labor today remains key to the area’s growth and agricultural economy.

But due to the lack of affordable housing, Mexican Americans for years purchased land they could afford in rural areas outside of city limits, often lacking basic infrastructure and public services. Those communities are known now as the colonias.

Alamo, where Santos de Torres lives, and San Juan, where LUPE is based, are neighboring cities. The landscape varies depending on the side of town. In the southern parts of the cities, closer to the border with Mexico, modest residential homes with green front lawns adorn along palm tree-lined streets. Shopping centers, chain restaurants, stadiums, and commercial developments lie to the north of the cities, along Interstate Highway 2, reflecting the transition from the once primarily agricultural community to a growing metropolitan hub. The Valley has for years relied on its trade of goods and services with Mexico. It has a population of more than 1.4 million people and 90% of them are Hispanic or Latino, according to Census data.

About 24% of people in the Valley live below the poverty line, which is more than double the national rate. And about 30% of Valley residents don’t have health insurance – one of the highest uninsured rates in the country. The area also has one of the highest rates of diabetes in the country; Nemorio Torres’ blindness is a complication of the disease.

LUPE and other advocacy groups have long worked with residents in the colonias and all over the Valley, providing resources to find affordable housing and medical treatment, or helping with complex procedures such as filing taxes. Voter education and outreach was part of the mission.

Now, instead of providing one-on-one assistance, LUPE hosts group sessions with a screen projector showing what mail ballot applications and mail ballots look like. Facilitators point at the screen indicating what the instructions say and explaining how the forms should be filled out.

The limitations are frustrating, Chavez Camacho said, especially “si una persona no sabe leer” — if a person can’t read. “It doesn’t matter that we’re doing those sessions because a person who doesn’t know how to read has to do it on their own and we can’t help them to know where to mark,” she said.

Instead, LUPE’s workers and volunteers now focus on letting people know key deadlines are coming up. They also have fewer volunteers willing to guide and interpret for voters at the polls, she said, because the law now requires such people to sign an oath affirming the voter is qualified to receive help because they are disabled or need an interpreter, and detail their relationship with the voter. They must also affirm they are not being paid by a candidate or political committee, which would be illegal. Volunteers fear any misstep while assisting voters could get them in trouble, Chavez-Camacho said.

“We really feel that the people are not getting the support they need,” Chavez Camacho said.

Election and voting law experts say the courts have interpreted “compensation” prohibited from going to volunteers by SB1 as any type of benefit. That interpretation is so broad that it makes it difficult for voter outreach organizations to know whether they are violating the law, said Zachary Dolling, litigation director at Texas Civil Rights Project, which works with groups to design trainings in voter outreach that comply with the law.

Dolling said some organizations historically provided unpaid volunteers dinner, T-shirts, or pens, and others have given volunteers college credit for their work.

“All of those things are items of value” and could be considered compensation, he said.

Texas Republicans passed SB1, the sweeping overhaul of election law, in part responding to false claims and conspiracy theories about the 2020 election.

Republicans claimed the law would increase public trust and confidence in the elections. Democrats argued the legislation would disproportionately burden voters of color and people with disabilities, and staged two walkouts and a 15-hour Senate filibuster in their failed attempt to defeat the bill.

Despite lawsuits from voting rights organizations including LUPE, the League of United Latin American Citizens and organizations representing Texans with disabilities, a federal appeals court ultimately upheld key provisions of SB1, including the restrictions on voter assistance.

Other attempts to expand voting help for people with disabilities were meanwhile unsuccessful.

In 2023, Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, vetoed a bipartisan bill that would have expanded vote-by-mail access for people with disabilities — specifically people who are blind or paralyzed and need assistance marking their ballot — by allowing such voters to request an electronic ballot and use a computer to mark their choices. Similar options in Texas are already available for military overseas voters and astronauts, but not for voters with disabilities.

The challenges Santos de Torres and her husband have faced are an example of what advocates worried about under SB1, said Lydia Nunez Landry, statewide coordinator for REV UP Texas, which works to get out the vote among people with disabilities.

“That was our worst fear and now it’s happening,” she said. Nunez Landry has muscular dystrophy, uses a power wheelchair, and needs help doing basic tasks such as opening the refrigerator.

The state has made voting “just so impossible and so arduous for people — and now people are also terrified of helping us,” she said.

Groups across the state have been changing their voter outreach work to comply with SB1.

Asian Texans for Justice conducts voter outreach in Asian communities, focusing on San Antonio, Houston, Austin, and North Texas.

The stricter rules associated with voting by mail under SB1 have created “a sense of anxiety” in those communities, Executive Director Nabila Mansoor said. She said that the process is now much more complicated for elderly voters, who must provide one of two forms of ID on their application and pay close attention to pages of instructions that are written in font that is small and hard for them to read. In addition, an error could force them to restart the whole process of applying for a ballot.

“That anxiety comes from this kind of fear that they’re going to do something wrong,” Mansoor said. “Whenever you have that kind of fear, it is one more barrier for that person to actually go out and vote.”

Now that Asian Texans for Justice can no longer provide one-on-one help, they’ve turned to providing checklists for voters, she said, which she believes is less effective when some voters may need help reading and understanding the ballot and instructions

Mansoor said she believes that SB1’s goal was to make it harder for people to vote.

“It means that we have to be more careful. It means that we have to dot our i’s and cross our t’s. It means that we have to take good records. It means that we have to be very thorough in terms of our training of our volunteers,” she said, adding that the organization assembled a legal team to defend against challenges to their work as well.

In the meantime, volunteers for LUPE and other groups say they are doing their best to fill the gap.

Maria Gomez, better known as Doña Mary, of Pharr, worked as a farmworker for years in Hidalgo County and has been a member of LUPE since the organization was founded. Gomez, 78, was involved in the farmworker movement years ago. She now ensures her elderly friends and neighbors are aware of election deadlines, know where to vote, and have a ride to the polls if they need one.

After she drops off her grandkids and great-grandkids at school, she makes her rounds around the Colonias in San Juan in her small red SUV. She chats up her neighbors, and asks them what they need help with or if they need resources or a ride. She’s always fielding calls.

“People don’t vote because sometimes they can’t leave their home and because they might not have access to that piece of paper that they need to sign to receive their ballot,” Gomez said in Spanish, referring to voter registration forms and ballot-by-mail applications.

One of her friends, 80-year-old Teresa Corona Garza of San Juan, has relied on Gomez for rides to the polls for some time now. Corona Garza struggles to stand for long periods of time and can’t see very well out of her left eye. Even though she qualifies to vote by mail, she prefers to go to the polls in person.

“There’s so much on there you have to fill out, and those letters are small,” Corona Garza said in Spanish. “No, I prefer to go, quiero ver que mi voto cuenta,” she said – I want to see that my vote is counted.

The laws have gotten so complicated and strict that Gomez worries state leaders may even try to prevent volunteers like her from providing rides to the polls.

“I don’t know what’s going to happen, if they’re going to keep making this harder for people,” she said, “but I would like to see people who want to vote to be able to do it.”

Natalia Contreras covers election administration and voting access for Votebeat in partnership with the Texas Tribune. Natalia is based in Corpus Christi. Contact her at ncontreras@votebeat.org.

Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization covering local election integrity and voting access. Sign up for their newsletters here.

#6120. War Insurance Dries Up for Gulf Events as U.S.-Iran Conflict Continues

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: The Riyadh Skyline Wikimedia Commons / B.alotaby

Gulf events can still insure against cancellation but not against war. That is pushing organizers to postpone events or to take on the risk themselves. It’s a growing issue, and Saudi Arabia’s calendar has been paying the price.

Event organizers in the Gulf can still insure against cancellation for many reasons, such as bad weather, a declared period of national mourning, or an IT failure. What they increasingly can’t buy is protection if an event is canceled because of war or political violence, industry executives told Skift.

Standard event-cancellation policies exclude war and political violence, so organizers routinely have to buy that coverage as a separate layer. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, it is something that has become very hard to find for Gulf events.

Only one insurer, possibly two on very limited terms, is currently willing to consider war exposure for events in the region, according to Panteha Peters, head of sports, entertainment, media and special risks at insurance broker Marsh Middle East and Africa. It does so case by case, and generally no earlier than about one week before the event.

War and political violence cover for events in the Gulf has largely disappeared, and organizers are absorbing the risk themselves, industry executives told Skift. Standard event-cancellation policies exclude war, so that protection is normally bought as a separate layer — and since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, only one insurer, possibly two on limited terms, will consider war exposure for Gulf events, according to Marsh Middle East and Africa's Panteha Peters, typically case by case and no earlier than about a week before the event. Marsh said in May that political violence premiums in the Gulf have risen at least 20-fold since the war began, while capacity to write that cover shrank from about $1 billion to roughly $200 million. Saudi Arabia is the sharpest pressure point: Morningstar DBRS's Marcos Alvarez said the Houthi missile and drone campaign on Riyadh, Abha, and Dammam in October turned war from a theoretical exclusion into a live, priced peril, and a long list of events has slipped, including the Future Investment Initiative conference, the EU-Gulf summit, Intersec Saudi Arabia 2026, the Saudi Retail Forum, the 2027 Dakar Rally, the Saudi International golf tournament, the Red Sea Film Festival, and Riyadh Fashion Week. Pricing for standard cancellation cover has generally held stable this year, Gallagher's Yasmin Dacuycuy said, so the squeeze is concentrated in the war layer. Events that proceed are doing so with lower limits, more exclusions, and in some cases no cancellation insurance at all.

#6118. The global rise of listening bars

A version of this story first appeared in The Swell, Salon's culture newsletter. Sign up for early access to articles like this, for more culture that's made to last.

Nothing about Shibuya HiFi is loud. From its unmarked front door to its low-lit lounge, the Seattle vinyl bar is a subtle, pensive ballad of a place. So much so, in fact, that on the Wednesday night that we visited for a sold-out event, the sparsely populated lounge area was nearly silent.

That is intentional, said general manager Jerry Stotler. Wednesday nights are closed to everyone but ticket holders. “These are what we call deep listening sessions,” he explained, “so when you walk in, there isn’t any music playing. We want to ensure a pristine listening environment when we’re in the hi-fi room.”

Seattle has many vinyl bars, but Shibuya, open since 2023, sets the local standard for premium listening experiences. Every inch of its intimate sanctum contains the story of the venue’s principal owners, Quentin Ertel and Brian Rauschenbach. It’s named for the Tokyo district known for its jazz kissa, cafés dating back to post-war Japan where visitors listen to vinyl on premium sound equipment. Rauschenbach’s parents met in such a place nearly six decades ago, Stotler said.

Ertel, an interior designer, painstakingly curated the room. Cedar planks line the walls. Louis Poulsen chandeliers hang from the ceiling, along with several plush, crescent-shaped loveseats, acquired from Benaroya Hall when the concert hall underwent a redesign. A pair of deep seats covered in nubby upholstery sit close to this sacred space’s altar — a vinyl-stacked media console holding a vintage receiver and turntable, flanked by two ATC SCM50 loudspeakers. But one set of equipment reigns over everything: a pair of 1976 Klipschorns.

Shibuya’s schedule favors favorites such as D’Angelo’s “Voodoo,” Radiohead’s “Kid A,” or Charles Mingus’ self-titled opus. But on this Wednesday, the venue hosted a special listening session for Michael Kiwanuka’s fifth album, “Fudge,” a week before its Oct. 23 release.

Stotler humbly acknowledged the venue’s good fortune to be included on the very short list of people and organizations invited to preview the record, a relatively recent development. Previous pre-release sessions have debuted work by the Beastie Boys’ Mike D and Thundercat.

But I’m getting ahead of myself. While waiting for the magic to start, we listened to the hi-hat riff of ice cubes click-clacking as Stotler worked a cocktail shaker. Once the listening room doors open, all drinks, distractions and shoes must be left at the door. “So enjoy a cocktail in advance of the session to relax and reset,” he calmly says, sliding one of his potions across the bar to a fellow patron. “Then we’ll go back and drop the needle.”

I’ve been curious about the recent rise of listening bars. Life has gotten faster, noisier and increasingly disconnected. Low-friction digital convenience has sapped life and music of their organic weight.

Places like Shibuya, then, are a natural fit for what Ertel describes as a renaissance of meaning, driven by vinyl’s resurgence. “There’s a search for new ways to be together, but also, I think, just new ways to be,” he said when I caught up with him by phone a few days later.  “We live in sort of this two-dimensional world of scrolling. Everything’s flat and fragmented and fractured. When you have something that has kind of a wholeness to it, that is also linked to something that most of us love so much, which is music, it makes sense that people want vinyl records again.”

Younger audiophiles revived the medium from the dead starting in 2008 for many reasons, the simplest being that digital downloads don’t include eye-popping cover art. By 2020, vinyl record sales revenue hit $596.2 million, surpassing CDs ($531.1 million) for the first time since 1986, according to the Recording Industry Association of America. In 2025, vinyl purchases in the U.S. alone reached $1.04 billion, the RIAA reported in March.

Listening bars, meanwhile, have popped up worldwide. Tracks & Tales, a site founded by British writer Rafi Mercer, reports finding bars, hi-fi cafés and sound-first venues across 171 countries and 6,465 cities. That doesn’t count traveling experiences like The Listening Room, created by Seattle DJ Joshua Fields.

Fields was inspired by listening to “Voodoo” at Shibuya and wishing that he could talk about it with the other attendees. (He credits Rauschenbach as a mentor.) A little later, a back injury forced him to slow down and think about what he’d do differently — a “divine download,” he called it during a recent phone chat, that transformed into a monthly series of phone-free listening sessions that have so far taken place in Portland and Seattle venues.

The rules of engagement are consistent. Soft, comfortable seating is a must. No phones for the duration, or talking, singing or other interruptions once the needle hits vinyl until the very last track finishes. Afterward, he sets aside time for quiet journaling and discussion.

“The music is really the medium that gets us to this opening up,” Fields told me, “because what I’m solving for is the lack of human connection, with all our technology and our robots, all our things.”

As such, his model is a little more relaxed than Shibuya’s. Participants are served food and drinks, with each event inspiring a signature cocktail. For a recent sit with “Purple Rain,” he direct-messaged its co-star, Apollonia Kotero, to let her know he was naming a drink after her.  “She responded, which blew my mind,” Fields said. “She told me, ‘Make sure it’s spicy.’”

Listening events remind us that music can be a full-bodied, meditative journey, however you do it. There’s a ritual to setting the turntable stylus, or needle, into a vinyl LP’s groove for the first time, hearing the soft, crackling prelude to an opening melody and listening to a body of work front to back with silent focus. We can create that feeling at home, setting up a dedicated space to be comfortably still and take in your favorite records, or an unfamiliar one, from start to finish.

Still, there’s real value in leaving home and finding a place to listen — not simply hear, but listen —alongside strangers who love the art and spirit of music as much as you do. At events like Fields’, you may even meet someone you otherwise wouldn’t. He teased that a Dec. 4 Listening Room event in Seattle for India Arie’s “Acoustic Soul” will feature a special guest.

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

I look forward to inhaling “Fudge” many times on my stereo. But I’ll never be able to recreate the rush of hearing its blossoming piano and strings for the first time, sensing the soundwaves from those Klipschorn speakers penetrate my skin. It made me well up, which embarrassed me until I glanced around the room and noticed a few others dabbing their eyes, too.

“In a true kissa or a well-kept basement bar, the first thing you feel is not volume; it’s presence,” Mercer writes. “The room seems to steady itself around a note. The air thickens. You sit differently. Your breath slows without negotiation.

“Good sound doesn’t overwhelm you,” Mercer adds. “It invites you. That’s the quiet truth at the heart of every listening bar: the room listens back.”

Beyond welcome bonuses, points and miles aren't always the easiest to earn. That's why I advocate for stacking your card's earning rates with shopping portal bonuses and other promotions whenever you can.

That's exactly what I did recently when I purchased three tickets for my parents and me to see the Portland Timbers while they were visiting. The total charge was about $180; if I’d paid with a card earning just 1 point per dollar spent and skipped the other offers, I’d have earned only 180 points.

But by paying close attention to my Chase Freedom Flex®'s (see rates and fees) quarterly categories and promotions offered by Rove and Paze, I was able to walk away with just shy of 4,000 points (or over $75 in value back). Here's exactly how my earnings break down.

For Q3 2026, the Freedom Flex offered select live entertainment as one of its rotating 5% quarterly bonus categories (activation required; on up to $1,500 in combined quarterly category spending per quarter).

Despite being marketed as a cash-back card, the Freedom Flex actually earns Ultimate Rewards points. That means my earning rate for live entertainment purchases in Q3 was effectively 5 points per dollar spent, since I have an eligible card that allows me to convert my Freedom Flex rewards into fully transferable points.

On its own, this category earned me about 900 points, a solid haul considering I'd earn only 180 points during quarters when live entertainment isn't offered. Still, while planning my purchase, I knew I could do better.

I've been a big fan of Rove over the past several months, using it for a variety of events and travel bookings. Rove offers members the opportunity to earn Rove miles, which are transferable to over 20 airline and hotel partners. This includes partners that aren't offered by any credit card loyalty programs, such as Frontier Miles and Lufthansa Miles & More.

It's free to join. Rove has its own travel booking portal, but for this particular purchase, I focused solely on its shopping portal. At the time, Rove offered 6.5 miles per dollar spent on StubHub purchases.

By booking my tickets through StubHub, I earned over 1,100 Rove miles. An unfortunate downside to shopping through Rove is that your miles often take an extended amount of time to post, which isn't uncommon with shopping portals. I'm still waiting for my miles to land in my account, which Rove indicates could take until early December.

Don't forget to start your purchase in the Rove app, on Rove's website or via its browser extension. If you're using the browser extension or accessing Rove via desktop, make sure all other shopping portal browser extensions are disabled.

With my decision to book through StubHub, there was one more way I could make my purchase work for me: Paze.

Currently, eligible Chase cardholders can earn 10 additional Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent when checking out with Paze at select merchants (through Dec. 31). StubHub is among those eligible for this promotion, meaning I could triple-dip on my purchase.

Checking out with Paze instead of the standard StubHub checkout process earned me roughly 1,800 additional points.

Using Paze at checkout is easy. You should be able to select it as a payment method on your eligible merchant's checkout screen, just as you would with a digital wallet or credit card.

One technical snag to note: I wasn't able to get Paze to work on mobile, but it worked on the first try on desktop. My transaction didn't say anything about Paze, so don't fret if the same is true for you. My points posted with no problem after a few days, but I recommend screen recording your purchase as proof if you're worried.

To summarize, here's how my earnings and their value broke down in the end:

*Valuations are according to TPG's November 2026 valuations and are not provided by credit card or program issuers.

My Freedom Flex is one of my oldest cards, but I still pull it out regularly, thanks in large part to strategies like this. While Chase's Paze promotion isn't limited to this card, the Freedom Flex is the only Chase card currently open to applicants that offers rotating 5% quarterly bonus categories.

Live entertainment reliably appears as a quarterly category every year, so I expect I'll be able to replicate this strategy (or a similar one) in 2027.

The more credit cards you open, the harder it becomes to find new welcome bonuses to earn. With welcome offers being the main way to earn heaps of rewards at once, it's important to have other ways to earn points and miles when that well starts to dry up.

Knowing how to maximize your purchases, especially larger ones or those you're splitting with friends or family, will help you maintain a large rewards balance even when you're not actively applying for new credit cards.

If you're currently not a Freedom Flex cardholder, you can apply and, upon approval, have the chance to earn $250 cash back (or 25,000 bonus points) after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. That's one of the easiest welcome bonuses to earn right now, but this offer ends soon.

If you hold an eligible Ultimate Rewards card, such as the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see ), you can transfer the points you earn with your Freedom Flex to Chase's 14 transfer partners.

The Timbers weren't able to walk away with the win, but the more than 3,800 points and miles I earned from the tickets I purchased helped ease the sting of that loss.

You can create a strategy like this with virtually any card in your wallet. Consider the offers, limited-time earning rates and promotions that are available for your specific card; take a look at shopping portals like Rakuten and Rove to see what they offer; and use sites like Cashback Monitor to make sure you're getting the best deal.

Effectively maximizing your card's earning potential means thoroughly understanding which offers and deals are available to you and knowing how to combine them. It requires a little extra work on your part, but that effort will be worth it when those extra rewards help take you on your next dream trip.

#6115. It’s scary how watchable these stories are

A version of this story first appeared in The Swell, Salon's culture newsletter. Sign up for early access to articles like this, for more culture that's made to last.

Iâve never been great at the whole Halloween thing. By the time I remember itâs happening, all the good sweets are gone from grocery store shelves, so any visiting trick-or-treaters get butterscotch suckers, breath mints or candy corn. I donât do costume parties. I never got the point of carving pumpkins.

But movie and TV marathons? Sign me up â along with a lot of other homebodies. The horror genre is bigger than ever, according to a San Francisco Chronicle report that says this yearâs domestic box office reached nearly $1.3 billion as of the start of October.

Horrorâs surge has also yielded more films designed to play with our perception as opposed to the âSawâ-style torture porn dominating years past. Think âObsessionâ or âBackrooms,â both of which are among the 10 highest-earning movies of 2026 thus far. Thatâs good news for anyone who isnât partial to splatter flicks or slashers but still enjoys a creep show that makes you think, especially ones that are more thoughtful than scary. If thatâs your speed, the following options may be perfect for your reclusive Samhain.

I will bet good money the first bong-ripping undergrad to declare that all horror is metaphor cited George Romeroâs âNight of the Living Deadâ as a prime example. Thatâs not wrong; Romeroâs 1968 benchmark established the modern cinematic zombie as a stand-in for mindless capitalist consumption. But âBlack Zombieâ rewinds to the monsterâs Haitian roots to examine an even darker origin tied to that countryâs shared history with ours.

You may be wondering why Iâd recommend a documentary in a horror roundup, let alone one that explains how the modern movie flesh gobbler began as a manifestation of white fear. The answer is that Maya Annik Bedwardâs film doubles as an impressive cinematic syllabus.

By braiding Americaâs media history with its national history, Bedward and her assemblage of academics, creatives, authors and Vodou practitioners invite us to think differently about the prejudices driving movies like, say, Victor Halperinâs 1932 effort âWhite Zombie,â or 1943âs âI Walked with a Zombie.â

âBlack Zombieâ opens with a truth that has long escaped those fascinated by the shambling undead. To some, theyâre simply mindless hunters. But Haitians understand the horror of zombies to be one of dispossession, a curse enacted by enslavers that binds victims to mindless servitude, denying them liberation in the afterlife. But long after Romero transformed them from blank-eyed puppets to ravenous murder machines, Bedwardâs film demonstrates how Hollywoodâs version of the zombie impacts Americaâs perception of Vodou, Haitians and immigration.

âBlack Zombieâ not only asks us to think differently about an overexposed subgenre, but also thoughtfully examines Vodouâs central role in the revolution that drove out French colonizers, and Franceâs imposition of debt to punish Haitians for winning their freedom.

All of this informs the zombieâs continued proliferation across popular culture, in films like âWorld War Zâ and shows such as âThe Last of Usâ and âThe Walking Dead.â Theyâre terrific entertainment, certainly. But each is, in its own way, built upon decadesâ worth of misrepresenting Haitiâs syncretic faith to the detriment and demonization of a people. At the same time, âBlack Zombieâ recognizes this subgenreâs cultural resilience, arguing that recognizing the zombieâs true roots broadens its narrative possibilities.

Proving that point, one of Bedwardâs subjects, a Vodou priest, says he grew up loving Wes Cravenâs âThe Serpent and the Rainbow,â despite its message that visitors to his country risk having their nuts nailed to a chair. Â âItâs a fantastical world to scare children,â he says, before adding that his main problem is its inaccurate messaging about his faith. âWe say, âWow â Haitians are devils.â Thatâs what weâre taught.â

Iâd nearly forgotten about that movie. Now I might rewatch it for the first time in decades and expect to be horrified for entirely different reasons.

Available to rent on Prime Video, Apple TV, and Fandango.

Stephen Kingâs classic may be more than half a century old and has undergone multiple adaptations, but it endures because its central moral that high school is hell never ages. Still, Mike Flanaganâs interpretation has divided the audience. Some, including King, appreciate Flanaganâs kinder portrait of Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) as an innocent unjustly sequestered from the world by fundamentalist parents who repudiate her extraordinary power. Others disagree with Flanaganâs alteration to the storyâs climactic scene, which shifts culpability for the prom massacre from Carrie to a character created expressly for the series.

Pretty much everyone questions the season finale, which hints at taking an âX-Menâ-style turn for its recently greenlit second season.

As someone who accepts nothing is sacrosanct now, not to mention a fan of the creatorâs other adaptations, including âThe Fall of the House of Usher,â I appreciated Flanagan using Carrieâs story to critique ignorance, knowledge suppression, and the dehumanizing effect of social media.

Besides, nearly all the key elements of âCarrieâ remain. The bullies are still awful, and the famous âplug it upâ shower scene in Brian DePalmaâs 1976 standard-setter is worsened by her tormentors posting Carrieâs frightened sobs on social media.

Some changes retain the spirit of past performances. Carrieâs mother Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) is still an abusive religious zealot fond of locking her daughter in a prayer closet, for instance. But after the law forces her homeschooled girl to join the festering sin den that is their local public school, Margaret throws herself into advocating for parentsâ rights, entirely disregarding her teenâs desire for a ânormalâ adolescence.

Part of the additional fun Flanagan has with this marquee property is strewing cultural Easter Eggs throughout. Some nod to whatâs happening in America, such as when Carrie discovers the school library and gravitates straight to books that have been banned from classrooms and community libraries across the country. Another winks at âArmy of Darknessâ fans; look for the logo on Margaretâs work uniform.

By the time we reach Carrieâs bloodbath, we may be left to question whether sheâs simply a bullied victim pushed beyond her limit or some version of a Final Girl empowered to vanquish tormentors who earn their reckoning. Even if you donât ultimately see Howellâs Carrie that way, itâs a fine dance with one of horrorâs oldest friends.

âCarrieâ is streaming on Prime Video.

For adults, Halloween is an excuse to mingle sensuality with morbid themes. Why cosplay as a grizzled cop when you can be a flirty detective? Why settle for pretending to be a humpbacked wiccan when you can troll for hookups as a sexy witch?

âYagaâ has it all ways, resplendent with softcore interludes dangled between clue-finding excursions and unexpected chicken violence. The latest infatuation bait from Crave, the Canadian streamer that brought us âHeated Rivalry,â also gives us a new view of Hudson Williams and his naked hindquarters.

Only now, theyâre humping away in a mystery taking place in a verdant seaside community called Whittock. There, dirtbag P.I. Charlie Rapp (Noah Reid) is drawn into a tense partnership with Carson (Clark Backo), a no-nonsense cop fatigued with her colleaguesâ disrespect.

At first, Carson is repulsed by Rappâs slimy overstepping, but she slowly learns not to loathe him. Implied in this, perhaps, is that a spell has ensnared the two as they probe the disappearance of rich playboy Henry Park (Williams). This pursuit leads them to encounter free-range poultry in odd places, along with strange symbols, a variety of nubile temptresses and a roommate, Logan (also Williams), who resembles Henry to an unsettling degree.

The showâs title has nothing to do with John Wick. It refers to the mythical Slavic crone, Baba Yaga, who either gives heroes a boon or lures wayward children to a forest hut that moves around on bird legs. Playwright Kat Chandlerâs interpretation leaves open the question of whether our impressions of its witch are unwarranted or dead right, further muddling our judgment with the introduction of Carrie-Anne Mossâ university professor, Katherine Hargrove.

Katherine announces herself by cozying up to Rapp over the manuscript for her new book titled âSexy Bones,â thrilling him with her mature lady erotic energy. As she flirts with and antagonizes the private dick, along with other townies, it grows increasingly baffling as whether sheâs friend or foe. Much like our titular enchantress.

This adaptation of Chandlerâs play looks like a cop drama tangled with witchy murder, but from a longer TV perspective itâs really a haunting by the ghosts of erotic TV shows past. Remember âRed Shoe Diariesâ and its moaning sax riffs? Like that anthology once did, âYagaâ banks on the power of smut to compel you. Itâs a cheap indulgence, but what Halloween candy isnât?

#6113. Inside the Unraveling of the Tollman Family Travel Dynasty

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

The company was doing fine. The family wasn’t.

For 104 years, The Travel Corporation was owned by a single family, and that ownership was a key selling point of the company.

The Tollmans built TTC into one of the world's largest guided-tour companies and kept full control. It presented itself to travel agents and customers as a family business with no outside investors to answer to.

Then, in July 2024, Brett Tollman, TTC’s chairman, announced a sale to Apollo. He gave only one reason: there was no next generation to lead the business. While that was true, it wasn’t the whole story.

Credit rating reports, UK filings and interviews with more than half a dozen former executives and advisers point to a profitable tour business that was underfunded, while the family’s luxury hotel chain, Red Carnation, lost money and relied on financial support from TTC on cheap terms. Ultimately, the family sold the tour business and kept the hotels.

Skift's review of credit rating reports, UK filings, and interviews with more than half a dozen former executives and advisers fills in what sat behind The Travel Corporation's 2024 sale to Apollo. Brett Tollman publicly cited the absence of a next generation to lead the business. The documents show a profitable but underfunded tour group — roughly $190 million in EBITDA on an implied $1.3 billion in revenue — sold for about $1.1 billion, less than six times earnings, despite Uniworld's roughly 45% share of luxury river cruise and Trafalgar's 15% of guided tours. S&P and Fitch both described reduced marketing spend and agent commissions, weak direct sales, and outdated systems, with an EBITDA margin of 14% against more than 20% at competitors. Apollo set aside $50 million to upgrade operations. The family kept Red Carnation Hotels, which UK filings show had been funded by a loan of more than £50 million from Travcorp Financial Services at the Bank of England base rate — terms the hotel group's own audited accounts call below market. The London hotel group's losses widened from £1.6 million in 2023 to £7.2 million in 2025, while capital spending rose from £2 million to £7.6 million over the same period.

#6111. Norway makes toilets great again

President Donald Trump called Norway a “shithouse country” after failing to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Norway’s tourism officials decided to take that as a compliment.

Visit Norway, the Scandinavian country’s tourism agency, responded to Trump’s insult with a cheeky campaign celebrating its spectacular public restrooms, declaring that Norway makes “shithouses great again.”

The campaign features some of the country’s most architecturally impressive toilets, many situated along scenic routes overlooking fjords, mountains and waterfalls. Some have even won international design awards.

Trump delivered the insult last Sunday during a campaign rally in Port Huron, Michigan, while complaining about the Nobel Peace Prize, which was awarded earlier this month to international jurist Navi Pillay.

“Norway has become a shithouse country, actually,” Trump told supporters. He also suggested he no longer wanted Norwegian immigrants coming to the United States because he had not received the prize.

The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded by an independent Norwegian committee, not the country’s government.

Rather than engage in a diplomatic spat, Visit Norway embraced the president’s characterization, promoting restrooms that include the award-winning Stegastein viewpoint toilet overlooking Aurlandsfjord and the triangular Golden Toilet on Senja Island.

The agency repurposed material originally developed for World Toilet Day, which falls on Nov. 19.

The response has been an unexpected tourism success.

According to travel industry publication Skift, Visit Norway’s toilet webpage attracted more than 80,000 views from over 170 countries in five days, with traffic surging to more than 540 times the previous week’s level. Roughly a quarter of visitors were American.

The tourism agency spent less than $10,000 promoting the campaign, with approximately 90% of its traffic arriving organically. A Times Square advertisement was also planned for this weekend.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The campaign marks a reversal from Trump’s first presidency, when he disparaged Haiti and African nations as “shithole countries” while expressing a preference for immigrants from Norway.

Now, Norway is making the most of its presidential publicity, inviting visitors to discover some of the world’s most scenic places to answer nature’s call.

#6105. Are Mount Everest climbers dreamers, or just cultists?

In the title of his 1997 bestselling adventure tale, “Into Thin Air,” mountaineer and writer Jon Krakauer employs a double entendre so clever that its effect is extraordinary. Throughout the book, Krakauer recounts his attempt to summit Mount Everest the year earlier in what would become, at the time, the mountain’s deadliest season. I’ve been momentarily halted by that title each time I’ve picked up my tattered $5 thrift-store copy over the last few weeks. It’s witty, but not grim; accurate but also imaginative. In three words, “Into Thin Air” conveys not only the literal effect of Everest’s high altitude and how quickly the mountain can take a life, but also the ardent, almost fatuous confidence of those who choose to climb it.

The dissonance between reason and ambition is what makes “Into Thin Air” such a compelling read. For someone like myself, who knows next to nothing about climbing, Krakauer powerfully elucidates the pull of a mountain like Everest and the trance-like state in which it ensnares its adversaries. Unlike some climbers, Krakauer can wax poetic while staying honest about the stakes. He writes about mountaineering as a spiritual practice, good for the mind and body alike, while questioning why some find that clarity only by staring death in the face. In that respect, extreme climbing is an incredibly selfish endeavor. Before he begins his push for the summit, Krakauer remembers his wife, Linda, telling him before he left for Nepal: “If you get killed, it’s not just you who will pay the price. I’ll have to pay, too. For the rest of my life.”

That sentiment echoed in my mind throughout “Everest: The Other Side,” the remarkable new documentary from National Geographic, helmed by “Free Solo” and “Nyad” co-directors Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin. The film is brutally honest in its depictions of cold human narcissism and the relentless pursuit of glory in the name of nebulous spiritual fulfillment. Yet it’s just as candid about humanity’s collective desire for all those things in one form or another.

Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, “Everest: The Other Side” forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.”

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

As “Everest: The Other Side” asserts, nothing in this already mystifying life is ever so simple. The film’s subjects, mountaineer Jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson, found love at the edge of the world and made a life together, with Morrison becoming co-parent to Nelson’s two young sons. But their shared lust for adventure created a prickly tension within their family unit, a strain between their passion and parentage that sits at the documentary’s emotional center.

Like those pulled by devout religion or extreme acts of faith, Morrison and Nelson are powerless before their distinct higher calling — especially with the literal highest calling of all, Everest, in their sights. They don’t just want to summit the mountain from its treacherous north face; they want to be the first people ever to ski down it. In their quest, personal glory and public vanity are forever at odds. Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, “Everest: The Other Side” forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.

Because this is National Geographic, the film is only partially concerned with relaying that price. This documentary is made for IMAX-loving, secondhand adventure seekers. Those who want sweeping shots of impossible sights won’t be disappointed.

But while “Everest: The Other Side” includes countless breathtaking sequences of Earth’s tallest mountain and plenty of nail-biting anxiety in the eventual summit push and ski attempt, those moments are merely the film’s selling points. The crux of this story is on Nelson and Morrison’s shoulders, and their sincerity flies in the face of good judgment and self-editing, giving viewers a palpable sense of their egos. This isn’t to say that either of them is a raging narcissist who cares only about themselves, but there’s no doubt that their sport’s seismic, life-altering dangers are on full display, warts and all.

Early in the film, Nelson tries to communicate the draw of climbing, and how fundamentally at odds it is with her role as a mother. “People ask me, ‘How do you find balance?’” she says. “There isn’t. It’s just chaos. You’re just hanging on. You want to be with your family, but you have a passion, and you want to work, and you need to make money. You’re all over the map.”

It would be easy to dismiss Nelson as selfish, or, at the worst and most damning, a bad parent. How can someone have young children and decide to part with them for two months for a climb that is about, at face value, little more than bragging rights? How can a parent let their children spend two months wondering if their mother is dead or alive?

These are easy questions to ask from the comfort of a living room or the cushion of a theater seat, but much harder to answer when you’re living the life. It’s important to remember that, in life, most of us have desires that would yank us in severe directions. It reminds me that cult experts will tell you that any of us could fall into the clutches of a cult, and those of us who argue otherwise are likely among the most vulnerable. Anyone who insists they are too self-aware to be pulled into something that goes against their own interests is admitting that they don’t know themselves or humanity very well. That’s one of life’s great mysteries: Why do we do things that we know are wrong, or bad for us? Death and taxes might be certain, but so are mistakes and regret, no matter how much we’d like to believe that we’re big enough to let go.

Conflict is ever-present in Morrison, who chooses to climb Everest despite its perils. For him, the adventure is about more than pride or titles; it’s about honor and love. The journey is intended both to strengthen his bond with Nelson and honor the memory of his late wife and their two children, who died in a horrific commuter plane crash in 2011, a decade before he and Nelson decide to attempt Everest. Recalling the aftermath, Morrison tells how climbing brought him clarity. Unable to move from the edge of his driveway, consumed by grief, he eventually found the strength to simply walk up the slight incline and into his home — a microscopic example of the human spirit’s extraordinary tenacity he hopes to commemorate in the Everest climb.

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

But more tests lie ahead. The route to Everest proves demanding in heart and health. And while training together for the big summit push by climbing a lower peak in Nepal in 2022, Nelson loses her footing in an avalanche the size of a small snow drift. On a ski slope, the drift would be minor. But on a mountain, every movement is measured. Nelson is swept away and under the snow, toward a cliff. We see it happen in real time, captured on a helmet GoPro. The moment is almost unassuming in its speed, but it permanently shapes everything that follows. Nelson is lost amid a series of avalanches, and the clock starts ticking.

Counting the seconds seems futile. But climbing is futile, too. For Morrison, left to search for his partner amid the snow, hazardous ridges and cliffs, it all seems like a waste. More pain, more trauma, more memories that are left for only one person to hold onto. I was immediately reminded of what Krakauer’s wife told him by satellite phone before he began his push from Everest’s base camp. “Saying goodbye to you was one of the saddest things I’ve ever done,” he remembers her saying. “I guess I knew on some level that you might not be coming back, and it seemed like such a waste. It seemed so f**king stupid and pointless.”

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

It’s hard not to dwell on that sentiment, already knowing what and who Nelson would leave behind if disaster struck. On some level, and to some people, it is all stupid and pointless. But that split second fortifies Morrison, confirming that his quest to Everest is for everyone that he’s lost, and every heartstopping moment along the way. It’s a spiritual pursuit, the kind that we make when we travel to a family member or friend’s favorite place to scatter their ashes; the kind that we make when we give eulogies, or just sit in the grass, staring into space, thinking about everything and nothing, everyone and no one.

Some may be driven to climb Everest just to say that they did it, while others are looking for something else, something with no name. They want to pierce the heavens and reach through the atmosphere to grasp the indescribable truth that unites us all. And if they don’t make it back down to share that peace with the rest of us, it might be enough to experience it just once.

Chinese arrivals to Thailand fell to 49,494 in the week of October 18–24, down about 24% from the week before, The Nation reported, with Thai officials attributing the decline partly to post-Golden Week seasonality and partly to weaker confidence after a Chinese embassy safety advisory. The reversal lands after a period of rebuilding: Minor Hotels had told Skift Chinese room nights across its Thailand portfolio were 78% ahead of last year heading into Golden Week, and China had retaken the top source market spot with about 4.2 million arrivals through October 31. #6097. Right-wing media and the mystery of Texas’ transgender mailers

On Thursday night, the smear at the heart of the mysterious transgender mailers that have rocked the final weeks of the midterm elections in Texas completed its journey. What began as baseless social media whispers quickly ascended the ladder of conservative influence, jumped into mailboxes across the Lone Star State and ultimately into the comforting prime-time embrace of Fox News.

At a town hall in Fort Worth, a Texas mother of six named Rebekah Smith told Vice President JD Vance that her 11-year-old daughter had received a letter explaining how to transition without her parents ever knowing, and asked how Republicans would keep the government out of her family. “I don’t know who sent that letter to your child,” the vice president said, “but I think the person who sends a letter to an 11-year-old about gender transition, what I call that in my family is a pervert, and that person ought to go to prison.” Host Jesse Watters, never one to let a grievance go to waste, promised that Fox would investigate “this perverted letter.” Vance asked Smith to talk to his staff because he would “like the Department of Justice to investigate that” as well.

Watters rushed to promote the spectacle. “WHOA! Texas MOM tells JD Vance her DAUGHTER received a letter telling her TO TRANSITION TO A BOY,” he posted on X, followed by Vance’s promise. Missing from that framing was the question that should have governed the segment: Who actually sent the material?

Nobody on that stage mentioned that the pamphlet was a fake. Nobody mentioned that the real transgender advocacy group named inside it had disavowed the mailer. Nobody mentioned that sworn testimony filed that same week had tied the text messages that accompanied it to a national Republican organization. The vice president was asking federal prosecutors to chase a forgery that may well have originated in his own party’s orbit — and he was doing it on a network whose viewers had been marinating in that forgery for weeks.

The race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico has become a crucible for dark-money maneuvers. As polls show the Republican grip on the Lone Star State slipping, conservative campaigns and their surrogates have resorted to increasingly desperate tactics. In early October, for example, Talarico took a brief hiatus from the campaign trail to recover from a severe case of the flu. Rather than accepting a routine human illness, the right-wing echo chamber treated a temporary absence as evidence of mental illness. Within days, the fabricated scandal has collapsed — yet the machinery of right-wing media simply pivoted to amplifying a more insidious operation designed to trigger visceral outrage.

This second October surprise involved millions of unsolicited text messages and a wave of physical mailers sent to Texas households with materials that directed readers to the website of the Transgender Education Network of

It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward.

Texas while inserting provocative advice on child emancipation that the real organization says it never authored or authorized. By flooding the electorate with extreme material disguised as progressive advocacy, right-wing operatives appear to have sought to create a fake controversy that could be weaponized in attack ads and campaign speeches. Vance, for instance, told the Fox News audience that Talarico has “a weird fascination with trans kids,” and that “he’ll probably defend the right of the person sending the letter, not the right of the parent who is rightfully creeped out by this.” Vance claimed that Talarico “has actually called it abusive when parents try to prevent their children from transitioning” and that Paxton “has fought hard to prosecute those people, whereas James Talarico has fought hard to protect those people.” Even the distortion had been laundered by then — Talarico called denying a child’s gender identity abusive, a different claim from saying parents must permit medical transition, but at the top of the ladder the difference no longer exists.

That is how a smear works in the closed ecosystem of the American right. It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward. An anonymous account posts it; an influencer adopts it; a donor-funded outlet reports the influencer’s outrage as news; an elected official demands an investigation, and the demand becomes proof the story matters; cable news books the controversy; a vice president promises federal action. Each rung launders the one below it. The correction, when it comes, travels in the opposite direction and arrives nowhere.

The paper trail looks like what you would expect from a covert operation. Texas Transgender Student Union LLC was formed in Wyoming on Sept. 2 through a commercial registered agent that helps owners stay anonymous. After CBS News Texas visited the agent’s address in Sheridan, Wyoming, the agent announced it was resigning. The mailers listed a Houston-area post office box. The Texas Observer reported that the barcode on the envelopes traced to a mail-tracking company that has taken federal campaign money from only one group this year, the National Republican Congressional Committee. The committee said it had nothing to do with the mailers, and the company would not say who paid. CBS News Texas reported that the bulk-mail permit belongs to an Illinois printer owned by the Zerrusen family, who have given heavily to Republican PACs and been photographed with Donald Trump.

When the real Transgender Education Network of Texas filed a petition in Travis County court to unmask the perpetrators behind the impersonation campaign, the partisan safety nets of the Texas judiciary eventually snapped into action. A deposition of Infobip, the messaging company that delivered the texts, which a Travis County judge ordered made public, indicated that the texts were sent on behalf of the Republican Women’s Caucus Fund and a man named John Braun. But on Friday, the Texas Supreme Court, composed entirely of judges appointed by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, issued an administrative stay that blocked its release. Chris Hilton, an attorney who previously served under Paxton, defended him during his impeachment trial and was later pushed out of office amid sexual harassment allegations, argued on behalf of the company that the mailers were not political speech because they named no candidate or party.

Dirty tricks are an old tradition of American politics. This cycle, Republican PACs in Nevada mailed a flyer calling a nonpartisan candidate, Danielle Ford, the “AOC of Nevada,” hoping voters would mistake her for the actual Democratic nominee, Aaron Ford. This week also brought word that the group that funded Cornel West’s 2024 ballot drives raised every dollar through a dark-money network bankrolled by Elon Musk.

The president’s party whines about decoy candidates in Alaska while running them at home. Ratf**king is a long and proud Republican tradition, and the Texas operation fits inside perfectly.

#6081. Skift Commerce Summit 2026: Five Decisions in the Room

AI agents are here. Travel isn’t ready. Decisions made today will determine who controls the booking, the customer relationship, and the economics of travel commerce.

AI agents are already booking travel. One invite-only booking agent reported more than $1 billion a year in transaction volume, half of which was travel. Investors have already placed their bets on who wins and who loses. Most travel companies are still built for a traveler who searches, scrolls, and clicks.

Direct or third-party distribution used to be the primary choice travel suppliers had to make. Now an agent may decide which brands show up, which system can complete the booking, which card pays, and which loyalty program earns. Hotels alone spend more than $105 billion a year on distribution, and AI companies want a share of it.

The agents are here. Travel is not ready. Travel companies have to connect the dots inside the new travel commerce stack, and Skift Commerce Summit brings senior commerce leaders together around five decisions travel companies have to make now.

Operator Ticket $275 · for the people who run commerce at travel companies. Vendor Ticket $1,500 · capped, limited supply. Group rates: events@skift.com

AI has moved quickly into the travel customer journey for inspiration and planning, but not booking… yet. According to Skift Research, direct suppliers lead with a 49% net comfort score, followed by packaged tours at 37%, travel agents at 34%, loyalty portals at 31%, and OTAs at 20%. AI and chatbots score -7%. [1]

However, Skift Research describes the discovery path shifting from “search-scroll-compare” toward “ask-shortlist-decide.” As soon as travelers gain confidence in booking through AI platforms, space for brands “on the shelf” is poised to shrink. [2]

Hotels, airlines, or other travel retailers are racing to optimize for AI discoverability, but the more control they give to AI platforms, the more they risk losing direct customer relationships. They have to decide how to prioritize what they value most, and whether distribution alone is worth it if they become interchangeable within someone else’s interface.

Travelers are comfortable booking across a wide range of channels, but that also means today’s marketplace has a wider swath of competitors.

Travel’s AI discussion is moving downstream. It’s not only a customer relationship question, but also a technological one. Even if they’re discovered, booked, and integrated into the loyalty ecosystem, brands have to ensure the infrastructure works when an AI agent starts to handle trip management.

It’s one thing for an AI assistant to drive traffic to a brand’s site. The open decision is whether travel companies find it worthwhile to give an agent the tools to compare offers, change or cancel an order, and fix problems on the traveler’s behalf.

A better conversational front end can’t compensate for fragmented inventory, legacy servicing systems, or commerce technology designed for humans.

Banks, card issuers, retailers, membership programs, and technology platforms have built businesses around the traveler without having to own (or even sell) an airline seat or hotel room. They can make money from payments, rewards, subscriptions, advertising, financing, and the broader customer relationship surrounding a trip.

That changes the competitive economics for travel companies. A bank can use travel to increase card spend. A membership business can use it to make a subscription more valuable. A technology platform can influence the purchase while monetizing the customer elsewhere. These companies can compete for the same traveler without depending on the booking itself for most of their economics.

The decision is how much of that value suppliers and other travel-native companies can capture themselves as more of the commercial relationship moves into ecosystems built outside the industry.

Non-travel companies are profiting more and more off travel, stepping in to sell ancillaries and earn loyalty. 32% of travelers rank credit-card or bank loyalty programs as the most rewarding, ahead of hotel programs at 26% and airline programs at 20%. [1]

The direct-versus-third-party debate has shaped travel distribution strategy for decades. The economics have never been as simple as choosing one side. A direct booking can carry marketing, loyalty, technology, and acquisition costs of its own. An intermediary can bring incremental demand, reach a customer the brand would not have acquired directly, or fill inventory that otherwise would have gone unsold.

The channel mix is also getting more crowded. OTAs remain important, but banks, credit-card programs, membership platforms, social channels, AI interfaces, and other partners are creating new paths to the customer. Each comes with different costs, different access to customer data, and a different ability to generate demand.

The decision is which channels produce the strongest return for a particular customer, market, and trip. The best distribution strategy may use direct channels to deepen valuable customer relationships while paying intermediaries when they can deliver demand more efficiently than the brand can acquire it on its own.

“The competition to be a travel distributor has never been this intense,” says Skift Research, pointing to credit cards, social platforms, AI-native tools, OTAs, and suppliers all competing for a larger role in the booking journey. [3]

Travel companies can find unique growth opportunities by leveraging an existing customer base, brand, asset, or operating capability to create a new revenue stream. The challenge occurs when they find themselves wading into businesses they were not originally built to run.

The decision is how far that expansion should go. Some adjacencies strengthen the core business because they use capabilities the company already has. Others require new technology, operations, capital, or customer behavior that the company has never had to manage before. Growth can create leverage. It can also create complexity faster than revenue.

A Skift and ZS survey found that 75% of senior travel executives have non-core assets they can monetize, but only 32% described their current approach to doing so as “very” innovative. [4]

Discovery no longer guarantees ownership. Distribution extends beyond an OTA or supplier website and, indeed, beyond travel-native companies themselves. Payments and loyalty can generate value beyond the booking. AI is becoming another intermediary, another channel, and eventually the buyer itself.

Every travel company now faces the same question: which parts of the customer relationship, the transaction and the economics do you need to own before an agent stands between you and the traveler, and which can sit on someone else’s platform?

The Skift Commerce Summit is built to help you answer it, and to show you where your company is least ready.

#6075. Skift Aviation Forum 2026: Five Decisions in the Room

Jet fuel prices are still rising, and just about every variable affecting air travel is in flux — aircraft supply, air traffic volume, global partnerships, input costs. Decisions made today will determine who succeeds in aviation.

Passenger demand and airline revenues seem to be holding at a macro level. For now. Jet fuel prices continue to rise, aircraft remain scarce, and labor and airport costs keep rising. Meanwhile, global air traffic has been unpredictable throughout 2026, with wide regional differences.

Airlines at all levels of the market are shifting toward premium offerings to offset these headwinds and keep their revenues afloat. They’re redesigning cabins, loyalty programs, networks, ancillaries, and customer experiences. Skift Research describes the premium push as a normalizing trend: it’s now a baseline offering underpinning revenue expectations, rather than a stopgap strategy. [1]

The decisions industry leaders have to make today center on how to yield a competitive advantage within this industry-wide shift. The decisions underpinning every conversation at the 2026 Skift Aviation Forum will provide foundational evidence for these answers.

Fuel has become the industry’s biggest near-term margin test. Airlines entered the year with strong passenger revenue and high load factors, but the economics changed quickly as jet fuel prices climbed.

The impact is not uniform. Some airlines have more pricing power, stronger premium demand, better hedging positions, or networks that can absorb a shock more easily. Others compete in markets where travelers are more price-sensitive or where adding a fuel surcharge risks pushing demand to a rival.

The decision is how much of the fuel increase airlines can absorb before fares have to rise.

IATA expected the airline industry’s net profit to halve in 2026, a forecast made months before jet fuel prices peaked above $200 a barrel in October. [2] [3]

Airlines have spent the past several years reallocating space toward travelers who generate more revenue per seat. It’s not just major international carriers, either. Low-cost airlines have nearly doubled premium capacity since 2019.

Demand has kept up so far. More than 70% of travelers surveyed by Skift Research said they would consider paying for a premium cabin. [1]

The decision is how much further to push. Premium now affects cabin configuration, route planning, revenue management, airport strategy, and loyalty. Airlines need to know where demand still supports expansion and where the market is beginning to crowd.

U.S. domestic premium-seat capacity has grown 33% since 2020, roughly twice the 16% growth in economy seats. Premium revenues are significantly outpacing overall revenue growth and driving disproportionate value within airline revenue streams. [1]

The global traffic story has fractured by region. Middle East passenger traffic is expected to contract by 11.4% in 2026 amid airspace closures and reduced transfer demand, while Africa and Asia-Pacific will benefit from the shift. [4] Global load factors are reaching record levels because capacity remains constrained even as demand slows.

The decision is how to create the strongest return if capacity becomes more scarce. Slower global growth raises the cost of getting that call wrong.

Global air traffic growth is expected to slow to 2.1% in 2026 from 5.3% in 2025, while capacity increase is expected to be even lower at 1.6%. [4]

For many travelers, the ease of knowing they’ll get some miles and a few perks outweighs the headache of price comparison. AI changes this calculation, even for those who consider themselves somewhat loyal. Shopping tools can compare fares and products across airlines immediately. A traveler carrying points or status can still be presented with a better-priced or better-matched option somewhere else.

The decision for airlines is what loyalty has to deliver beyond points. Service, recognition, card economics, access, flexibility, and personalization can all strengthen the relationship. To avoid commoditization, airlines need to prove to travelers at every level of their programs that they can offer differentiated value.

The shift to premium is buoying revenue numbers, but AI platforms may not-so-quietly siphon off loyalty value from otherwise brand-agnostic travelers.

The industry has to make long-term commitments while near-term conditions remain volatile. Those investments have to make some assumptions about how the industry will operate years from now.

The decision is which bets deserve capital allocation. Growth alone is no longer enough justification. Airlines, airports, and manufacturers need a clear view of what each investment changes — capacity, economics, reliability, service, or competitive position.

Global airline passenger revenue is expected to approach $883 billion in 2027, but annual growth is projected to slow to about 3%. [5]

The airline industry’s next set of decisions centers on where to commit.

Airlines need to decide how much further to push premium, where capacity belongs, which rising costs customers can absorb, what keeps loyalty valuable, and which long-term investments deserve capital now.

Each decision comes back to the same constraint: airlines cannot pursue every opportunity at once. Skift Aviation Forum is focused on helping industry leaders identify where the economics still justify the strategy.

In a masterstroke of historical or perhaps biblical irony, Israelâs Arab minority â which is not a monolithic group in political or cultural terms, and until now has never been electorally significant â holds the balance of power, and perhaps the nationâs future, in its hands.

As Gideon Levy of the left-leaning Israeli newspaper Haaretz explains it,Â

The future of Israel now depends on its Arab citizens and on the attitude of its Jewish citizens toward its Arab ones. Eighty years after the Nakba and the establishment of the Jewish state, Israeli Palestinians may determine its fate. Is there greater historical justice than that?

The electionâs unexpected results are âa cause for rejoicing,â Levy writes, in that they have presented Israelis with a clear choice âbetween a government led by Benjamin Netanyahu and a government that includes the Arab parties.â If the âchange blocâ within the Zionist majority cannot accept a coalition with Arab Israelis, he continues, âthey will make it clear that they are actually the same as Netanyahu, that they prefer even the devil Netanyahu over repressing their racism. â¦ [E]veryone will know that racism is the supreme value in this country, across the board, above any other value.â
